The length of a fatty acid is determined by the length of the longest carbon chain, including the carbon of the carboxy group. Common natural fatty acids usually have an even number of carbons in the longest chain and can be either saturated or unsaturated. In many organisms they are often modified by branching, hydroxylation, methylation, epoxidation and other types of modifications. Inside living cells fatty acids are rarely found in free form. They are usually bound to coenzyme A or acyl-carrier proteins, or form part of |FRAME: Triacylglycerides triglycerides|, |FRAME: Phospholipids phospholipids|, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharides|, and |FRAME: Cholesterol-esters cholesterol esters|. To classify these enzymes, it is helpful to divide the substrates into smaller groups based on their chain length. Most of the natural fatty acids have an even number of carbon atoms, since their biosynthesis involves the addition of two-carbon-atom units. When a fatty acid contains only single bonds, it is referred to as |FRAME: Saturated-Fatty-Acids|. When it contains one or more double bonds, it is referred to as |FRAME: Unsaturated-Fatty-Acids|. Compound.name: an A vitamin
Comment: Vitamin A is a group of related compounds that include |FRAME: Retinols retinol|, |FRAME: Retinals retinal|, |FRAME: Retinoates retinoate|, and several provitamin A carotenoids, among which |FRAME: CPD1F-129| is the most important. Vitamin A has multiple functions: it is important for growth and development, for the maintenance of the immune system and for vision. Vitamin A is needed by the retina of the eye in the form of retinal, which combines with protein |FRAME: Opsins opsin| to form the light-absorbing molecule rhodopsin (see |FRAME: PWY-6861|). Vitamin A, in the form of retinoic acid, is also an important hormone-like growth factor for epithelial and other cells. In foods of animal origin, the major form of vitamin A are |FRAME: Retinyl-Esters esters|, primarily |FRAME: CHOCOLA_A|, which are converted to retinol in the small intestine.

Compound.name: a phytoestrogen
Comment: Estrogens are hormones that stimulate or control the development and maintenance of female sex characteristics in mammals by binding to estrogen receptors. They are important in both the menstrual and the estrous reproductive cycles. Estrogens are synthesized in all vertebrates as well as some insects, suggesting that estrogenic sex hormones have an ancient evolutionary history. The estrogens that occur naturally in the body are steroids, however other types of molecules acquired in the diet are known to bind to the estrogen receptors and are thus also considered estrogens. They include molecules produced by plants (phytoestrogens), molecules produced by fungi (mycoestrogens), and synthetic compounds (xenoestrogens). Phytoestrogens are a diverse group of naturally occurring nonsteroidal plant compounds that, because of its structural similarity with |FRAME: CPD-352|, have the ability to cause estrogenic and/or antiestrogenic effects. Most phytoestrogens are mainly substituted natural phenolic compounds such as |FRAME: coumestans coumestans|, |FRAME: PRENYLFLAVANONES prenylflavonoids|, and |FRAME: Isoflavones isoflavones|. The best-researched are |FRAME: Isoflavones isoflavones|, which are commonly found in soy and red clover.

Compound.name: a malbrancheamide
Comment: |FRAME: CPD-25411 Malbrancheamide| is a complex halogenated indole alkaloid produced by the terrestrial fungus |FRAME: TAX-78605| Martinez-Luis06 and by the fungus |FRAME: TAX-465706|, which was isolated from a marine invertebrate 21682275. The compound was identified during a search for calmodulin antagonists, and several later studies have confirmed its significant vasorelaxant effect |CITS: [20939762][25643751]|. The malbrancheamides belong to a diverse family of biologically active prenylated indole alkaloids isolated mainly from various |FRAME: TAX-5073| and |FRAME: TAX-5052| species of fungi that contains a unique bicyclo[2.2.2]diazaoctane core ring system, and are derived from |FRAME: TRP|, a cyclic amino acid (|FRAME: PRO|, |FRAME: L-PIPECOLATE| or a derivative of one of those compounds), and one or two isoprene units (see |FRAME: PWY-8345|). In addition to their structural diversity, members of this family have been attributed a variety of bioactivities, including (but not limited to) insecticidal, cytotoxic, anthelmintic, and antibacterial. They are also promising calmodulin inhibitiors 20939762 The bicyclo[2.2.2]diazaoctane-containing compounds can be divided into two sub-categories: the diketopiperazines (DKPs) and the monoketopiperazines (MKPs). DKPs include the |FRAME: Stephacidins stephacidins|, |FRAME: Brevianamides brevianamides|, and |FRAME: Notoamides notoamides|, while MKPs include the |FRAME: Paraherquamides paraherquamides|, |FRAME: Asperparalines asperparalines|, |FRAME: Marcfortines marcfortines|, |FRAME: Chrysogenamides chrysogenamides|,and |FRAME: Malbrancheamides malbrancheamides|.

Compound.name: a cobamide lower ligand ribotide
Comment: |FRAME: Cobamides "A cobamide"| is a corrinoid molecule based on the structure of |FRAME: CPD-20843|, a cobalt-corrinoid hexaamide that is formed from |FRAME: COBINAMIDE| by the attachment of an alpha-D-ribofuranose 3-phosphate residue at the 2 position of the aminopropanol chain. Cobamides serve as cofactors for a number of important enzymes. A key structural feature of cobinamides is a corrin ring with a cobalt ion in its center. Four of the six coordination sites of the cobalt ion are provided by the corrin ring, while the other two are provided by |FRAME: Cobamide-Upper-Ligands upper| (beta) and |FRAME: Cobamide-Lower-Ligands lower| (alpha) ligands, which are located above and below the ring plane, respectively. The best known cobamide, |FRAME: Cobalamins cobalamin|, contains |FRAME: DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE| as the lower ligand and either a methyl group or 5'-deoxyadenosyl group as the upper ligand. At least 16 different cobamides with structural variability in the lower ligand have been described. The 16 bases reported so far are |FRAME: BENZIMIDAZOLE|, |FRAME: CPD-18320|, |FRAME: CPD-18321|, |FRAME: CPD-18497|, |FRAME: CPD-18495|, |FRAME: DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE|, |FRAME: ADENINE|, |FRAME: CPD-18323|, |FRAME: GUANINE|, |FRAME: HYPOXANTHINE|, |FRAME: PHENOL|, |FRAME: CPD-108|, |FRAME: CPD-5723|, |FRAME: CPD-20865|, |FRAME: CPD-20864|, and |FRAME: CPD-20885| 24055007. Different cobamides may not be functionally equivalent as cofactors for cobamide-dependent enzymes |CITS: [14351147][13796808][13796809][21696461][22923412][23417488]|.

Compound.name: a phenylurea herbicide

In addition, ecotoxicological data show that phenylurea herbicides and their main metabolites are environmental hazards and are carcinogenic to animals and humans |CITS: [2279779][8402576]|.

Compound.name: an N 10 -formyltetrahydrofolate
Comment: |FRAME: THF-GLU-N Tetrahydrofolate| (vitamin B9) and its derivatives, commonly termed folates, are required in a variety of reactions in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, where they act as carriers of one-carbon units in various oxidation states. These one-carbon units are utilized in the biosynthesis of various cellular components, including glycine, methionine, formylmethionine, thymidylate, pantothenate and purine nucleotides. During folate biosynthesis (as described in FOLSYN-PWY) the enzyme |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.12|, adds a glutamate residue to |FRAME: 7-8-DIHYDROPTEROATE|, resulting in |FRAME: DIHYDROFOLATE|, also known as H 2 PteGlu 1 . This molecule in turn is reduced by EC-1.5.1.3 (FolA) to |FRAME: THF| (H 4 PteGlu 1 , or tetrahydrofolate), which can be converted to several other folate molecules 11501996. Most folate molecules are modified in cells by successive additions of glutamate residues, forming folate polyglutamates (or folylpoly-gamma-glutamates). The glutamate residues are added by an amide linkage to the gamma-carboxylate group of the folate or folate derivative. Since these isopeptide bonds are not the normal amide bonds they are not hydrolyzed by peptidases or proteases, which are specific for alpha-carboxyl-linked peptide bonds. The addition of glutamyl residues probably occurs after the reduction of newly synthesized dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate and its conversion to other tetrahydrofolate derivatives. The glutamylation of folate residues serves several goals: it prevents the efflux of folates out of the cell, it increases the binding of folate cofactors to the enzymes of folate interconversion and biosynthesis, and in mammals, it allows the accumulation of folates in the mitochondria, which is required for glycine synthesis 10598551. This class stands for 10-formyltetrahydrofolates with an unspecified number of glutamate residues.

Compound.name: globo H
Comment: The Globo-H antigen was first isolated from the breast cancer cell line MCF-7 in 1983 6863318. Globo H is overexpressed on a variety of epithelial cell tumors such as colon, ovarian, gastric, pancreatic, lung, prostate, and breast cancers. Patients with Globo H-positive tumors show a shorter survival in comparison to patients with Globo H-negative tumors 2554552. Since globo H is not expressed in normal tissue except for weak expression in the apical epithelial cells at lumen borders, a site that is inaccessible to the immune system |CITS: [6711680][9334808]|, it is considered an ideal target for immunotherapy of many epithelial cancers. Two phase I trials of a Globo H-based vaccine in breast and prostate cancer, respectively, have shown promising results |CITS: [10318949][11248068]|, and efforts to develop a globo H cancer vaccine are continues 25665650.

Compound.name: a melleolide
Comment: The |FRAME: Melleolides melleolides| are a large family of aryl ester secondary metabolites produced by species of the basidiomycete genus |FRAME: TAX-47424|, which are composed of an |FRAME: CPD-47| moiety esterified to a tricyclic sesquiterpene (|FRAME: CPD-14796|) alcohol |CITS: [Midland82][Donnelly82]|. Both |FRAME: CPD-47| and protoilludane derivatives have been described from numerous other organisms |CITS: [11281843][12714063][19666480]|, but these two elements are combined into a single entity only in the melleolides, which are not found outside the |FRAME: TAX-47424|. Biosynthesis of the sesquiterpene protoilludene moiety is achieved by cyclization of |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP|, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-4.2.3.135|, and results in the tricyclic |FRAME: CPD-14796| backbone 21148562. In |FRAME: TAX-47429|, |FRAME: CPD-47| is biosynthesized by a seven-domain polyketide synthase whose terminal thioesterase domain also catalyzes the coupling of |FRAME: CPD-47| to protoilludene-based alcohols 23993460. Modifications of the basic structure include hydroxylation at various positions of the sesquiterpene, oxidation of the primary alcohol at C-1 to an aldehyde or carboxy group, shift or reduction of the cyclohexene double bond, methyl ether formation at O-5', and chlorination at C-6' 26655762, resulting in excess of 60 melleolide analogs and making the melleolides one of the most diverse groups of fungal natural products Misiek12. Various melleolides have been shown to inhibit microbial growth |CITS: [Arnone86][10805573]| and display phytotoxicity 1418682. The antifungal activity has been linked to the position of the double bond within the sesquiterpene moiety 24906293. Melleolides have also been reported to have cytotoxic effects on human cancer cell lines by decreasing DNA synthesis 21376582.

Compound.name: an oleanonic-acid-type saponin ginsenoside
Comment: |FRAME: Ginsenosides Ginsenosides| or panaxosides are a class of steroid glycosides and triterpene saponins found exclusively in the plant genus |FRAME: TAX-4053| (ginseng). They are the principal components responsible for the pharmaceutical activities of ginseng. Ginsenosides are composed of an aglycone and sugar moieties. Based on the structure of their aglycones, ginsenosides have been categorized into three broad types; |FRAME: Protopanaxadiol-type-ginsenosides "protopanaxadiol-type ginsenosides"| (PPD), which contain hydroxyl groups at positions 3 and 20, |FRAME: Protopanaxatriol-type-ginsenosides "protopanaxatriol-type ginsenosides"| (PPT), which contain hydroxyl groups at positions 3, 6 and 20, and |FRAME: Oleanonic-acid-type-ginsenosides "oleanonic-acid-type saponins"|. Although ginsenosides only have three kinds of aglycones, more than 60 kinds of ginsenosides have been identified by now due to the variability in the type of sugar moieties, their number, and the carbon positions they link to. The biological activity of ginsenoside increases with the decrease of the number of the sugar moieties. All of the ginsenosides found in large quantities in wild ginseng (known as major ginsenosides) are heavily glycosylated, while the more active less-glycosylated ginsenosides are found in much smalller quantities (and are commonly referred to as the minor ginsenosides). Following oral intake of ginseng, the large low-solubility and poor-permeability major ginsenosides cannot be absorbed by the human body directly Su06, and are deglycosylated into smaller forms in the gastrointestinal tract by intestinal bacteria and/or digestive enzymes 8923812. The bicyclo[2.2.2]diazaoctane-containing compounds can be divided into two sub-categories: the diketopiperazines (DKPs) and the monoketopiperazines (MKPs). DKPs include the |FRAME: Stephacidins stephacidins|, |FRAME: Brevianamides brevianamides|, and |FRAME: Notoamides notoamides|, while MKPs include the |FRAME: Paraherquamides paraherquamides|, |FRAME: Asperparalines asperparalines|, |FRAME: Marcfortines marcfortines|, |FRAME: Chrysogenamides chrysogenamides|,and |FRAME: Malbrancheamides malbrancheamides|. Compound.name: an unsaturated fatty acid
Comment: |FRAME: Fatty-Acids "A fatty acid"| is a carboxylic acid with a long unbranched aliphatic tail. Even though fatty acids derived from natural fats and oils, such as CPD-195, are usually at least 8 carbon atoms long, carboxylic acids as short as BUTYRIC_ACID (4 carbon atoms) are considered to be fatty acids. When a fatty acid contains only single bonds, it is referred to as |FRAME: Saturated-Fatty-Acids|. When it contains one or more double bonds, it is referred to as |FRAME: Unsaturated-Fatty-Acids|. If it contains a double bond in the trans configuration, it is often referred to as a trans fatty acid. Most fatty acids in the trans configuration are not found in nature and are the result of human processing. About nomenclature : Several nomenclatures are used for unsaturated fatty acids, and are not complementary. Systematic names (or IUPAC names) begin counting the carbon atoms from the carboxylic acid end, and the double bonds are labelled with cis / trans or E/Z notation, e.g. 8 E ,10 E ,12 Z -octadecatrienoate. However, unsaturated fatty acids are often described using the omega nomenclature, which begins counting the carbon atoms from the terminal methyl carbon (designated as n or ω). In addition, unsaturated fatty acids are often referred to by trivial names, or by the "lipid number" as in 18:3, where 18 is the number of carbons, and 3 is the number of double bonds. This notation is ambiguous, as it does not specify the location of the double bonds.

Compound.name: compound III
Comment: |FRAME: Compound-0 "Compound 0"|, |FRAME: Compound-I|, and |FRAME: Compound-II| are the names given to intermediate states of the heme-iron center that is formed at the active sites of cytochrome P-450 enzymes and peroxidases during catalysis. I. Cytochrome P-450 In cytochrome P-450 the proximal coordinatioin position of the heme iron, which is bound to the 4 nitrogen atoms of the tetrapyrrole ring, is tethered to the protein via a cysteine thiolate ligand. At its rest state, the iron is found at a low-spin ferric state (III valency). At this state the iron also binds a water molecule as a sixth ligand at the distal axial coordination position. Binding of a substrate to the low-spin ferric enzyme leads to displacement of the water as the sixth ligand and a high spin shift. The substrate-bound complex has a greater reduction potential and more easily accepts a single electron from the redox partner, which can be either |FRAME: EC-1.6.2.4 "a cytochrome P450 reductase"|, |FRAME: Ferredoxins|, or |FRAME: Cytochromes-b5|). After the first reduction, the heme iron binds oxygen, forming an oxy-heme complex. The oxygen is bound at the distal axial coordination position, from which the water molecule has been displaced. Following the transfer of the second electron from the redox partner and two subsequent protonations, a peroxo adduct is formed, known as |FRAME: Compound-0|. Next, the O-O bond is cleaved heterolytically, releasing a water molecule and leaving behind an oxygen atom with only six valence electrons. This highly active oxene oxygen removes one electron from the iron and one from the porphyrin, oxidizing the iron to the unusual valency of IV (ferryl iron) and generating an additional oxidizing equivalent that is delocalized over the porphyrin and thiolate ligands. This ferryl/porphyrin radical cation complex is known as |FRAME: Compound-I| 21071661. When the substrate nears the active site, |FRAME: Compound-I| abstracts an electron from it, converting the substrate into a radical and becoming a protonated non-radical ferryl compound known as |FRAME: Compound-II|. At this point the substrate radical reacts with the oxygen of |FRAME: Compound-II|, forming a new carbon oxygen bond. The product is released, and the iron returns to a valency of III (compound III) OrtizdeMontellano15. II. preoxidases In peroxidases the proximal coordinatioin position of the heme iron, which is bound to the 4 nitrogen atoms of the tetrapyrrole ring, is tethered to the protein via a histidine residue. |FRAME: Compound-I "Compound I"| is produced when the heme iron is oxidized by |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE|. A single one-electron reduction step of |FRAME: Compound-I| from an electron donor substrate yields |FRAME: Compound-II|, followed by a second one-electron transfer that returns the enzyme to the ferric oxidation state, thus completing the catalytic cycle. Each electron transfer event converts a substrate molecule to a radical cation, forming two such radicals during a catalytic cycle. In the presence of high concentrations of |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE| and the absence of a reducing substrate, |FRAME: Compound-II| can be oxidized to |FRAME: Compound-III|, a catalytically inactive form of the enzyme. |FRAME: Compound-III "Compound III"| is converted back to the resting state by spontaneous autoxidation or by oxidation with two molecules of the substrate radical cation 18581264.

Comment: Green sulfur bacteria (|FRAME: TAX-191412|) and green flimentous bacteria (|FRAME: TAX-1106|) contain chlorosomes - large organelles that are believed to be the most efficient light-harvesting antennae in nature |CITS: [20130996][Saga10]|. Green sulfur bacteria can grow at light intensities that are too low to support growth of any other phototroph, up to a million times lower light than normal sunlight Overmann92. Chlorosomes contain about 1,500 bacteriochlorophyll molecules per reaction center. They are filled with 10 30 rod-shaped elements which are oriented parallel to the long axis of the chlorosomes and have a diameter of 10 nm. Each rod consists of a tubular bilayer formed by self-organization of the antenna bacteriochlorophyll molecules. Unlike all other known photosynthetic antenna, in which the chlorophyll molecules are bound to proteins, chlorosomes do not contain accessory proteins. The chlorosomal bacteriochlorophyll pigments are able to self-aggregate due to their unique chemical characteristics. The bacteriochlorophylls found in chlorosomes are either |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c "|, |FRAME: CPD-9093 "bacteriochlorophyll d "| or |FRAME: CPD-9094 "bacteriochlorophyll e "|, depending on the species. Compound.name: a c-series ganglioside
Comment: c-Series gangliosides are formed during mammalian brain development where they are thought to be involved in growth, differentiation, and migration of neuronal cells. They are abundant in fish brain, and in adult rats; they occur in liver, kidney, and pancreas 10699494 and in tumors such as glioma. About the nomenclature of gangliosides Ganglioside naming is somewhat complex. Two ganglioside nomenclature systems are currently in use. The most commonly used is a short-hand nomenclature suggested by Svennerholm, which was initially based on the migration order of |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs "ganglio-series"| gangliosides in chromatography 14066623. The more comprehensive system formulated by IUPAC 9826173 is applied much less frequently. A typical ganglioside name using the old system looks like |FRAME: Ganglioside-GQ1b "ganglioside GQ1b"|. The first letter refers to the glycosphingolipid series. For example, the "G" stands for the |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs "ganglio series"|. The next letter describes the number of sialic acid residues: (A = 0, M =1, D = 2, T = 3, Q = 4, P = 5, H = 6, S = 7). The following number describes the number of the non-sialic residues, and is derived in a rather complex manner. It was initially assumed that the number of such residues does not exceed 5. The number in the name was calculated as (5 - the number of uncharged carbohydrates). In addition, several sub-series of gangliosides have been defined based on the number of sialic acids attached to the galactose residue of the lacosylceramide core. If no sialic residues are present at that position, the compounds belong to the |FRAME: 0-Series-Ganglioside "0-series |. Those with one sialic acid at that position are named the |FRAME: A-Series-Gangliosides a-series |, those with two sialic acids belong to the |FRAME: B-Series-Gangliosides b-series |, and so on. |FRAME: C-Series-Gangliosides "C-series"| or higher gangliosides are rare in adult mammals and birds, but are abundant in fish and amphibians. Confusingly, GM1b and GD1c are both 0-series gangliosides, despite having a b and c in their names. So, for example, the |FRAME: Ganglioside-GQ1b "ganglioside GQ1b"| is named as follows: G = belongs to the ganglio series, Q = 4 sialic acids, 1 = 4 non-sialic residues, and b = belongs to the b-series, meaning two of the sialic acids are attached to the inner galactose.

Quinones are organic compounds derived from aromatic compounds, with two carbonyl groups incorporated into the ring structure with rearrangement of the double bonds where necessary. Quinones are conjugated but not aromatic. A classic example of a quinone is |FRAME: P-BENZOQUINONE|. Quinones are commonly named with a prefix that indicates the parent aromatic hydrocarbon (for example, "benzo-" for benzene, "naphtho-" for naphthalene, and "anthra-" for anthracene) with a "-quinone" suffix. Quinones can carry two electrons, and when fully reduced they are referred to as |FRAME: Reduced-Quinones quinols|. Many quinone derivatives often have other biological activities, such as |FRAME: CPD-11501 "vitamin K"|.

Comment: Penicillins are medically important |FRAME: Beta-Lactams "beta-lactam"| antibiotics biosynthesized as end products by certain filamentous fungi, including |FRAME: TAX-5076| and |FRAME: TAX-162425|. Β-Lactam antibiotics inhibit the formation of peptidoglycan cross-links in the bacterial cell wall by the irreversible binding of their four-membered beta-lactam ring to the so-called |FRAME: Penicillin-Binding-Proteins "penicillin binding proteins"| (PBPs). The PBPs are proteins that contain a D,D-peptidase domain, most commonly used for hydrolyzing the |FRAME: D-ALA-D-ALA| bond found in the pentapetide moiety of peptidoglycans. Since the beta-lactam moiety of |FRAME: PENICILLIN "penicillins"| is similar to the D-Ala-D-Ala structure, these enzymes bind penicillin irreversibly and become inactive. Several groups of enzymes belong to this family - carboxypeptidases, transpeptidases, and endopeptidases. The carboxypeptidase remove the terminal |FRAME: D-ALANINE| from the pentapeptide, the transpeptidase form crosslinks between the pentapeptides of adjacent glycan threads, and the endopeptidases hydrolyze these crosslinks. This irrevesible binding prevents the enzyme from catalyzing the formation of these cross-links, resulting in a defective cell wall and cell death. Penicillin antibiotics were the first drugs that were effective against many previously serious diseases, such as syphilis, and infections caused by staphylococci and streptococci. They are still widely used today, although more and more types of bacteria have acquired resistance.

Though the existence of polyketide quinones was known since 2008 18364359, their role was not understood at the time. A new understanding of polyketide quinones was achieved in 2015, when it was reported that these molecules can serve as alternate mobile electron carriers in the respiratory electron transport chain during respiration in oxygen-deficient niches. The authors, who studied the enzymes from |FRAME: TAX-1772|, found that the enzymes are specifically expressed in biofilms and other oxygen-deficient niches. They also reported that the system is conserved in all mycobacteria as well as in several other Actinobacterial and a few Proteobacterial species 26585386. A study of the freshwater bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1573406| has shown that the organism switches from using menaquinone to using polyketide quinone during its development cycle. It is not usually found in higher plants, although trace amounts have been identified in |FRAME: TAX-46147|. Humans require either |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| or EPA to produce |FRAME: CPD-10244|, a primary structural component of the human brain cerebral cortex, sperm, testicles and retina. They are laid out in the cell wall at a high density and can constitute up to 50% of the algae dry mass. The basic units of |FRAME: Carrageenans carrageenans| are repeats of alternating alpha-1,3-linked D-galactose and beta-1,4-linked D-galactose units, which are often substituted by sulfate. Carrageenans are classified according to the number and the position of sulfated ester 1367970. In |FRAME: Carrageenoses carrageenoses| the alpha-1,3-linked galactose units are modified by having a 3,6-anhydro bridge. These bridges, which form a double helix during aggregation, are responsible for the gelation that is typical to these compounds. Despite this distinction, carrageenoses are often referred to as carrageenans. The three most industrially exploited carrageenans, namely, |FRAME: kappa-Carrageenan|, |FRAME: iota-Carrageenan| and |FRAME: Lambda-Carrageenan|, are distinguished by the presence of one, two or three ester-sulfate groups per repeating disaccharide unit respectively.

However, |FRAME: Glucuronoarabinoxylans Glucuronoarabinoxylans| consist of |FRAME: Arabinoxylan| backbone that contains about ten times more alpha-L-arabinofuranose side chains than glucuronate ones, while |FRAME: Arabinoglucuronoxylans arabinoglucuronoxylans| are |FRAME: Glucuronoxylans| with a small proportion of the xylopyranose residues of the backbone disubstituted by two alpha-L-arabinofuranose residues. Another difference is that |FRAME: Glucuronoarabinoxylans glucuronoarabinoxylans| contain some xylopyranose units that are doubly substituted by both 4- O -methylglucuronate and alpha-L-arabinofuranose Ebringerova05. Some of the arabinofuranose side chains in AGX are further substitued by either a beta-D-xylopyranose attached by a (1->2) linkage. This sugar moiety has been found usually esterified by ferulate at position 5 of the arabinofuranose unit and occur as a widespread component of grass cell walls Ishii97. The AGX type polymers occur in appreciable quantity in coniferous species, although it is usually not the dominant hemicellulosic component (an exception is the hemicellulose of the tropic conifer |FRAME: TAX-1030197| Bochicchio03). They are also the dominant hemicelluloses in the cell walls of lignified supporting tissues of grasses and cereals.

Compound.name: melanin

Compound.name: hemicellulose
Comment: Please note that hemicellulose is a not a precise biological term. The plant cell wall is composed of |FRAME: CELLULOSE| and many additional complex polymers. Unlike cellulose, which is crystalline and resistant to hydrolysis, the other polymers are amorphous and are easily hydrolyzed by dilute acid or base. Hemicellulose is a heterogeneous term that is used for all the plant cell wall components that are soluble in dilute alkali solutions, or that go into solution quite readily in hot dilute mineral acids with the formation of simple sugars. The term is often used to describe all the polysaccharide components of the cell wall other than cellulose. Hemicelluloses constitute about one-fourth of perennial plants and about one-third of annual plants. Since the term does not refer to a particular chemical entity, hemicelluloses extracted from different plant sources are rarely identical. However, D-xylose is the dominant building unit of the hemicelluloses of most woods and annual plants. D-xylose occurs as the polymer |FRAME: Xylans|, as derivatives of xylan, such as |FRAME: Glucuronoxylans glucuronoxylan| and |FRAME: Arabinoxylan arabinoxylan|, and as side chains on other types of backbones, such as |FRAME: Xyloglucan xyloglucan| and |FRAME: Xylogalacturonan xylogalacturonan|. D-Mannose is also very abundant, and occurs as the polymer |FRAME: 1-4-Mannan mannan| or in combination with D-glucose or D-galactose as |FRAME: Glucomannans glucomannans|, |FRAME: Galactomannans galactomannan|, or |FRAME: Galactoglucomannans galactoglucomannan|. Arabinose is common as well, either in the form of |FRAME: Arabinans "L-arabinan"| or in the form of side chains on other polysaccharides. Other sugars common in hemicellulose include |FRAME: Galactose galactose|, |FRAME: Rhamnose rhamnose|, |FRAME: Galacturonate galacturonate| and |FRAME: Mannuronate mannuronate|. Hemicellulose consists of shorter chains than cellulose, typically 500 - 3,000 sugar units, and is usually branched.

Compound.name: a bacteriochlorophyll c
Comment: Green sulfur bacteria (|FRAME: TAX-191412|) and green flimentous bacteria (|FRAME: TAX-1106|) contain chlorosomes - large organelles that are believed to be the most efficient light-harvesting antennae in nature |CITS: [20130996][Saga10]|. Green sulfur bacteria can grow at light intensities that are too low to support growth of any other phototroph, up to a million times lower light than normal sunlight Overmann92. Chlorosomes contain about 1,500 bacteriochlorophyll molecules per reaction center. They are filled with 10-30 rod-shaped elements which are oriented parallel to the long axis of the chlorosomes and have a diameter of 10 nm. Each rod consists of a tubular bilayer formed by self-organization of the antenna bacteriochlorophyll molecules. Unlike all other known photosynthetic antenna, in which the chlorophyll molecules are bound to proteins, chlorosomes do not contain accessory proteins. The chlorosomal bacteriochlorophyll pigments are able to self-aggregate due to their unique chemical characteristics. The bacteriochlorophylls found in chlorosomes are either |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c "|, |FRAME: CPD-9093 "bacteriochlorophyll d "| or |FRAME: CPD-9094 "bacteriochlorophyll e "|, depending on the species. They all possess a hydroxyl group at the C3 1 position that allows them to chelate the Mg atom of a neighboring molecule and to interact with the C13-oxo carbonyl group of another neighboring pigment molecule, affording the self-aggregation |CITS: [16121276][19435848][22210764]|. In addition, all of these bacteriochlorophylls lack C-13 2 -methylcarboxyl side chains, which are found in all other (bacterio)chlorophylls but would interfere with the ability to form aggregates 16245042. Despite of their names, |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c "|, |FRAME: CPD-9093 "bacteriochlorophyll d "| and |FRAME: CPD-9094 "bacteriochlorophyll e "| are actually chlorins rather than bacteriochlorins. All three are usually found with an unsaturated farnesyl tail rather than phytyl tails |CITS: [2350541][Borrego99]|, although exceptions have been reported. In chlorosomes of |FRAME: TAX-191412| (but not |FRAME: TAX-1106| |CITS: [Risch79][3442679]|) all three types of bacteriochlorophyll appear in several forms with different degrees of methylation at the C-8 2 and C-12 1 carbons |CITS: [12656478][14610639]|. The variety in methylation is depicted in the structure shown here by the R groups. In general, pimgents produced by cultures grown at lower light intensities are more highly methylated at the C-8 2 position than pigments produced by cells of the same organism grown at higher light intensities. Different methylation states result in different aggregation properties and light absorbance of the chlorosome, and thus methylation is used as an adaptation to altering envireonmental conditions. Most of the green sulfur bacteria growing in stratified lakes contain CPD-9093, and species containing |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c "| are rarely found vanGemerden95. Some examples for bacteria that possess |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c "| are the green sulfur bacteria |FRAME: TAX-1092| and |FRAME: TAX-1097| and the green filamentous bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1108|.

Compound.name: a dolichal
Comment: |FRAME: DOLICHOL "Dolichol"| is the name given to a family of long-chain polyprenols that contain a varying number of cis -linked isoprene units, terminating with three isoprene units, two of which are trans -linked. The first (alpha) unit in dolichols is always saturated 11442630. Additional modifications are found. For example, dolichols from certain halobacteria contain an additional saturation in the terminal (omega) isoprene unit |CITS: [9363431][21091511]|. The length of dolichol molecules varies within a range in a species, and the range varies among species (reviewed in 9878760). In mammals dolichols are usually within the range of 80 to 105 carbons. Archaea prefer dolichols of 55-60 carbons. The main function of dolychols is to act as a membrane anchor for the formation of oligosaccharides, which are then transferred to certain asparagine residues within proteins through a modification process known as |FRAME: MANNOSYL-CHITO-DOLICHOL-BIOSYNTHESIS "N-glycosylation"|. In eukaryotes dolichol is also involved in the transfer of some of the monosaccharides to the forming oligosaccharide. Dolichols are the major lipid component (14% by mass) of human substantia nigra |FRAME: CPD-12419| 15686500.

Compound.name: a lipopolysaccharide
Comment: This compound class stands for generic and unspecified lipopolysaccharides. The structure shown here is intended to provide a general overview and does not describe a lipopolysaccharide from a specific species. Lipopolysaccharides (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of almost all Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. Lipopolysaccharides that comprise all three regions are called |FRAME: Smooth-Form-LPS "smooth (S)-form LPS"|, while LPS lacking the O -antigen are named |FRAME: LOS "rough (R)-form LPS"| or lipooligosaccharide (LOS). Lipid A, which is common to most Gram negative bacteria, is the most toxic part. The core polysaccharide is genus specific, and contains unusual 7-carbon and 8-carbon sugars, and the O -antigen's side chains are variable in structure and toxicity. The O -antigen usually consists of about 20-40 repeated subunits.

In individuals that do express the Fs antigen, the |FRAME: HS07505| gene contains a mutation that results in an arginine to glutamine change at residue 296. Transfection experiments and molecular modeling showed that the Agr296Gln mutation reactivates the human Fs synthase. Based on these findings, the authors suggested to name a new histo-blood group system in man, FORS 23255552.

Compound.name: a ginsenoside
Comment: |FRAME: Ginsenosides Ginsenosides| or panaxosides are a class of steroid glycosides and triterpene saponins found exclusively in the plant genus |FRAME: TAX-4053| (ginseng). They are the principal components responsible for the pharmaceutical activities of ginseng. Ginsenosides are composed of an aglycone and sugar moieties. Based on the structure of their aglycones, ginsenosides have been categorized into three broad types; |FRAME: Protopanaxadiol-type-ginsenosides "protopanaxadiol-type ginsenosides"| (PPD), which contain hydroxyl groups at positions 3 and 20, |FRAME: Protopanaxatriol-type-ginsenosides "protopanaxatriol-type ginsenosides"| (PPT), which contain hydroxyl groups at positions 3, 6 and 20, and |FRAME: Oleanonic-acid-type-ginsenosides "oleanonic-acid-type saponins"|. Although ginsenosides only have three kinds of aglycones, more than 60 kinds of ginsenosides have been identified by now due to the variability in the type of sugar moieties, their number, and the carbon positions they link to. The biological activity of ginsenoside increases with the decrease of the number of the sugar moieties. All of the ginsenosides found in large quantities in wild ginseng (known as major ginsenosides) are heavily glycosylated, while the more active less-glycosylated ginsenosides are found in much smalller quantities (and are commonly referred to as the minor ginsenosides). Following oral intake of ginseng, the large low-solubility and poor-permeability major ginsenosides cannot be absorbed by the human body directly Su06, and are deglycosylated into smaller forms in the gastrointestinal tract by intestinal bacteria and/or digestive enzymes 8923812. Glycosidase enzymes that can convert the major ginsenosides to minor ginsenosides are not common and are of commercial interest.

Compound.name: a chlorophyll
Comment: Chlorophyll is a green pigment found in most plants, algae, and cyanobacteria. The name is derived from Greek (chloros "green" and phyllon "leaf". Chlorophyll absorbs light strongly in the blue and red spectra and has a strong green color. Chlorophylls play a crucial role in photosynthesis, both in the antennae and in the reaction centers. By far most of the chlorophylls are found in the antennae, where they absorb light and transfer that light energy by resonance energy transfer to the reaction center. Some of the cholorophylls (known as P700 and P680) are part of the photosystems reaction centers, where they perform the charge separation reaction, sending electrons to a transfer chain that ultimately results in the reduction of |FRAME: NADP| to |FRAME: NADPH|.

Compound.name: a carrageenose
Comment: |FRAME: Carrageenans Carrageenans| and |FRAME: Carrageenoses carrageenoses| are sulfated polysaccharides that are extracted from sea weeds belonging to the |FRAME: TAX-2763| (red algae), mainly from |FRAME: TAX-2769|, and species from the |FRAME: TAX-31444| and |FRAME: TAX-33664| genera. They are laid out in the cell wall at a high density and can constitute up to 50% of the algae dry mass. The basic units of |FRAME: Carrageenans carrageenans| are repeats of alternating alpha-1,3-linked D-galactose and beta-1,4-linked D-galactose units, which are often substituted by sulfate. Carrageenans are classified according to the number and the position of sulfated ester 1367970. In |FRAME: Carrageenoses carrageenoses| the alpha-1,3-linked galactose units are modified by having a 3,6-anhydro bridge. These bridges, which form a double helix during aggregation, are responsible for the gelation that is typical to these compounds. Despite this distinction, carrageenoses are often referred to as carrageenans. The three most industrially exploited carrageenans, namely, |FRAME: kappa-Carrageenan|, |FRAME: iota-Carrageenan| and |FRAME: Lambda-Carrageenan|, are distinguished by the presence of one, two or three ester-sulfate groups per repeating disaccharide unit respectively.

Compound.name: a pyruvoyl cofactor
Comment: Several enzymes depend on a covalently bound |FRAME: CPD0-2654 "pyruvoyl cofactor"| for activity |CITS: [5681461][1989676]|. These enzymes catalyze either the reduction or the decarboxylation of amino acids and amino acid derivatives. Pyruvoyl-dependent reductases, such as |FRAME: EC-1.21.4.1|, |FRAME: EC-1.21.4.2|, |FRAME: EC-1.21.4.3|, and |FRAME: EC-1.21.4.4|, have been described mostly from Gram-positive anaerobes performing Stickland reactions, although they can be found in Gram-negative bacteria, such as the |FRAME: CPLX-9661| of |FRAME: TAX-876|. Decarboxylases, such as |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.11|, |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.22|, |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.65|, and |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.50|, have been described in a wide range of bacteria as well as in mammals. The pyruvoyl group is thought to act analogously to a |FRAME: PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE| cofactor by first forming a Schiff base between its carbonyl residue and the amino group of the substrate and then serving as an electron sink to facilitate the reaction 338609. In many cases, the eukaryotic homologs of these enzymes utilize |FRAME: PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE| instead of the pyruvoyl group. The pyruvoyl group is essential for catalytic activity and can be inactivated by carbonyl reagents. Pyruvoyl-containing enzymes are expressed as proenzymes (also known as zymogens or π proteins), which undergo a post-translational self-maturation/cleavage that generates two chains, beta and alpha (by convention beta is the N-terminal chain and alpha is the C-terminal chain). An |FRAME: CYS| residue was shown to be the precursor of the pyruvoyl group in the reductases, while an |FRAME: SER| residue is the precursor in the decarboxylases 11422384. While the exact process of pyruvoyl group formation in reductases (from an |FRAME: CYS| residue) is still not understood, the process is much better understood in the case of the decarboxylases. The self-cleavage reaction occurs through nonhydrolytic serinolysis, in which the side chain hydroxyl group of the serine residue attacks the C-N bond between the serine and the amino acid preceeding it, forming an oxyoxazolidine intermediate. Breakage of the C-N bond results in formation of an ester intermediate |CITS: [9546220][11583148]|, which is resolved by beta-elimination, generating the two chains. The beta chain ends with a carboxylate, in which pne of the oxygens originates in the side chain hydroxyl group of the serine residue. The remainder of that residue is attached to the N-terminus of the alpha chain as a 2-aminoprop-2-enoyl group. The last reaction converts that group to purovoyl group, releasing ammonia 3944098. The serinolysis process is described in the pathway |FRAME: PWY-8057|.

Compound.name: a chaxalactin
Comment: The |FRAME: Chaxalactins chaxalactins| are a group of macrolactone polyketides produced by |FRAME: TAX-1437453|, an organism that was isolated from a soil sample collected from the Chaxa Lagoon, located in the Salar de Atacama in northern Chile. The Chaxa Lagoon is a hyper-arid and hypersaline lake and possesses an extremely high content of sodium, sulfate, magnesium, bicarbonate, chlorine, nitrate and arsenic ions. |FRAME: TAX-1437453| produces a variety of specialized metabolites, some of which were shown to possess antibiotic, anti-cancer and anti-inflammatory activities. Among those are two families of polyketide antibiotics, the chaxalactins 21879726 and the ansamycin-like |FRAME: Chaxamycins chaxamycins| 21553813 (see |FRAME: PWY-8036|) 26122045. The chaxalactins belong to the family of 22-membered macrolactone polyketides, which is rather rare in nature (most macrocyclic lactones have a 34-member ring). They were shown to have strong activity against the Gram-positive bacteria |FRAME: TAX-1280| , |FRAME: TAX-1639|, and |FRAME: TAX-1423|, and only weak activity against the Gram-negative bacteria |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-670| 21879726.

Compound.name: a Rieske [2Fe-2S] iron-sulfur cluster
Synonyms: a Rieske Fe 2 S 2 iron-sulfur cluster // a Rieske type [2Fe-2S] iron-sulfur cluster // a Rieske type [2Fe-2S]
Comment: Iron-sulfur centers consist of nonheme iron complexed to sulfur in several ways. Iron-sulfur clusters are prosthetic groups of many proteins, which function as intracellular electron carriers with a low reduction potential. In addition to their roles in electron transfer reactions, iron-sulfur clusters are also known to participate in the activation of substrates, the stabilization of radicals and structures, the protection of proteins from enzymes and the storage of iron and sulfur. In addition, they act as sensors of iron, dioxygen, the superoxide ion, and possibly nitric oxide, and participate in gene expression 16466637. Rieske iron-sulfur clusters contain two iron atoms and two sulfur atoms, similar to an |FRAME: CPD-6|. However, while in |FRAME: CPD-6| the irons are coordinated to the sulfurs of 4 cysteine side chains, in Rieske clusters a pair of cysteinyl residues on one of the iron centers are replaced by 2 imidazole ligands from the side chain of two histidine residues.

Le y is expressed predominately during embryogenesis, and expression on adult tissue is restricted to granulocytes and epithelial surfaces 11037972, where it acts as a ligand for lectin-like proteins |CITS: [18711002][22101897]|. However, Le y is overexpressed in the majority of carcinomas, including breast, ovary, pancreas, prostate, colon, and non-small cell lung cancers, and has been correlated to the pathological staging and prognosis |CITS: [2537068][7714977][8621218][9824007][21512109]|. In these cases, Le y occurs either at the plasma membrane as a glycolipid or linked to surface receptors |CITS: [2436750][14871842]|. Le y was shown to play an important role in promoting cell proliferation, tumorigenecity and adhesion |CITS: [21152298][18205178]|, and several clinical trials were conducted using Le y monoclonal antibodies for targeted immunotherapy of tumors |CITS: [1327079][8577771][8640770][10829049][10861456][16963623][17545534][17909358][19825951][26026738]|. The human pathogenic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-210| is known to express the Le y antigen in its lipopolysaccharide, mimicking human cell surface glycoconjugates |CITS: [8890213][10096092][11237846][11741906]|.

Compound.name: an actinomycin

The first actinomycin was isolated from |FRAME: TAX-1890| in 1940, and was the first antibiotic obtained in pure form from an actinomycete Waksman40. |FRAME: ACTINOMYCIN-D "Actinomycin D"| was the first antibiotic shown to have anti-cancer activity |CITS: [13112124][4130354]|, and was approved as an anticancer drug in 1964, making it one of the oldest anticancer drugs. Actinomycin D inhibits transcription by binding DNA at the transcription initiation complex and preventing elongation of RNA chain by RNA polymerase 2410919. A common feature of all actinomycins is the chromophoric moiety |FRAME: CPD-18447|, which is a unique phenoxazinone dicarboxylic acid to which two pentapeptide lactone rings are attached with amide linkages |CITS: [15395378][13505348][13790233]|.

Synonyms: an alpha-L-fucosyl-(1->2)-beta-D-galactosyl-R // a glycoprotein-alpha-L-fucosyl-(1,2)-beta-D-galactose // a 2-O-(6-deoxy-alpha-L-galactopyranosyl)-beta-D-galactopyranosyl // an alpha-L-fucosyl-1,2-beta-D-galactoside // an alpha-L-fucosyl-1,2-beta-D-galactosyl-R
Comment: The |FRAME: H-antigen "H antigens"| are fucosylated oligosaccharides that decorate proteins on the surface of red blood cells in people with O blood type. In people with A or B blood types an additional monosaccharide is attached to one of the beta-D-galactosyl residues of the H antigen (|FRAME: CPD-12557| in |FRAME: A-antigen "A antigens"| and |FRAME: GALACTOSE| in |FRAME: B-antigen "B antigens"|). These fucosylated structures are found not only on blood cells but also on many other cell types (mainly epithehal), and it has been suggested that they should be called histo-blood group antigens. The majority of the A, B and H antigens are linked to the ends of long polylactosamine chains attached mainly to band 3 protein (encoded by SLC4A1), the anion exchange protein of the red blood cells. A minor fraction of the antigens is attached to a ceramide moiety, forming neutral glycosphingolipids. Several H antigens exist, differing in their core disaccharide 2093726. The different types are: |FRAME: Type-1-H-Antigen "Type 1"|: alphaFuc-(1,2)-betaGal-(1->3)-betaGlcNac-(1->R) |FRAME: Type-2-H-Antigen "Type 2"|: alphaFuc-(1,2)-betaGal-(1->4)-betaGlcNac-(1->R) |FRAME: Type-3-H-Antigen "Type 3"|: alphaFuc-(1,2)-betaGal-(1->3)-alphaGalNac-(1->R) |FRAME: Type-4-H-Antigen "Type 4"|: alphaFuc-(1,2)-betaGal-(1->3)-betaGalNac-(1->R) |FRAME: Type-5-H-Antigen "Type 5"|: alphaFuc-(1,2)-betaGal-(1->3)-betaGal-(1->R) |FRAME: Type-6-H-Antigen "Type 6"|: alphaFuc-(1,2)-betaGal-(1->4)-betaGlc-(1->R) Most of the H antigens found in the cell are either type 1 or type 2, followed by type 3 and 4. It is not clear if type 5 H antigens exist, although the type 5 precursor has been characterized 2093726.

Compound.name: a glucomannan
Comment: |FRAME: Glucomannans Glucomannans| (GM), along with |FRAME: Galactoglucomannans galactoglucomannans| (GGM), are the major hemicellulosic components of the secondary cell walls of softwoods, but occur only in minor amounts in the secondary cell walls of hardwoods. |FRAME: Glucomannans Glucomannans| consist of a backbone composed of beta(1->4)-linked glucopyranose and mannopyranose residues, and are often branched. Unlike GMs, GGM chains are substituted by galactopyranose residues. Glucomannans show some variations in structural features depending on the plant species and stage of plant development Ebringerova05. Low-molecular-weight GMs, acetylated at position 2 or 3 of some mannopyranose residues, were isolated from aspen and birch wood 12668108. Soluble, often partially acetylated GMs occur as constituents of bulbs, tubers, seeds, roots, and leaves of some non-gramineousmonocotyl plants. An example are the GMs from plants of the genus |FRAME: TAX-25641|, which are known for their medicinal value. A GM from the potato-like plant |FRAME: TAX-78372| is known as konjac mannan in Japanese food applications. Studies of konjac mannan showed that is is branched (8%), with branches joined through the C-6 position of only the glucose residues. Both glucopyranose and mannopyranose residues (in the ratio of 1 : 2) were suggested to terminate the branches Katsuraya03.

Compound.name: a [4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur cluster
Synonyms: Iron-sulfur (4Fe-4S) // a 4Fe-4S iron-sulfur cluster // a 4Fe-4S center // a 4Fe-4S cluster // a 4Fe-4S iron-sulfur center // a Fe 4 S 4 iron-sulfur center // a [4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur center // [4Fe-4S] // 4Fe-4S // [4Fe-4S] cluster // Fe 4 S 4 cluster
Comment: Iron-sulfur centers consist of nonheme iron complexed to sulfur in several ways. They serve as cofactors of many proteins, which function as intracellular electron carriers with a low reduction potential. In addition to their roles in electron t ransfer reactions, iron-sulfur clusters are also known to participate in the activation of substrates, the stabilization of radicals and structures, the protection of proteins from enzymes and the storage of iron and sulfur. They can also act as sensors of iron, dioxygen, the superoxide ion, and possibly nitric oxide, and participate in gene expression 16466637. In some cases iron-sulfur clusters serve as sources of sulfur in enzymatic reactions 29051382 (see below). [4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur clusters feature four iron ions and four sulfide ions placed at the vertices of a cubane-type structure. The Fe centers are typically further coordinated by cysteinyl ligands. Two main types of [4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur clusters are low-potential (bacterial-type) clusters and high-potential (HiPIP) clusters. The bacterial clusters shift between the oxidation states +1 and +2, while the HiPIP clusters shift between the oxidation states +2 and +3. In some enzymes the [4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur clusters bind substrates. For example, in radical SAM enzymes the cluster binds and reduces S-adenosylmethionine, generating a radical that interacts with the enzyme's substrate. In a few cases, as in |FRAME: EC-2.8.1.8|, the cluster serves as the source of sulfur atoms for a sulfuration reaction. In such cases the cluster needs to be reassembled before the enzyme can catalyze the next round.

Compound.name: a short chain fatty acid
Synonyms: SCFA // a volatile fatty acid // VFA
Comment: The term "fatty acid" was originally coined to describe aliphatic monocarboxylic acids derived from or contained in esterified form in an animal or vegetable fat, oil or wax. However, over the years the term has been expanded to refer to additional, shorter monocarboxylic acids with an aliphatic tail such as |FRAME: PROPIONATE| and |FRAME: BUTYRIC_ACID| (but not the shorter |FRAME: FORMATE| and |FRAME: ACET|). The length of a fatty acid is determined by the length of the longest carbon chain, including the carbon of the carboxy group. Common natural fatty acids usually have an even number of carbons in the longest chain and can be either saturated or unsaturated. In many organisms they are often modified by branching, hydroxylation, methylation, epoxidation and other types of modifications. Inside living cells fatty acids are rarely found in free form. They are usually bound to coenzyme A or acyl-carrier proteins, or form part of |FRAME: Triacylglycerides triglycerides|, |FRAME: Phospholipids phospholipids|, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharides|, and |FRAME: Cholesterol-esters cholesterol esters|. Many enzymes that act on fatty acids, as well as the corresponding |FRAME: Fatty-Acyl-CoAs "fatty acyl-CoAs"|, alcohols, and aldehydes, have evolved to recognize substrates with a limited range of chain lengths. To classify these enzymes, it is helpful to divide the substrates into smaller groups based on their chain length. The following subgroups have been defined: |FRAME: Short-chain-fatty-acids "Short-chain fatty acids"| (SCFA) have 3-5 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Medium-chain-fatty-acids "Medium-chain fatty acids"| (MCFA) have 6-12 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Long-Chain-Fatty-Acids "Long-chain fatty acids"| (LCFA) have 13-22 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Very-long-chain-fatty-acids "Very-long-chain fatty acids"| (VLCFA) have 23-27 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Ultra-long-chain-fatty-acids "Ultra-long-chain fatty acids"| (ULCFA) have more than 27 carbons in the longest chain. Most of the natural fatty acids have an even number of carbon atoms, since their biosynthesis involves the addition of two-carbon-atom units. When a fatty acid contains only single bonds, it is referred to as |FRAME: Saturated-Fatty-Acids|. When it contains one or more double bonds, it is referred to as |FRAME: Unsaturated-Fatty-Acids|. If it contains a double bond in the trans configuration, it is often referred to as a trans fatty acid. Most fatty acids in the trans configuration are not found in nature and are the result of human processing.

Compound.name: a 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate
Synonyms: (-)CH 2 H 4 folate // (-)5,10-methylene-5,6,7,8-tetrahydrofolate // methylene-H4PteGlu(n) // methylene-THF(glu) n // methylene-H 4 PteGlu n // methylene-tetrahydropteroylpolyglutamates
Comment: |FRAME: THF-GLU-N Tetrahydrofolate| (vitamin B9) and its derivatives, commonly termed folates, are required in a variety of reactions in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, where they act as carriers of one-carbon units in various oxidation states. These one-carbon units are utilized in the biosynthesis of various cellular components, including glycine, methionine, formylmethionine, thymidylate, pantothenate and purine nucleotides. During folate biosynthesis (as described in FOLSYN-PWY) the enzyme |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.12|, adds a glutamate residue to |FRAME: 7-8-DIHYDROPTEROATE|, resulting in |FRAME: DIHYDROFOLATE|, also known as H 2 PteGlu 1 . This molecule in turn is reduced by EC-1.5.1.3 (FolA) to |FRAME: THF| (H 4 PteGlu 1 , or tetrahydrofolate), which can be converted to several other folate molecules 11501996. Most folate molecules are modified in cells by successive additions of glutamate residues, forming folate polyglutamates (or folylpoly-gamma-glutamates). The glutamate residues are added by an amide linkage to the gamma-carboxylate group of the folate or folate derivative. Since these isopeptide bonds are not the normal amide bonds they are not hydrolyzed by peptidases or proteases, which are specific for alpha-carboxyl-linked peptide bonds. The addition of glutamyl residues probably occurs after the reduction of newly synthesized dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate and its conversion to other tetrahydrofolate derivatives. The glutamylation of folate residues serves several goals: it prevents the efflux of folates out of the cell, it increases the binding of folate cofactors to the enzymes of folate interconversion and biosynthesis, and in mammals, it allows the accumulation of folates in the mitochondria, which is required for glycine synthesis 10598551. This class stands for 5,10-methylene-tetrahydrofolates with an unspecified number of glutamate residues.

Compound.name: λ-carrageenan
Comment: |FRAME: Carrageenans Carrageenans| and |FRAME: Carrageenoses carrageenoses| are sulfated polysaccharides that are extracted from sea weeds belonging to the |FRAME: TAX-2763| (red algae), mainly from |FRAME: TAX-2769|, and species from the |FRAME: TAX-31444| and |FRAME: TAX-33664| genera. They are laid out in the cell wall at a high density and can constitute up to 50% of the algae dry mass. The basic units of |FRAME: Carrageenans carrageenans| are repeats of alternating alpha-1,3-linked D-galactose and beta-1,4-linked D-galactose units, which are often substituted by sulfate. The three most industrially exploited carrageenans, namely, |FRAME: kappa-Carrageenan|, |FRAME: iota-Carrageenan| and |FRAME: Lambda-Carrageenan|, are distinguished by the presence of one, two or three ester-sulfate groups per repeating disaccharide unit respectively. |FRAME: Lambda-Carrageenan| is sulfated at position 2 of the beta-1,4 linked D-galactose units and positions 2 and 6 of the alpha-1,3-linked galactose units. Some carrabiose units of the λ-carrageenan from |FRAME: TAX-2765380| are substituted with four sulfate groups (D2S,6S-G2S,4S) 16716278. Since λ-carrageenans do not feature 3,6-anhydro-bridges, they do not make physical gels.

Comment: This class contains glycosides composed of a di-rhamnose moiety joined in an O -glycosidic linkage to a lipid moiety. Methanofuran is also used by methylotrophic bacteria as a coenzyme to oxidize formaldehyde to formate |CITS: [9651254][11532013]|. Compound.name: a 0-series ganglioside
Comment: About the nomenclature of gangliosides Ganglioside naming is somewhat complex. Two ganglioside nomenclature systems are currently in use. The most commonly used is a short-hand nomenclature suggested by Svennerholm, which was initially based on the migration order of |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs "ganglio-series"| gangliosides in chromatography 14066623. The more comprehensive system formulated by IUPAC 9826173 is applied much less frequently. A typical ganglioside name using the old system looks like |FRAME: Ganglioside-GQ1b "ganglioside GQ1b"|. The first letter refers to the glycosphingolipid series. For example, the "G" stands for the |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs "ganglio series"|. The next letter describes the number of sialic acid residues: (A = 0, M =1, D = 2, T = 3, Q = 4, P = 5, H = 6, S = 7). The following number describes the number of the non-sialic residues, and is derived in a rather complex manner. It was initially assumed that the number of such residues does not exceed 5. The number in the name was calculated as (5 - the number of uncharged carbohydrates). In addition, several sub-series of gangliosides have been defined based on the number of sialic acids attached to the galactose residue of the lacosylceramide core. If no sialic residues are present at that position, the compounds belong to the |FRAME: 0-Series-Ganglioside "0-series |. Those with one sialic acid at that position are named the |FRAME: A-Series-Gangliosides a-series |, those with two sialic acids belong to the |FRAME: B-Series-Gangliosides b-series |, and so on. |FRAME: C-Series-Gangliosides "C-series"| or higher gangliosides are rare in adult mammals and birds, but are abundant in fish and amphibians. Confusingly, GM1b and GD1c are both 0-series gangliosides, despite having a b and c in their names. So, for example, the |FRAME: Ganglioside-GQ1b "ganglioside GQ1b"| is named as follows: G = belongs to the ganglio series, Q = 4 sialic acids, 1 = 4 non-sialic residues, and b = belongs to the b-series, meaning two of the sialic acids are attached to the inner galactose.

Compound.name: a menaquinol

Menaquinones and demethylmenaquinones are isoprenoid quinones of the naphthalene series, and are constituents of bacterial plasma membranes, where they play important roles in electron transfer and oxidative phosphorylation. Menaquinones are the most widespread respiratory quinones in biological systems Fujimoto12. Menaquinones and demethylmenaquinones are named MK- n or DMK- n , respectively, where the n refers to the number of prenyl units present in the side chain. The most common length of the side chain in bacteria is 8, although minor amounts of MK-1 through MK-14 have been found 7022156. Many bacteria and archaea have |FRAME: Dihydromenaquinones "dehydrogenated menaquinones"|, which are named MK- n (H 2 ). The degree and location of dehydrogenation depends on the species. Some organisms have menaquinones with modifications of the head group, for example |FRAME: TAX-2302| possess both |FRAME: CPD-15875 thermoplasmaquinones| (TPQ), which contains an extra methyl group, and |FRAME: CPD-15876 methionaquinones| (MTK), which contains a methylthio group 11157962. Menaquinones are also known as vitamin K 2 . Vitamin K is a name given to a group of derivatives of 2-methyl-1,4-naphthoquinone that are required by mammals for the posttranslational modification of certain proteins, mostly involved in blood coagulation. These compounds, while essential for mammals, are not synthesized by them, and are thus considered vitamins. The natural forms of the vitamin are vitamin K 1 (|FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE|) and vitamin K 2 (|FRAME: Menaquinones "menaquinone"|). Since menaquinones produced by different organisms have different tail lengths there are many variations of vitamin K 2 , usually specified based on the number of carbons in their tails, such as in Vitamin K 2 (45).

Compound.name: a bacteriochlorophyll e
Comment: Green sulfur bacteria (|FRAME: TAX-191412|) and green flimentous bacteria (|FRAME: TAX-1106|) contain chlorosomes - large organelles that are believed to be the most efficient light-harvesting antennae in nature |CITS: [20130996][Saga10]|. Green sulfur bacteria can grow at light intensities that are too low to support growth of any other phototroph, up to a million times lower light than normal sunlight Overmann92. Chlorosomes contain about 1,500 bacteriochlorophyll molecules per reaction center. They are filled with 10 30 rod-shaped elements which are oriented parallel to the long axis of the chlorosomes and have a diameter of 10 nm. Each rod consists of a tubular bilayer formed by self-organization of the antenna bacteriochlorophyll molecules. Unlike all other known photosynthetic antenna, in which the chlorophyll molecules are bound to proteins, chlorosomes do not contain accessory proteins. The chlorosomal bacteriochlorophyll pigments are able to self-aggregate due to their unique chemical characteristics. The bacteriochlorophylls found in chlorosomes are either |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c "|, |FRAME: CPD-9093 "bacteriochlorophyll d "| or |FRAME: CPD-9094 "bacteriochlorophyll e "|, depending on the species. They all possess a hydroxyl group at the C-3 1 position that allows them to chelate the Mg atom of a neighboring molecule and to interact with the C-13-oxo carbonyl group of another neighboring pigment molecule, affording the self-aggregation |CITS: [16121276][19435848][22210764]|. In addition, all of these bacteriochlorophylls lack C-13 2 -methylcarboxyl side chains, which are found in all other (bacterio)chlorophylls but would interfere with the ability to form aggregates 16245042. Despite of their names, |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c "|, |FRAME: CPD-9093 "bacteriochlorophyll d "| and |FRAME: CPD-9094 "bacteriochlorophyll e "| are actually chlorins rather than bacteriochlorins. All three are usually found with an unsaturated farnesyl tail rather than phytyl tails |CITS: [2350541][Borrego99]|, although exceptions have been reported. In chlorosomes of |FRAME: TAX-191412| (but not |FRAME: TAX-1106| |CITS: [Risch79][3442679]|) all three types of bacteriochlorophyll appear in several forms with different degrees of methylation at the C-8 2 and C-12 1 carbons |CITS: [12656478][14610639]|. The variety in methylation is depicted in the structure shown here by the R groups. In general, pimgents produced by cultures grown at lower light intensities are more highly methylated at the C-8 2 position than pigments produced by cells of the same organism grown at higher light intensities. Different methylation states result in different aggregation properties and light absorbance of the chlorosome, and thus methylation is used as an adaptation to altering envireonmental conditions. Most of the green sulfur bacteria growing in stratified lakes contain CPD-9093. CPD-9094 has been isolated from the chlorosomes of several strains of brown-colored |FRAME: TAX-191412|, including |FRAME: TAX-34090| and |FRAME: TAX-1096| 12029393.

The basic units of |FRAME: Carrageenans carrageenans| are repeats of alternating alpha-1,3 linked D-galactose and beta-1,4-linked D-galactose units, which are often substituted by sulfate. Carrageenans are classified according to the number and the position of sulfated ester 1367970. The three most industrially exploited carrageenans, namely, |FRAME: kappa-Carrageenan|, |FRAME: iota-Carrageenan| and |FRAME: Lambda-Carrageenan|, are distinguished by the presence of one, two or three ester-sulfate groups per repeating disaccharide unit respectively. |FRAME: alpha-Carrageenan| is sulfated only at position 2 of the alpha-1,3-linked 3,6-anhydrogalactose units.

Members of this family, such as |FRAME: CPD-25407|, were found to possess extremely potent cytotoxicity against various tumor cells |CITS: [1241159][628025][367597][3834790][20937594]|. Shortly after that discovery highly related compounds were discovered in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-42198| 593392. These new compounds, which were named |FRAME: Ansamitocins ansamitocins|, differed structurally from the maytansinoids only by carrying simpler acyl groups at C-3, and the two names (maytansinoids and ansamitocin) are now used interchangeably. Related compounds were later observed in moss species |CITS: [3204376][2298279]|. Structurally, the compounds belong to the |FRAME: Ansamycins ansamycin| family of polyketide macrolactams, which are defined by consisting of an aromatic moiety bridged at nonadjacent positions by an aliphatic chain 4148590. The bacterial-derived ansamitocins were found to have the same activity against tumor cells as the plant compounds |CITS: [6245801][7380728]|. This activity is a result of the compounds' affinity towards |FRAME: Beta-tubulins beta-tubulin| in eukaryotic cells, which inhibits microtubule assembly and chromosome segregation during the interphase and mitotic phase and causes cell apoptosis 24124473. The identified |FRAME: CPD-25407|-binding site was shown to be distinct from that of |FRAME: CPD-7858| 25114240. In bacteria, |FRAME: CPD-25396| was shown to bind to the cell division protein FtsZ 32365857. A derivative of |FRAME: CPD-25407|, named |FRAME: CPD-25409|, is used in several antibody-drug conjugates. One of those, trastuzumab emtansine, sold under the brand name Kadcyla, is currently used for treatment of HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer in some patients.

Compound.name: xanthan
Comment: |FRAME: Xanthan Xanthan| is an exopolysaccharide produced by the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-339| and related species. Because of its rheological properties, including high viscosity and pseudo-plasticity, and stability in extreme conditions, xanthan gum has been used in food, agriculture and industry as an emulsifying, thickening or suspending agent. It was approved for use in foods in 1968. Xanthan gum has been implicated as the pathogenic substance causing black rot in crucifers 9144435. The polymer is composed of repeating pentasaccharide units with the structure of a beta-1,4-linked D-glucose backbone with trisaccharide side chains composed of mannose-(beta-1,4)-glucuronic acid-(beta-1,2)-mannose attached to alternate glucose residues in the backbone by alpha-1,3 linkages 1212669. The terminal repeat unit is anchored to the cytoplasmic membrane by an undecaprenyldiphosphate lipid carrier, and assembley of the polymer occurs while anchored. Acetyl and pyruvyl residues are often added to one of the mannose units as non-carbohydrate decorations.

Attached to these rings are a number of unusual 2,6-dideoxy- or 2,3(4),6-trideoxysugars, such as |FRAME: CPD-13780|. Macrolide antibiotics are effective inhibitors of bacterial protein biosynthesis. They bind to the large 50S ribosomal subunit at or near the peptidyl transferase center and block the elongation of the peptide chain.

Comment: 'Heme' is usually understood as any tetrapyrrolic chelate of iron. Compound.name: an inositol
Comment: |FRAME: Inositols Inositol| is the generic name for 1,2,3,4,5,6-cyclohexanehexol. Epimerization of the six hydroxyl groups results in nine stereoisomers. Among the isomers, |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| is the most abundant in nature and it is an essential compound in eukaryotic cell membranes as a phosphatidylinositol moiety, which plays an important role in signal transduction. Some other forms, such as |FRAME: CPD-8050|, are also found in nature, although they are less abundant. Nomenclature of cyclitols can be quite confusing. Two alternative naming schemes are possible for inositol compounds since carbon-1 could be assigned to either of two enantiotopic carbons. The two methods result in 1D-stereochemistry and 1L-stereochemistry based names. If carbon-1 is placed at the top of the molecule, L-numbering proceeds clockwise, while D-numbering proceeds counter-clockwise. Both the 1D or 1L designations can be employed currently. However, the symbol Ins implies myo-inositol with D- numbering. Additional information on the nomenclature of myo -inositol compounds can be found in the 1973 document Nomenclature of cyclitols by the Nomenclature Committee of the International Union of Biochemistry (NC-IUB), and the 1988 publication Numbering of atoms in myo -inositol , published by the same body, whose aim was to relax some of the rules specified in the 1973 publication. To aid in following the transformations in inositol compounds in pathways, the structures of inositol stereoisomers in MetaCyc have been formatted to show carbon 1 at the top of the ring, with numbering proceeding clockwise. An exception is the structure of |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL|, which is presented with carbon 3 at the top and counter-clockwise numbering. The reason is that carbon 3 of |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| (which is based on L-numbering) matches the carbon-1 of 1D numbering, which is used for the various phosphorylated and otherwise modified forms, and by presenting the molecule in this way, it is much easier to show structural relationships in reactions and pathways (see for example |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL-1-KINASE-RXN "EC 2.7.1.64"|).

The adenine cytokinins are classified further by the configuration of their N6-side chain as isoprenoid or aromatic cytokinins. The authors noted its anticancer activity, which they described as "remarkable" Pettit82. Other samples, collected in the Gulf of Mexico, the Gulf of California, and other locations, afforded other members. Currently 20 members of the bryostatin family are known Pettit91. In 1990 it was suggested that the bryostatins may be produced by endosymbiotic bacteria Anthoni90. The presence of such endosymbionts was confirmed in 1997, and based on small-subunit rRNA gene sequence the organisms were found to belong to a new genus within the gamma-proteobacteria. They were named |FRAME: TAX-62101| 9361448. The bacteria cannot be cultivated outside the host; however, the discovery of genes encoding polyketide synthases in the bacterial DNA provided proof for a bacterial origin of the bryostatins 11571152. Most, but not all, of the bryostatins pharmacological effects are attributed to their interaction with the |FRAME: Diacyl-sn-Glycerols diacylglycerol| binding site of the C-1, C-19 and C-26 regulatory domain of |FRAME: EC-2.7.11.13| 20971628. More than 30 clinical trials have been conducted with |FRAME: CPD-21475| in monotherapy or in combination with clinically used cytotoxic drugs, testing its efficacy against different tumor types such as sarcoma, melanoma, ovaria, cervical, neck and head carcinoma, esophageal, gastric, pancreatic, renal cell carcinoma, as well as a variety of leukemias, e.g., chronic lymphocytic leukemia, non-Hodgkin s lymphoma, or multiple myeloma. However, phase II studies of |FRAME: CPD-21475| have failed to demonstrate any clinically meaningful activity, and bryostatin has not progressed to phase III clinical trials as a cancer treatment Newman12. On the other hand, |FRAME: CPD-21475| has been shown to reverse synaptic loss and facilitate synaptic maturation in animal models of Alzheimer's disease, Fragile X, stroke, and other neurological disorders. Advanced Alzheimer patients treated with bryostatin demonstrated return of major functions such as swallowing, vocalization, and word recognition, and currently Phase II clinical trials are conducted with |FRAME: CPD-21475| as a potential treatment for Alzheimer's disease 28482641.
