Comment: |FRAME: Gangliosides "Gangliosides"| are molecules composed of |FRAME: Glycosphingolipids| (|FRAME: Ceramides| and |FRAME: Oligosaccharides|) with one or more sialic acids (usually |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE|) linked to the sugar chain. They are components of the cell plasma membrane that modulates cell signal transduction events, and appear to concentrate in lipid rafts. The name ganglioside is derived from the ganglion cells of the brain, from which the first gangliosides were isolated by the German scientist Ernst Klenk in 1942 Klenk42. Indeed, gangliosides dominate the composition of the glycocalyces of most of the cells of the vertebrate nervous system. Although gangliosides with various glycan structures are found in every vertebrate tissue, they are markedly more abundant in the nervous system, where each cell has on average about 10 million cell surface gangliosides 27261254. Variations in the sialoglycan and lipid components of the gangliosides result in hundreds of distinct ganglioside structures with a variety of functions that ranges from regulating receptor tyrosine kinases to directing cell-cell communication, cell-substrate interaction, adhesion, and protein targeting 17991443. Mammalian brain gangliosides, however, are dominated by only four types of gangliosides - |FRAME: CPD-7188 "ganglioside GM1a|, |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINYL-ETCETERA-GLUCOSYLCERA "ganglioside GD1a"|, |FRAME: Ganglioside-GD1b "ganglioside GD1b"| and |FRAME: Ganglioside-GT1b "ganglioside GT1b"| 22735313. The ceramide lipid components of brain gangliosides are dominated by a single fatty acid (|FRAME: STEARIC_ACID|) attached to one of two sphingoid bases, |FRAME: SPHINGOSINE| and |FRAME: CPD-19684| 21113547. While many non-human mammals synthesize gangliosides that contain two types of sialic acids - |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE| and |FRAME: CPD-273|, mammalian brain gangliosides almost exclusively carry the former. Like other glycosphingolipids, gangliosides are biosynthesized stepwise by a series of glycosyltransferases that use nucleotide sugar donors to first glucosylate ceramide and then elongate the saccharide chain .|FRAME: Lactosyl-Ceramides Lactosylceramide|, a product of the second glycosylation step in the biosynthesis of many glycosphingolipids, is an important branching point, being a common precursor for the synthesis of the four major classes of glycosphingolipids: the |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs "ganglio series"|, the |FRAME: Globo-Series-GSLs "globo series"|, the |FRAME: Lacto-Series-GSLs "lacto series"|, and the |FRAME: Neolacto-Series-GSLs "neolacto series"| 10320813. The ceramide lipid of glycosphingolipids is embedded in the outer leaflet of the lipid bilayer of the plasma membrane, with the glycan extending 2-2.5 nm outward, perpendicular to the plane of the lipid bilayer 19056784. What makes gangliosides different from other glycosphingolipids is the incorporation of sialic acids. With a mean Pka value of around 2.6, sialic acids are more acidic than the majority of carboxylic acids and negatively charged at most physiological pH values. About the nomenclature of gangliosides Ganglioside naming is somewhat complex. Two ganglioside nomenclature systems are currently in use. The most commonly used is a short-hand nomenclature suggested by Svennerholm, which was initially based on the migration order of |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs "ganglio-series"| gangliosides in chromatography 14066623. The more comprehensive system formulated by IUPAC 9826173 is applied much less frequently. A typical ganglioside name using the old system looks like |FRAME: Ganglioside-GQ1b "ganglioside GQ1b"|. The first letter refers to the glycosphingolipid series. For example, the "G" stands for the |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs "ganglio series"|. The next letter describes the number of sialic acid residues: (A = 0, M =1, D = 2, T = 3, Q = 4, P = 5, H = 6, S = 7). The following number describes the number of the non-sialic residues, and is derived in a rather complex manner. It was initially assumed that the number of such residues does not exceed 5. The number in the name was calculated as (5 - the number of uncharged carbohydrates). In addition, several sub-series of gangliosides have been defined based on the number of sialic acids attached to the galactose residue of the lacosylceramide core. If no sialic residues are present at that position, the compounds belong to the |FRAME: 0-Series-Ganglioside "0-series |. Those with one sialic acid at that position are named the |FRAME: A-Series-Gangliosides a-series |, those with two sialic acids belong to the |FRAME: B-Series-Gangliosides b-series |, and so on. |FRAME: C-Series-Gangliosides "C-series"| or higher gangliosides are rare in adult mammals and birds, but are abundant in fish and amphibians. Confusingly, GM1b and GD1c are both 0-series gangliosides, despite having a b and c in their names. So, for example, the |FRAME: Ganglioside-GQ1b "ganglioside GQ1b"| is named as follows: G = belongs to the ganglio series, Q = 4 sialic acids, 1 = 4 non-sialic residues, and b = belongs to the b-series, meaning two of the sialic acids are attached to the inner galactose.

Compound.name: a mycobacterial arabinogalactan
Comment: |FRAME: Arabinogalactan Arabinogalactans| are biopolymers consisting mostly of arabinose and galactose residues. Two main classes of arabinogalactans are found in nature: |FRAME: Plant-Arabinogalactans "plant arabinogalactan"| and |FRAME: Mycobacterial-Arabinogalactans "microbial arabinogalactan"|. The |FRAME: Mycobacterial-Arabinogalactans "microbial arabinogalactan"| consists of arabinose and galactose monosaccharides in their furanose configurations and is a major structural component of the mycobacterial cell wall, where it is covalently attached to the peptidoglycan. The galactan portion of the polymer is linear, consisting of approximately 30 units with alternating beta-(1-5) and beta-(1-6) glycosidic linkages. |FRAME: Arabinans Arabinan| chains are attached at three branch points within the galactan chain (believed to be at residues 8, 10 and 12) 16040600. These chains consist of about 30 residues 18303028. The arabinan portion of the polymer is a complex branched structure with glycosidic linkages of alpha-(1-3), beta-(1-5). The chains are capped by a D-arabinofuranose residue attached by a beta-(1-2) linkage. In the Mycobacterial cell wall, the arabinan portion is usually capped with mycolic acids that are attached to the beta-(1-2) linked residue. Arabinogalactan molecules in slow-growing mycobacterial strains possess a single galactosamine (GalN) residue attached via an alpha-linkage to a highly branched arabinofuranose residue in the arabinan core |CITS: [9359425][23043372]|.

Important androgens include |FRAME: TESTOSTERONE|, |FRAME: 17-BETA-HYDROXY-5ALPHA-ANDROSTAN-3-O| (DHT) and |FRAME: ANDROST4ENE androstenedione|. |FRAME: TESTOSTERONE Testosterone| is the major androgen in adult males, while DHT plays a crucial role in utero, causing differentiation of the penis, scrotum and prostate. Despite its small size, it, is the most structurally complex pectin component. Its alpha-1,4-linked D-galacturonate backbone is decorated with four side branches (named A D) consisting of 12 different types of sugars in over 20 different linkages 18486536. Some of the sugars are quite rare, including |FRAME: CPD-13046|, |FRAME: CPD-20946| (3-C-carboxy-5-deoxy-L-xylose), and |FRAME: CPD-20949| (Dha). RG-II exists in the primary wall as a dimer that is cross linked by a 1:2 borate-diol diester 12226238. The borate diester cross link is formed between the apiosyl residue in side chain A of each monomer subunit |CITS: [8798473][10224062]|. Despite this complexity the structure of RG-II is largely conserved across plant species. It has been reported that the structure is virtually the same in members of the Brassicacea, Cucurbitaceae, Leguminoseae, Apiaceae, Liliaceae, Araceae, Amaryllidaceae, Gramineae, and more families 12765781. However, later work reported some variation in the side chains and methylation status within and across different plant speces 23802881. Please note that the structure shown here is not entirely accurate, due to the inability of software to depict unusual monosaccharides. |FRAME: CPD-13046|, |FRAME: CPD-20946| and |FRAME: CPD-20949| are depicted as generic pentose, hexuronate, and heptose, respectively.

Compound.name: a 1-phosphatidyl-1D-myo-inositol 5-phosphate
Comment: The phosphorylated derivatives of |FRAME: L-1-phosphatidyl-inositols "phosphatidylinositol"| (PtdIns), collectively called phosphoinositides (PIs), are eukaryotic cell membrane phospholipids whose inositol head group is phosphorylated at position D3, D4, or D5, singly or in all combinations, to yield seven PI metabolites. The seven phosphoinositides found in animals include: Phosphatidylinositol monophosphates: |FRAME: CPD-177|, |FRAME: CPD-1108| and |FRAME: 1-PHOSPHATIDYL-1D-MYO-INOSITOL-5-PHOSPHA|. Phosphatidylinositol bisphophosphates: |FRAME: 1-PHOSPHATIDYL-1D-MYO-INOSITOL-34-BISPH|, |FRAME: 1-PHOSPHATIDYL-1D-MYO-INOSITOL-35-BISPH|, and |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYL-MYO-INOSITOL-45-BISPHOSPHA|. Phosphatidylinositol trisphophosphate: |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYLINOSITOL-345-TRIPHOSPHATE|. About phosphatidylinositol 5-phosphate (PI5P): PI5P represents only 0.5% of the PI pool present in most cells. However, its levels strongly fluctuate due to external stimuli such as TCR activation, insulin treatment, oxidative stress, and pathogen cellular invasion 28302928. Several studies found changes in intracellular PI5P levels during cell cycle progression, as well as upon thrombin treatment and osmotic stress |CITS: [10854858][11463365][11716778]|. The plant homeodomain-containing ING2 protein, a candidate tumor suppressor, was shown to act as a nuclear PI5P receptor, a function that regulates its ability to activate p53 12859901. PI5P has also been tied to tumor suppression via its potential regulation of Akt. It was demonstrated that the loss of PI5P, via a conversion to |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYL-MYO-INOSITOL-45-BISPHOSPHA|, resulted in a decrease in Akt activity 12897244. In addition, PI5P was shown to enhance the activity of various myotubularin phosphatases (MTM1, MTMR3, and MTMR6) toward their preferred substrate |FRAME: 1-PHOSPHATIDYL-1D-MYO-INOSITOL-35-BISPH|, presumably through allosteric regulation 12646134). Together these studies stress the importance of PI5P as a bona fide signaling molecule 15247229.

Compound.name: heparin
Comment: |FRAME: HEPARIN "Heparin"| is a glycosaminoglycan polymer with a molecular weight ranging from 3 to 30 kDa. It is composed of a variable sulfated repeating disaccharide units composed of hexuronic (either iduronic or glucuronic) acid and glucosamine residues, in which the 2 position of the hexuronic acid and the 2, 3, or 6 positions of glucosamine may be sulfated. The two residues within a disaccharide are linked by a (1->4) bond, as are the disaccharides to each other. The main disaccharide unit consists of |FRAME: CPD-12518| and |FRAME: CPD-12533| [it is often referred to as IdoA(2S)-(1->4)-GlcNS(6S)]. However, |FRAME: CPD-12518| can be substituted by |FRAME: CPD-12521|, and |FRAME: CPD-12533| can be replaced by |FRAME: N-ACETYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSAMINE|, |FRAME: N-sulfo-D-glucosamine|, |FRAME: CPD-12545| or |FRAME: CPD-12565|. The basic IdoA(2S)-(1->4)-GlcNS(6S) disaccharide accounts for at least 85% of heparin isolated from beef lung and about 75% of heparin from porcine intestinal mucosa |CITS: [Casu89][Gatti79]|. Variations in the extent and location of sulfation, as well as the conformation of the alternating hexuronic acid residues, lead to a high degree of heterogeneity. By convention, heparin refers to molecules which possess a high sulfate content and large amounts of iduronic acid. The structure of |FRAME: HEPARIN| is very similar to that of |FRAME: Heparan-Sulfate| (also known as heparitin sulfate). Heparan sulfate contains lower amounts of sulfate and less iduronic acid than heparin 5484472. In addition, heparan sulfates disaccharide units are organized into distinct sulfated and non-sulfated domains, while heparin disaccharides are sulfated more uniformly 15047699.

The carboxyl group of the distal chain is usually free, but in a few cases it is esterified with a short alkyl group. The fatty acid chains may be saturated, mono-unsaturated, or poly-unsaturated and the chain length may vary from C 8 to C 16 . In rare cases the rhamnose 2-hydroxyl group distal to the glycosidic bond may be acylated with a long chain alkenoate |CITS: [16160828] [20336292]|.

Compound.name: a short-chain 3-oxo-fatty acid
Comment: The term "fatty acid" was originally coined to describe aliphatic monocarboxylic acids derived from or contained in esterified form in an animal or vegetable fat, oil or wax. However, over the years the term has been expanded to refer to additional, shorter monocarboxylic acids with an aliphatic tail such as |FRAME: PROPIONATE| and |FRAME: BUTYRIC_ACID| (but not the shorter |FRAME: FORMATE| and |FRAME: ACET|). The length of a fatty acid is determined by the length of the longest carbon chain, including the carbon of the carboxy group. Common natural fatty acids usually have an even number of carbons in the longest chain and can be either saturated or unsaturated. In many organisms they are often modified by branching, hydroxylation, methylation, epoxidation and other types of modifications. Inside living cells fatty acids are rarely found in free form. They are usually bound to coenzyme A or acyl-carrier proteins, or form part of |FRAME: Triacylglycerides triglycerides|, |FRAME: Phospholipids phospholipids|, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharides|, and |FRAME: Cholesterol-esters cholesterol esters|. Comment: Cytokinins are a class of plant hormones that promote cell division, or cytokinesis, in plant roots and shoots. While their main role is to control cell growth and differentiation, they also affect apical dominance, axillary bud growth, and leaf senescence. The cytokinins are structurally diverse, and have been divided into two main types: |FRAME: Adenine-Cytokinins "adenine-type cytokinins"| and |FRAME: Phenylurea-Cytokinins "phenylurea-type cytokinins"|. All the natural cytokinins fall into the first type - phenylurea-type cytokinins are synthetic. The adenine cytokinins are classified further by the configuration of their N6-side chain as isoprenoid or aromatic cytokinins. The most prevalent cytokinins are by far those with an unsaturated isoprenoid side chain, and in particular those with a trans -hydroxylated N6-side chain, such as |FRAME: CPD-4210| and its derivatives. Most of the adenine-type cytokinins are modified by glucosylation of the adenine ring at the 3-, the 7-, or 9-position and conjugation of alanine at the 9-position of zeatin, forming lupinic acid. With the exception of the 3-glucosides, the N -glucosyl and alanyl conjugates generally exhibit no or low activity. The most important modifications are those affecting the N6-side chain, where even small substitutions have pronounced effects on cytokinin activity. The most common modifications of the side chain include reduction (e.g. trans-zeatin to dihydrozeatin), conjugation to O-glycosides (O-glucosides and O-xylosides), and side chain cleavage by cytokinin oxidases 11337393.

Cobamides serve as cofactors for a number of important enzymes. A key structural feature of cobinamides is a corrin ring with a cobalt ion in its center. Four of the six coordination sites of the cobalt ion are provided by the corrin ring, while the other two are provided by |FRAME: Cobamide-Upper-Ligands upper| (beta) and |FRAME: Cobamide-Lower-Ligands lower| (alpha) ligands, which are located above and below the ring plane, respectively. The best known cobamide, |FRAME: Cobalamins cobalamin|, contains |FRAME: DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE| as the lower ligand and either a methyl group or 5'-deoxyadenosyl group as the upper ligand.

Comment: |FRAME: THF-GLU-N Tetrahydrofolate| (vitamin B9) and its derivatives, commonly termed folates, are required in a variety of reactions in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, where they act as carriers of one-carbon units in various oxidation states. These one-carbon units are utilized in the biosynthesis of several cellular components, including glycine, methionine, formylmethionine, thymidylate, pantothenate and purine nucleotides. During folate biosynthesis (as described in FOLSYN-PWY) the enzyme |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.12|, adds a glutamate residue to |FRAME: 7-8-DIHYDROPTEROATE|, resulting in |FRAME: DIHYDROFOLATE|, also known as H 2 PteGlu 1 . This molecule in turn is reduced by EC-1.5.1.3 (FolA) to |FRAME: THF| (H 4 PteGlu 1 , or tetrahydrofolate), which can be converted to several other folate molecules 11501996. Most folate molecules are modified in cells by successive additions of glutamate residues, forming folate polyglutamates (or folylpoly-gamma-glutamates). The glutamate residues are added by an amide linkage to the gamma-carboxylate group of the folate or folate derivative. Since these isopeptide bonds are not the normal amide bonds they are not hydrolyzed by peptidases or proteases, which are specific for alpha-carboxyl-linked peptide bonds. The addition of glutamyl residues probably occurs after the reduction of newly synthesized dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate and its conversion to other tetrahydrofolate derivatives. The glutamylation of folate residues serves several goals: it prevents the efflux of folates out of the cell, it increases the binding of folate cofactors to the enzymes of folate interconversion and biosynthesis, and in mammals, it allows the accumulation of folates in the mitochondria, which is required for glycine synthesis 10598551. This class stands for 5-methyltetrahydrofolates with an unspecified number of glutamate residues.

Comment: About the nomenclature of gangliosides Ganglioside naming is somewhat complex. Two ganglioside nomenclature systems are currently in use. The most commonly used is a short-hand nomenclature suggested by Svennerholm, which was initially based on the migration order of |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs "ganglio-series"| gangliosides in chromatography 14066623. The more comprehensive system formulated by IUPAC 9826173 is applied much less frequently. A typical ganglioside name using the old system looks like |FRAME: Ganglioside-GQ1b "ganglioside GQ1b"|. The first letter refers to the glycosphingolipid series. For example, the "G" stands for the |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs "ganglio series"|. The next letter describes the number of sialic acid residues: (A = 0, M =1, D = 2, T = 3, Q = 4, P = 5, H = 6, S = 7). The following number describes the number of the non-sialic residues, and is derived in a rather complex manner. It was initially assumed that the number of such residues does not exceed 5. The number in the name was calculated as (5 - the number of uncharged carbohydrates). In addition, several sub-series of gangliosides have been defined based on the number of sialic acids attached to the galactose residue of the lacosylceramide core. If no sialic residues are present at that position, the compounds belong to the |FRAME: 0-Series-Ganglioside "0-series |. Those with one sialic acid at that position are named the |FRAME: A-Series-Gangliosides a-series |, those with two sialic acids belong to the |FRAME: B-Series-Gangliosides b-series |, and so on. |FRAME: C-Series-Gangliosides "C-series"| or higher gangliosides are rare in adult mammals and birds, but are abundant in fish and amphibians. Confusingly, GM1b and GD1c are both 0-series gangliosides, despite having a b and c in their names. So, for example, the |FRAME: Ganglioside-GQ1b "ganglioside GQ1b"| is named as follows: G = belongs to the ganglio series, Q = 4 sialic acids, 1 = 4 non-sialic residues, and b = belongs to the b-series, meaning two of the sialic acids are attached to the inner galactose.

The primary nucleobases are |FRAME: CYTOSINE|, |FRAME: GUANINE|, |FRAME: ADENINE| (found in both DNA and RNA), |FRAME: THYMINE| (found only in DNA) and |FRAME: URACIL| (found only in RNA), abbreviated as C, G, A, T, and U, respectively. There are many additional nucleobases, usually derived from the primary ones. Based on their structure, nucleobases are divided into |FRAME: Purines purines| and |FRAME: Pyrimidine-Bases pyrimidines|.

These antibiotics exhibit remarkable antitumor activity and share several common structural features 11996547. Some of the compounds included in this class are |FRAME: CPD-16513| 567065, |FRAME: CPD-18026| 16314293, |FRAME: CPD-18027| 7174530 and |FRAME: CPD-18028| 6860429. Among them, |FRAME: CPD-18026| exhibits the most potent antitumor activity and has been approved as an anticancer drug for use in patients with soft-tissue sarcoma 25273374.

JA-Ile has also been detected in |FRAME: TAX-49451| and plays a role in defense responses 17085687 but it is unclear which form of JA-Ile is active in this process.

Compound.name: a galactan
Comment: Galactans are polymers composed of repeating units of galactose residues. In many plants galactans are often found as a constituent of complex polysaccharides such as |FRAME: Arabinogalactan arabinogalactan|, often forming a component of hemicellulose. Two main classes of arabinogalactans are found in nature: |FRAME: Plant-Arabinogalactans "plant arabinogalactan"| and |FRAME: Mycobacterial-Arabinogalactans "microbial arabinogalactan"|. A completely different form of galactan polymers is found in red algae. |FRAME: Red-Alage-Galactans "Red algal galactans"| are polysaccharides having usually a linear backbone built up of alternating 3-linked beta-D-galactopyranose and 4-linked alpha-galactopyranose residues. The beta-galactose residues always belong to D-series, whereas the alpha-galactose residues are D in carrageenans and L in agars. A substantial part of the alpha-galactose residues may exist in the form of a 3,6-anhydro derivative Truus06. Red algal galactans are usually sulfated.

Compound.name: a flavin electron carrier/enzyme cofactor
Comment: Flavin compounds are based on the tricyclic heterocycle |FRAME: CPD-23399| structure. They are capable of undergoing oxidation-reduction reactions, and can accept either one electron in a two-step process or two electrons at once. Reduction is made with the addition of hydrogen atoms to specific nitrogen atoms on the isoalloxazine ring system. Flavin compounds participate in many reactions as electron acceptors or donors, and some of the compounds (particularly |FRAME: FAD| and |FRAME: FMN|) can also serve as enzyme cofactors. Enzymes that contain flavin cofactors are often referred to as flavoenzymes or flavoproteins. The flavin compounds are synthesized from GTP, via the precursor |FRAME: RIBOFLAVIN|.

Compound.name: a [cullin]- N 6 -[NEDD8-protein]-yl-L-lysine
Comment: |FRAME: Cullins Cullins| are a family of proteins that provide a scaffold for some RING-type E3 ubiquitin transferases (|FRAME: EC-2.3.2.27 "EC 2.3.2.27"|), which are not able to bind a substrate protein directly. These E3 proteins form a complex with a cullin protein and a substrate recognition subunit (SRS). Some complexes also include an adaptor that links the SRS to the complex. The complexes are known as CRLs for Cullin-RING ubiquitin Ligases. CRLs comprise the largest known category of ubiquitin ligases, and regulate an extensive number of dynamic cellular processes, including multiple aspects of the cell cycle, transcription, signal transduction, and development 18282298. There are five major types of cullins in metazoa, each of which forms a distinct class of CRL complex, with distinct adaptors and/or substrate-recognition subunits. CRLs are activated by the covalent attachment of the ubiquitin-like protein |FRAME: NEDD8 NEDD8| to the cullin, and are inhibited by binding to the CAND1 inhibitor 15688063. The human genome contains eight cullin genes.

Compound.name: a monounsaturated fatty acid
Comment: |FRAME: Fatty-Acids "A fatty acid"| is a carboxylic acid with a long unbranched aliphatic tail. Even though fatty acids derived from natural fats and oils, such as CPD-195, are usually at least 8 carbon atoms long, carboxylic acids as short as BUTYRIC_ACID (4 carbon atoms) are considered to be fatty acids. When a fatty acid contains only single bonds, it is referred to as |FRAME: Saturated-Fatty-Acids|. When it contains one or more double bonds, it is referred to as |FRAME: Unsaturated-Fatty-Acids|. If it contains a double bond in the trans configuration, it is often referred to as a trans fatty acid. Most fatty acids in the trans configuration are not found in nature and are the result of human processing. About nomenclature : Several nomenclatures are used for unsaturated fatty acids, and are not complementary. Systematic names (or IUPAC names) begin counting the carbon atoms from the carboxylic acid end, and the double bonds are labelled with cis / trans or E/Z notation, e.g. 8 E ,10 E ,12 Z -octadecatrienoate. However, unsaturated fatty acids are often described using the omega nomenclature, which begins counting the carbon atoms from the terminal methyl carbon (designated as n or ω). In addition, unsaturated fatty acids are often referred to by trivial names, or by the "lipid number" as in 18:3, where 18 is the number of carbons, and 3 is the number of double bonds. This notation is ambiguous, as it does not specify the location of the double bonds.

Compound.name: an amide
Comment: Amides are derivatives of oxoacids in which an acidic hydroxy group has been replaced by an amino or substituted amino group. Most amide compounds fall under |FRAME: Carboxamides carboxamides|, where the nitrogen atom is bonded with a carbon atom. However, the term amide also refers to compounds where the nitrogen is bonded to a non-carbon atom (see for example |FRAME: Sulfonamides|).

Compound.name: a phycobilin
Comment: Phycobilins are photosynthetic chromophores found in |FRAME: TAX-1117| and in the chloroplasts of |FRAME: TAX-2763 rhodophytes|, |FRAME: TAX-38254 glaucocystophytes|, and some |FRAME: TAX-3027 cryptomonads|, but not in green algae and higher plants. They are bound to proteins called |FRAME: Phycobiliproteins phycobiliproteins|, which are organized into large complexes called |FRAME: Phycobilisomes phycobilisomes|, which pass the light energy captured by the phycobillins to |FRAME: Chlorophylls chlorophylls| in the photosystems. The phycobilins are efficient at absorbing wavelengths that are not absorbed well by |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-A|, including red, orange, yellow, and green light. The phycobilins are divided into four main types: |FRAME: Phycoerythrobilins phycoerythrobilins|, |FRAME: Phycourobilins phycourobilins|, |FRAME: Phycoviolobilins phycoviolobilins|, and |FRAME: Phycocyanobilins phycocyanobilins|.

Compound.name: a glycogen
Comment: Glycogen is a highly branched glucose polymer found in archaea, bacteria, and eukaryotes. It resembles plant-produced |FRAME: Starch starch| and is sometimes called "animal starch". Glycogen serves multiple functions, including energy reserve, osmotic regulation, blood glucose homeostasis, and pH maintenance. Glycogen is formed of small chains of 8 to 12 glucose molecules linked together by alpha (1->4) bonds. These small chains, also known as |FRAME: Maltodextrins maltodextrins|, are in turn linked together by alpha (1->6) bonds. The alpha-1,4 linkages make up approximately 95% of the total molecule. The alpha-1,6 branches accounts for 7–10% of the linkages and are evenly distributed within the glycogen particle. Since each chain (with the exception of the outer unbranched chains) supports two branches, glycogen particles grow spherically by adding tiers (a tier corresponds to the spherical space separating two consecutive branches from all chains located at similar distance from the center of the particle). Two structural levels of glycogen particles have been reported, which are tightly associated with their physiological functions: small quasi-spherical beta particles, as found in muscle cells, and large rosette-shaped alpha particles, as found in liver cells. The diameter of beta particles normally range from 10 to 50 nm, with an average at around 20—30 nm. The beta particles can stick together to form large alpha particles with diameters up to 300 nm |CITS: [20196533][31244022][33996916]|. Two types of alpha particles have been observed: fragile and dense particles, which comprise large and dense beta particles with long average chain length, and stable light particles, which comprise smaller, compact beta particles with short average chain length 31244022. Mathematical modelling predicts a maximal size for the beta particle beyond which further growth is impossible, as there would not be sufficient space for interaction of the chains with the catalytic sites of glycogen metabolism enzymes. The predicted upper limit is a particle consisting of 12 tiers corresponding to a 42 nm maximal diameter and including about 55,000 glucose residues. 36% of this total number rests in the outer (unbranched) shell and is thus readily accessible to glycogen catabolism without the need for debranching 12179957. Although glycogen and starch are two distinct physical states of the same type of storage polysaccharide, starch is solid semi-crystalline while glycogen particles are entirely hydrosoluble 21220783.

Compound.name: a sialyl-Lewis x epitope
Synonyms: an sLe x antigen // alphaNeuNAc-(2->3)-betaGal-(1->4)-[alphaFuc-(1->3]-betaGlcNAc-[protein] // a sialyl Lewis x antigen // a histo-blood group sialyl Lewis x antigen
Comment: The sialyl Lewis-X (SLeX) antigen is expressed on glycolipids and glycoproteins on the cell surfaces. In adults, SLeX antigen is expressed principally on the surfaces of granulocytic cells. It plays an important role during early steps of inflammatory response as a ligand of the three known selectins - E-selectin (also known as endothelial leucocyte adhesion molecules, ELAM-1), P-Selectin, and L-selectin, resulting in the capture of leucocytes from the plasma and their attachment to blood endothelial cells |CITS: [2210723][7591266]|. The antigen is expressed in high frequency in tumor tissue where it plays a role in adhesion between tumor cells and blood endothelial cells during tumor metastases |CITS: [6386148][12029441][1699667][1701275]|. The SLeX antigen is synthesized from |FRAME: B-Gal-14-NacGlc-R| by the action of two enzymes, |FRAME: EC-2.4.3.6| and |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.152| |CITS: [1339443][25498912]|.

Compound.name: a rhodoquinol
Comment: Rhodoquinone (RQ) is a modified ubiquinone, where the methoxyl group in position 3 is replaced by an amino group. Rhodoquinone is not limited to prokaryotes. It was soon discovered that some eukaryotic parasites such as the nematodes |FRAME: TAX-6253| and |FRAME: TAX-6252| |CITS: [5796154][811785]|, as well as parasitic helminths 4795616 also contain rhodoquinone, which is essential for fumarate reduction under anaerobic conditions 2843227. Later it was shown that rhodoquinone is present in all eukaryotes that reduce fumarate during anoxia, including freshwater snails, mussels, lugworms, and oysters 8537365. The reduced form of rhodoquinone is rhodoquinol.

Algae of the |FRAME: TAX-3009| order produce fucose-rich polysaccahrides known as |FRAME: Fucoidans fucoidans|. However, fucose is a common sugar, found in N -linked glycans on the mammalian, insect and plant cell surface, in many bacterial glycans, and in other biomolecules. Most of the fucose found in biology is in the |FRAME: L-fucoses "L conformation"|, and the use of |FRAME: D-Fucoses| is rather rare (for example in some |FRAME: Cardenolide-Glycosides "cardenolide glycosides"|). Note that fucose is a reducing sugar that exists in solution in multiple configurations. The open-chain structure shown here is provided only as a schematic illustration of chirality. Compound.name: a pectate
Synonyms: poly(1,4-alpha-D-galacturonate)(n) // (1,4-alpha-D-D-galactosyluronate)n // 1,4-alpha-D-galacturonide // a pectic acid // an alpha-D-polygalacturonic acid // a poly(1,4-alpha-D-galacturonate)
Comment: |FRAME: Pectin "Pectin"| is a structural heteropolysaccharide consisting of a complex set of polysaccharides that is present in most primary cell walls and is particularly abundant in the non-woody parts of terrestrial plants. It s involved in crosslinking cellulose and hemicellulose fibers, which provides rigidity to the cell wall. The characteristic structure of pectin is a linear chain of alpha-(1-4)-linked |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| that forms the pectin-backbone, |FRAME: 1-4-alpha-D-galacturonosyl|. Different components of pectin have different substitutions and additions. A common type is |FRAME: Rhamnogalacturonans-I "rhamnogalacturonan I"| (RG-I), which makes up 20-35% of pectin. In RG-I some of the |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| units in the backbone are replaced by (1-2)-linked |FRAME: L-rhamnose|, to which side chains of various neutral sugars branch off, mostly |FRAME: D-Galactose|, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE| and |FRAME: CPD-25028|. Another common type is |FRAME: CPD-14581 "rhamnogalacturonan II"| (RG-II), which makes up about 10% of pectin. RG-II is based on a backbone of 8-9 galacturonate units, which are decorated by four side chains consisting of 12 different types of sugars in more than 20 different linkages. RG-II usually forms dimeric structures via the formation of crosslinks by a 1:2 borate diol ester between apiosyl residues in one of the side chains. Other types of pectin include chains of apiogalacturonan, homogalacturonan, and xylogalacturonan. There is currently no consensus as to how the pectic polysaccharides are linked to each other, or to other polymers, in the wall. However, it is thought that the different peptides are covalently linked to each other via their backbones, forming a large linear structure with many side branches |CITS: [11423143][12162553][Coenen07]|. In nature, around 80% of the carboxyl groups of the galacturonate units are esterified with |FRAME: METOH|. Some plants, including sugar beet, potatoes and pears, contain pectins with acetylated galacturonate in addition to methyl esters. Partially esterified pectins are often referred to as pectinate, and if the degree of esterification is below 5%, |FRAME: PECTATE|.

This modification is likely to lead to solubilization of the starch 19325165. Starch is a combination of two polymeric carbohydrates (polysaccharides) called |FRAME: Alpha-Amyloses| and |FRAME: CPD-7043|. |FRAME: Alpha-Amyloses| contains up to several thousand alpha-glucosyl units linked almost exclusively in linear alpha(1->4) linkages, with very few branches of alpha(1->6) linkages. In |FRAME: CPD-7043|, on the other hand, branching is common, and occurs approximately every 24-30 glucose monomer units. |FRAME: Alpha-Amyloses| accounts for 30% of starch, while |FRAME: CPD-7043| accounts for the other 70%.

Comment: |FRAME: Compound-0 "Compound 0"|, |FRAME: Compound-I|, and |FRAME: Compound-II| are the names given to intermediate states of the heme-iron center that is formed at the active sites of cytochrome P-450 enzymes and peroxidases during catalysis. I. Cytochrome P-450 In cytochrome P-450 the proximal coordinatioin position of the heme iron, which is bound to the 4 nitrogen atoms of the tetrapyrrole ring, is tethered to the protein via a cysteine thiolate ligand. At its rest state, the iron is found at a low-spin ferric state (III valency). At this state the iron also binds a water molecule as a sixth ligand at the distal axial coordination position. Binding of a substrate to the low-spin ferric enzyme leads to displacement of the water as the sixth ligand and a high spin shift. The substrate-bound complex has a greater reduction potential and more easily accepts a single electron from the redox partner, which can be either |FRAME: EC-1.6.2.4 "a cytochrome P450 reductase"|, |FRAME: Ferredoxins|, or |FRAME: Cytochromes-b5|). After the first reduction, the heme iron binds oxygen, forming an oxy-heme complex. The oxygen is bound at the distal axial coordination position, from which the water molecule has been displaced. Following the transfer of the second electron from the redox partner and two subsequent protonations, a peroxo adduct is formed, known as |FRAME: Compound-0|. Next, the O-O bond is cleaved heterolytically, releasing a water molecule and leaving behind an oxygen atom with only six valence electrons. This highly active oxene oxygen removes one electron from the iron and one from the porphyrin, oxidizing the iron to the unusual valency of IV (ferryl iron) and generating an additional oxidizing equivalent that is delocalized over the porphyrin and thiolate ligands. This ferryl/porphyrin radical cation complex is known as |FRAME: Compound-I| 21071661. When the substrate nears the active site, |FRAME: Compound-I| abstracts an electron from it, converting the substrate into a radical and becoming a protonated non-radical ferryl compound known as |FRAME: Compound-II|. At this point the substrate radical reacts with the oxygen of |FRAME: Compound-II|, forming a new carbon oxygen bond. The product is released, and the iron returns to a valency of III (compound III) OrtizdeMontellano15. II. preoxidases In peroxidases the proximal coordinatioin position of the heme iron, which is bound to the 4 nitrogen atoms of the tetrapyrrole ring, is tethered to the protein via a histidine residue. |FRAME: Compound-I "Compound I"| is produced when the heme iron is oxidized by |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE|. A single one-electron reduction step of |FRAME: Compound-I| from an electron donor substrate yields |FRAME: Compound-II|, followed by a second one-electron transfer that returns the enzyme to the ferric oxidation state, thus completing the catalytic cycle. Each electron transfer event converts a substrate molecule to a radical cation, forming two such radicals during a catalytic cycle. In the presence of high concentrations of |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE| and the absence of a reducing substrate, |FRAME: Compound-II| can be oxidized to |FRAME: Compound-III|, a catalytically inactive form of the enzyme. |FRAME: Compound-III "Compound III"| is converted back to the resting state by spontaneous autoxidation or by oxidation with two molecules of the substrate radical cation 18581264.

While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. Lipopolysaccharides contain three parts: a lipid (|FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|), a |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, and polysaccharide side chains known as the O -antigen. The composition of the O-antigen varies among different strains, but in general it consists of |FRAME: O-Antigen-Repeat-Units "repeating oligosaccharide subunits"| made up of two to eight sugar residues. At least 20 different sugars are known to occur, and many of these sugars are unique dideoxyhexoses that are rarely found elsewhere in nature. The variations in sugar content of the O-antigens contribute to the wide variety of antigenic types between species and even strains of Gram-negative bacteria 12007641. The presence or absence of O chains determines whether the LPS is considered smooth or rough, respectively. In addition, particular sugars in the structure, especially the terminal ones, confer immunological specificity of the O-antigen, in addition to the "smoothness" of the strain.

The cytokinins are structurally diverse, and have been divided into two main types: |FRAME: Adenine-Cytokinins "adenine-type cytokinins"| and |FRAME: Phenylurea-Cytokinins "phenylurea-type cytokinins"|. All the natural cytokinins fall into the first type - phenylurea-type cytokinins are synthetic. The adenine cytokinins are classified further by the configuration of their N6-side chain as isoprenoid or aromatic cytokinins. The most prevalent cytokinins are by far those with an unsaturated isoprenoid side chain, and in particular those with a trans -hydroxylated N6-side chain, such as |FRAME: CPD-4210| and its derivatives.

Compound.name: an aromatic compound
Comment: An aromatic compound contains one or more aromatic rings (an aromatic ring is a planar ring in which every atom must have an occupied p orbital, which overlaps with p orbitals on either side). The pi orbitals of the ring's atoms form a conjugated system and are in resonance, giving increased stability compared to saturated compounds having a similar structure. As a result aromatic rings are very stable and do not break apart easily. The least complex aromatic hydrocarbon is benzene. The name stems from a time when compounds were characterized by their smell rather than their chemical structure. Similar structures in which at least one of the ring's carbon atoms is replaced by one of the heteroatoms oxygen, nitrogen, or sulfur, are called heteroarenes.

Compound.name: a carotenoid
Comment: |FRAME: carotenoids Carotenoids| are isoprenoid pigments in the yellow to red color range. They have conjugated double bond chains of varying length with varying substituents, which determines their light absorption spectrum. They are produced by photosynthetic organisms and some non-photosynthetic fungi and bacteria. Animals, including humans, cannot synthesize carotenoids, although they are an essential source of retinoids and vitamin A. Carotenoids have diverse functions that include participation in photosynthetic light-harvesting complexes, serving as antioxidants, virulence factors, and modulation of membrane function. In photosynthetic organisms carotenoids provide protection against photooxidative stress through energy-dissipation of excess light absorbed by the antenna pigments as well as light-harvest. The prominent |FRAME: CPD1F-119|, as well as |FRAME: CPD1F-130|, are involved in the reduction of cataract and macular degeneration; others are exploited as coloring agents in flowers and fruits to attract pollinators (and in industry as food colorant) and agents of seed dispersal. Carotenoids serve as precursors for the plant growth hormone |FRAME: Abscisic-Acid| and |FRAME: Vitamin-A| (for a succinct review of the applications of carotenoids, see 15012246). In addition, they may be cleaved to |FRAME: Apocarotenoids apocarotenoids|, whose functions include serving as a cofactor for light-sensing proteins, acting as hormones, or acting as antifungals. Carotenoids have been the subject of metabolic pathway engineering studies because microbial carotenoid production is environmentally preferable to chemical synthesis. Over 700 carotenoids have been identified. The two main structural classes of carotenoids are the |FRAME: Carotenes carotenes| and the |FRAME: Xanthophylls xanthophylls|, which are composed of hydrocarbons and oxygenated hydrocarbons, respectively. Most carotenoids have a C40 chain length derived from the symmetric precursor |FRAME: CPD-12321| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6287|). |FRAME: CPD-12321| is derived from |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP|, which is in turn derived from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| and |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5120|). Larger, C50 carotenoids also occur in nature and appear to be derived from the addition of two isoprene units to a C40 carotenoid. Although biosynthetic intermediates and novel bacterial genes involved in C50 carotenoid biosynthesis from |FRAME: CPD1F-114| have been identified and biosynthetic pathways postulated, details of all of the enzyme reactions involved in these pathways remain to be determined (as in |CITS: [20802040] [17008032] [11511870] [11432736]|). Smaller, C30 carotenoids have also been found in plants and microorganisms. In microorganisms they appear to be synthesized by a distinct C30 pathway, whereas in plants they appear to result from cleavage of C40 carotenoids. |FRAME: CPD-9911| is a bacterial C30 carotenoid derived from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP|. It is an intermediate in the biosynthesis of the secondary metabolite |FRAME: CPD-9916| in |FRAME: TAX-1280| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5875|). |FRAME: CPD-9911| has also been identified in a few other bacteria |CITS: [20303609] [9297464]|. Genes encoding the enzymes of carotenoid biosynthesis have been cloned from many plants, cyanobacteria and other microorganisms (|CITS: [20582313][11511870][18535920] [17257797] [17912511][12730708]|. Extensive comparative genomics analysis of microbial carotenoid biosynthetic proteins has shown new phylogenetic and evolutionary patterns of these pigments that had not been found in previous, more limited, analyses 20582313.

Naturally occurring |FRAME: Beta-Lactams "beta-lactam antibiotics"| are classified into several groups according to their chemical structure: In |FRAME: Monolactams monolactams| the beta-lactam ring is not fused to another ring. This class includes compounds such as the |FRAME: Nocardicins nocardicins| 3427723 and the |FRAME: Monobactams monobactams| 3909315. In |FRAME: Penams penams| the beta-lactam ring is fused to a saturated five atom ring (a 4:5 structure). Penams contain a sulfur atom at position 1 of the five atom ring (for example, the |FRAME: PENICILLIN penicillins|) 6335599. Related classes include the |FRAME: Carbapenams carbapenams|, which contain a carbon atom in that position 12890666, and the |FRAME: Clavams oxopenams| (also known as clavams), which contain an oxygen atom at that position (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-9261|) 3304182. |FRAME: Penems Penems| are molecues similar to penams in which the five atom ring is unsaturated at positions 2-3. Similarly, penems contain a sulfur atom at position 1 of the five atom ring, while |FRAME: Carbapenems carbapenems| contains a carbon atom in that position 16413506. In |FRAME: Cephams cephams| and |FRAME: Cephems cephems| the beta-lactam ring is fused to a six-atom ring (a 4:6 strcuture) that contains a sulfur atom at position 1. In cephams the ring is saturated, while cephems have an unsaturated bond at positions 3-4 |CITS: [1164170][12722308]|. 1-Oxocephams/1-oxacephems conain an oxygen atom at position 1 |CITS: [11671696][11078187]|.

Compound.name: acetoin
Comment: Acetoin, along with diacetyl, is one of the compounds that gives butter its characteristic taste. It is natuarally found in apples, butter, yogurt, asparagus, black currants, blackberry, wheat, broccoli, brussels sprouts, and cantaloupe. Acetoin is a common fermentation product, since it is a neutral compound that allows bacteria to degrade sugars without substantial acidification of the growth medium. Many bacteria can grow on acetoin, some of which degrade it to acetaldehyde and acetyl-CoA 8110297.

Compound.name: a glycoprotein
Comment: Glycoproteins are proteins that have been modified by the attachment of a glycan (carbohydrate) moiety. This process is known as "protein glycosylation". The most common forms of protein glycosylation include: N -linked glycosylation, where the glycan is attached to a nitrogen of asparagine or arginine side-chains. O -linked glycosylation, where the glycan is attached to the hydroxyl oxygen of serine, threonine, tyrosine, hydroxylysine, or hydroxyproline side-chains. Other, less common, forms of protein glycosylation include phosphoglycans, in which the glycan is linked through the phosphate of a phosphoserine, and C-linked glycans, where the glycan is attached to a carbon on a tryptophan side-chain. A special form of protein glycosylation is glypiation, in which a protein is attached to a lipid anchor via a glycan chain.

Comment: Vitamin D refers to a group of fat-soluble secosteroids responsible for enhancing intestinal absorption of calcium, iron, magnesium, phosphate and zinc. In humans, the most important compounds in this group are |FRAME: VITAMIN_D3| (cholecalciferol), which is produced in animal skin from |FRAME: CPD-4187| after exposure to |FRAME: UV-Light| and |FRAME: Heat|, and |FRAME: VITAMIN_D2| (ergocalciferol), which is produced in plants and fungi from |FRAME: ERGOSTEROL| after exposure to |FRAME: UV-Light|. In its activated form, |FRAME: VITAMIN_D3| is necessary for optimal absorption and regulation of dietary |FRAME: CA+2| and |FRAME: Pi|. This nutrient is essential for the prevention of rickets, a bone-softening disease (reviewed in |CITS: [15585789][15951480][16563471]|). There is controversy in the literature as to whether supplemental |FRAME: VITAMIN_D2| is as effective as |FRAME: VITAMIN_D3| in maintaining circulating levels of the |FRAME: CALCIDIOL| vitamin D metabolite |CITS: [17023693][18089691]|. The production of vitamin D analogs is n active area of research (reviewed in 15544953.

Compound.name: a quinone
Comment: Quinones are organic compounds derived from aromatic compounds, with two carbonyl groups incorporated into the ring structure with rearrangement of the double bonds where necessary. Quinones are conjugated but not aromatic. A classic example of a quinone is |FRAME: P-BENZOQUINONE|. Quinones are commonly named with a prefix that indicates the parent aromatic hydrocarbon (for example, "benzo-" for benzene, "naphtho-" for naphthalene, and "anthra-" for anthracene) with a "-quinone" suffix. Several types of quinones serve as electron acceptors in electron transport chains. Those quinones are usually prenylated with a lipid-soluble isoprenyl tail that anchors them in the membrane lipid bilayer. Quinones can carry two electrons, and when fully reduced they are referred to as |FRAME: Reduced-Quinones quinols|. The addition of a single H atom to a quinone results in formation of a free radical called |FRAME: Semiquinones|. Many quinone derivatives often have other biological activities, such as |FRAME: CPD-11501 "vitamin K"|.

Compound.name: a lipid A
Comment: Lipid A is a lipid component of the |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides "lipopolysaccharides"| (LPS) of Gram-negative bacteria. Its hydrophobic nature allows it to anchor the LPS to the outer membrane. Lipid A consists of two glucosamine units attached by a beta(1->6) linkage and decorated with four to seven acyl chains and one or two phosphate groups. Up to four acyl chains, often with a beta hydroxy group and usually 10 to 18 carbons in length, are attached directly to the glucosamine sugars at positions N-2 and O-3 (and N'-2 and O'-3, respectively), while additional acyl chains are attached to the beta hydroxy groups of some of those primary acyl chains. Phosphate groups can be attached at position O-1, O'-4, or both. Many variations are found in the structures of lipid A molecules. Further modifications are commonly observed, such as the addition or removal of phosphate groups (see |FRAME: EC-2.7.4.29|, |FRAME: EC-3.1.3.M9|, and |FRAME: EC-3.1.3.M11|), the addition of |FRAME: PHOSPHORYL-ETHANOLAMINE| (see |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.43|, |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.42|, and |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.M9|), the addition of |FRAME: 4-AMINO-4-DEOXY-L-ARABINOSE| units (see |FRAME: EC-2.4.2.43|), and further addition or removal of fatty acyl units (see |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.251| and |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.77|). Many bacterial species produce lipid A molecules that contain |FRAME: CPD-24440| (see |FRAME: PWY-8273|). Since the fully acylated lipid A is assembled only when attached to the core oligosaccharide, a "stand alone" lipid A, as depicted here, does not occur naturally.

Compound.name: a glyco-amino acid
Comment: The glycation reaction, also known as the Maillard reaction, as first identified by the French chemist L. Maillard, is ubiquitous in nature. The reaction involves the formation of Schiff's bases between reducing sugars (such as glucose) and biological amines such as an amino acid, which then rearrange to form stable ketoamine products, or amadori compounds.

Compound.name: a stephacidin
Comment: Stephacidin A and B are indole alkalids isolated from |FRAME: TAX-40380| that exhibit in vitro cytotoxicity against a number of human tumor cell lines 12465964. The stephacidins belong to a diverse family of biologically active prenylated indole alkaloids isolated mainly from various |FRAME: TAX-5073| and |FRAME: TAX-5052| species of fungi that contains a unique bicyclo[2.2.2]diazaoctane core ring system, and are derived from |FRAME: TRP|, a cyclic amino acid (|FRAME: PRO|, |FRAME: L-PIPECOLATE| or a derivative of one of those compounds), and one or two isoprene units. In addition to their structural diversity, members of this family have been attributed a variety of bioactivities, including (but not limited to) insecticidal, cytotoxic, anthelmintic, and antibacterial properties. The bicyclo[2.2.2]diazaoctane-containing compounds can be divided into two sub-categories: the diketopiperazines (DKPs) and the monoketopiperazines (MKPs). DKPs include the |FRAME: Stephacidins stephacidins|, |FRAME: Brevianamides brevianamides|, and |FRAME: Notoamides notoamides|, while MKPs include the |FRAME: Paraherquamides paraherquamides|, |FRAME: Asperparalines asperparalines|, |FRAME: Marcfortines marcfortines|, |FRAME: Chrysogenamides chrysogenamides|,and |FRAME: Malbrancheamides malbrancheamides|.

Compound.name: a galactoglucomannan
Comment: |FRAME: Glucomannans Glucomannans| (GM) and |FRAME: Galactoglucomannans galactoglucomannans| (GGM) are the major hemicellulosic components of the secondary cell walls of softwoods, but occur only in minor amounts in the secondary cell walls of hardwoods. Both polymers consist of a bakbone composed of beta(1->4)-linked glucopyranose and mannopyranose residues. GGM chains are substituted by galactopyranose residues and are often branched. Both polymers show some variations in structural features depending on the plant species and stage of plant development Ebringerova05. The mannan backbone of GGM from spruce wood consists of galactose, glucose, and mannose in the mole ratio 1 : 8 : 33, and contains segments of more than four mannopyranose residues, interrupted with a segment composed of both mannopyranose and glucopyranose, or two glucopyranose residues. Branches terminated by single galactose residues are attached at positions 2, 3, and 6 of mannose residues and at positions 3 and 6 of glucose residues of the backbone. Many of the mannose residues are acetylated at positions 2 and 3 11128591. The extent of GGM galactosylation governs its association tendency to the cellulose microfibrils Ebringerova05.

Compound.name: an anthracycline
Comment: Anthracyclines are a class of antibiotics produced by |FRAME: TAX-1883| bacteria that are used in cancer as chemotherapy drugs. This group of antibiotics is defined by the presence of a four fused-ring aromatic system, based on a 7,8,9,10-tetrahydro-5,12-naphthacenequinone framework, which usually occurs as a glycoside with a deoxy(amino)sugar. The framework is synthesized by a polyketide-synthase from an acetyl-CoA or propanoyl-CoA starter unit and malonyl-CoA extender units, and subsequently modified by other enzymes 11851469. The anthracyclines intercalate between base pairs of the DNA/RNA strand, inhibit topoisomerase II enzymes, and prevent DNA replication. They are among the most effective anticancer treatments ever developed and are effective against more types of cancer than any other class of chemotherapeutic agents.

Compound.name: jadomycin A
Comment: The jadomycins are a unique family of angucycline-derived antibiotics. Jadomycin A is produced by the organism |FRAME: TAX-953739| under stress conditions such as heat shock, phage infection, and particularly ethanol treatment. This compound is bioactive against Gram-positive (including the methicillin-resistant TAX-1280) and Gram-negative bacteria, but unlike |FRAME: Jadomycin-B|, it is not active against yeast 8514643. The difference between the two compounds is that |FRAME: Jadomycin-B| includes an |FRAME: CPD-11914| moiety 11932454. Jadomycin A exists as a diastereomeric mixture of |FRAME: CPD-12938| and |FRAME: CPD-21699| 7764672, with the former being the predominant form at a ratio of 10:1. The two forms can interconvert via an aldehyde intermediate 16468745.

Compound.name: a phenolphthiocerol
Comment: |FRAME: Phthiocerols Phthiocerol|-based lipids and glycolipids have been found in many species of |FRAME: TAX-1762|, including |FRAME: TAX-1773|, |FRAME: TAX-1765|, |FRAME: TAX-33894|, |FRAME: TAX-1781|, |FRAME: TAX-1768|, |FRAME: TAX-1777|, |FRAME: TAX-1769| and |FRAME: TAX-1809| 3149973. Phthiocerols comprise a linear carbohydrate molecule to which one methoxyl group, one methyl group, and two secondary hydroxyl groups are attached. Two types of phthiocerols have been described. In |FRAME: Phthiocerol-A "phthiocerol A"| the methoxyl and methyl groups are attached at positions 3 and 4, respectively, and the hydroxyl groups are at positions 9 and 11. In |FRAME: Phthiocerol-B "phthiocerol B"| a methyl group is missing from the beginning of the molecule, and thus the methoxyl and methyl groups are attached at positions 2 and 3, respectively, and the hydroxyl groups are at positions 8 and 10. The two hydroxyl groups serve as attachment points for fatty acids, in a manner analogous to the much more ubiquitous sn -glycerol. The phthiocerol molecules have a range of 28 to 34 carbon atoms in the main chain, indicating a promiscuity of the enzymes involved in their biosynthesis. Longer molecules have additional carbon atoms added at the ω end of the molecule. Many organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-1769|, |FRAME: TAX-1768|, |FRAME: TAX-1765|, |FRAME: TAX-1781|, and |FRAME: TAX-78331|, produce the related compound |FRAME: Phenolphthiocerols phenolphthiocerol|, which contains a phenol group at the ω end of the molecule 3113946. The phenol is usually glycosylated by a type or species-specific mono-, tri-, or a tetrasaccharide. For example, in |FRAME: TAX-78331| the trisaccharide (2,3,4-tri- O -methyl L-fucopyranosyl-(alpha1->3)-rhamnopyranosyl-(alpha1->3)-2- O -methyl L-rhamnopyranose) is attached. In addition, the two secondary alcohol functions are often esterified by |FRAME: Mycocerosic-Acids "mycocerosic acids"| or |FRAME: Phthioceranic-Acids "phthioceranic acids"| (see |FRAME: CPD-18579|) 3113946.

Compound.name: a carbapenem
Comment: This compound class stands for |FRAME: Lactams lactams| in which the amide bond is contained within a four-membered ring, which includes the amide nitrogen and the carbonyl carbon. beta-Lactam compounds imitate the naturally occurring |FRAME: D-ALA-D-ALA| substrate for the group of enzymes known as penicillin binding proteins (PBPs), which cross-link the peptidoglycan in bacterial cell wall, and thus act as powerful antibiotics 6109324. Naturally occurring |FRAME: Beta-Lactams "beta-lactam antibiotics"| are classified into several groups according to their chemical structure: In |FRAME: Monolactams monolactams| the beta-lactam ring is not fused to another ring. This class includes compounds such as the |FRAME: Nocardicins nocardicins| 3427723 and the |FRAME: Monobactams monobactams| 3909315. In |FRAME: Penams penams| the beta-lactam ring is fused to a saturated five atom ring (a 4:5 structure). Penams contain a sulfur atom at position 1 of the five atom ring (for example, the |FRAME: PENICILLIN penicillins|) 6335599. Related classes include the |FRAME: Carbapenams carbapenams|, which contain a carbon atom in that position 12890666, and the |FRAME: Clavams oxopenams| (also known as clavams), which contain an oxygen atom at that position (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-9261|) 3304182. |FRAME: Penems Penems| are molecues similar to penams in which the five atom ring is unsaturated at positions 2-3. Similarly, penems contain a sulfur atom at position 1 of the five atom ring, while |FRAME: Carbapenems carbapenems| contains a carbon atom in that position 16413506. In |FRAME: Cephams cephams| and |FRAME: Cephems cephems| the beta-lactam ring is fused to a six-atom ring (a 4:6 strcuture) that contains a sulfur atom at position 1. In cephams the ring is saturated, while cephems have an unsaturated bond at positions 3-4 |CITS: [1164170][12722308]|. 1-Oxocephams/1-oxacephems conain an oxygen atom at position 1 |CITS: [11671696][11078187]|.

The lipid portion is embedded in the outer plasma membrane leaflet and the sugar chains extended to the outer environment, acting as an antigen. Glycosphingolipids are synthesized by the sequential addition of sugar residues to ceramide by glycosyltransferases that are specific to each glycosidic linkage. Glycoshphingolipids have been classified into the following 12 series based on their structure: |FRAME: Arthro-Series-GSLs arthro|, |FRAME: Gala-Series-GSLs gala|, |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs ganglio|, |FRAME: Globo-Series-GSLs globo|, |FRAME: Isoglobo-Series-GSLs isoglobo|, |FRAME: Lacto-Series-GSLs lacto|, |FRAME: Muco-Series-GSLs muco|, |FRAME: Mollu-Series-GSLs mollu|, |FRAME: Neogala-Series-GSLs neogala|, |FRAME: Neolacto-Series-GSLs neolacto|, |FRAME: Schisto-Series-GSLs schisto| and |FRAME: Spirometo-Series-GSLs spirometo| 25969757. |FRAME: Lactosyl-Ceramides Lactosylceramide| is an important branching point, being a common precursor for the synthesis of the four major classes of glycosphingolipids: the |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs "ganglio series"|, the |FRAME: Lacto-Series-GSLs "lacto series"|, the |FRAME: Neolacto-Series-GSLs "neolacto series"|, and the |FRAME: Globo-Series-GSLs "globo series"| 10320813. The core structure that defines the |FRAME: Globo-Series-GSLs "globo series"| is GalNAcbeta(1,3)Galalpha(1,4)Galbeta(1,4)Glcbeta-Cer. Compound.name: a dolichyl diphosphate
Comment: |FRAME: DOLICHOL "Dolichol"| is the name given to a family of long-chain polyprenols that contain a varying number of cis -linked isoprene units, terminating with three trans -linked isoprene units. The first (alpha) unit in dolichols is always saturated 11442630. Additional modifications are found. For example, dolichols from certain halobacteria contain an additional saturation in the terminal (omega) isoprene unit. The length of dolichol molecules varies within a range in a species, and the range varies among species (reviewed in 9878760). In mammals dolichols are usually within the range of 80 to 105 carbons. Archaebacteria prefer dolichols of 55-60 carbons. |FRAME: DOLICHOLP "Dolichyl phosphate"| acts as a membrane-bound carrier in the assembly of pyrophosphate-linked oligosaccharides. It can accept the respective sugar residues from the donors |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE|, |FRAME: CPD-12575| and |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE|. When the complete oligosaccharide is transferred to a protein L-asparagine residue, |FRAME: Dolichol-PP| is produced. It can be converted back to |FRAME: DOLICHOLP| by |FRAME: EC-3.6.1.43|. The structure shown here is of a C80 dolichol diphosphate, containing 16 isoprene units.

Compound.name: a medium chain fatty acid
Comment: The term "fatty acid" was originally coined to describe aliphatic monocarboxylic acids derived from or contained in esterified form in an animal or vegetable fat, oil or wax. However, over the years the term has been expanded to refer to additional, shorter monocarboxylic acids with an aliphatic tail such as |FRAME: PROPIONATE| and |FRAME: BUTYRIC_ACID| (but not the shorter |FRAME: FORMATE| and |FRAME: ACET|). The length of a fatty acid is determined by the length of the longest carbon chain, including the carbon of the carboxy group. Common natural fatty acids usually have an even number of carbons in the longest chain and can be either saturated or unsaturated. In many organisms they are often modified by branching, hydroxylation, methylation, epoxidation and other types of modifications. Inside living cells fatty acids are rarely found in free form. They are usually bound to coenzyme A or acyl-carrier proteins, or form part of |FRAME: Triacylglycerides triglycerides|, |FRAME: Phospholipids phospholipids|, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharides|, and |FRAME: Cholesterol-esters cholesterol esters|. Many enzymes that act on fatty acids, as well as the corresponding |FRAME: Fatty-Acyl-CoAs "fatty acyl-CoAs"|, alcohols, and aldehydes, have evolved to recognize substrates with a limited range of chain lengths. To classify these enzymes, it is helpful to divide the substrates into smaller groups based on their chain length. The following subgroups have been defined: |FRAME: Short-chain-fatty-acids "Short-chain fatty acids"| (SCFA) have 3-5 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Medium-chain-fatty-acids "Medium-chain fatty acids"| (MCFA) have 6-12 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Long-Chain-Fatty-Acids "Long-chain fatty acids"| (LCFA) have 13-22 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Very-long-chain-fatty-acids "Very-long-chain fatty acids"| (VLCFA) have 23-27 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Ultra-long-chain-fatty-acids "Ultra-long-chain fatty acids"| (ULCFA) have more than 27 carbons in the longest chain. Most of the natural fatty acids have an even number of carbon atoms, since their biosynthesis involves the addition of two-carbon-atom units. When a fatty acid contains only single bonds, it is referred to as |FRAME: Saturated-Fatty-Acids|. When it contains one or more double bonds, it is referred to as |FRAME: Unsaturated-Fatty-Acids|. If it contains a double bond in the trans configuration, it is often referred to as a trans fatty acid. Most fatty acids in the trans configuration are not found in nature and are the result of human processing.

During the catalytic cycle, TTQ mediates electron transfer from substrate to a copper protein, amicyanin. These electrons are transferred to the respiratory chain via a c-type cytochrome 10721104.

The basic units of |FRAME: Carrageenans carrageenans| are repeats of alpha-1,3 linked D-galactose and beta-1,4- linked D-galactose units, which are substituted by sulfate. Different types of carrageenans have sulfate groups at different positions 1367970. In |FRAME: Carrageenoses carrageenoses| the alpha-1,3-linked galactose units are modified by having a 3,6-anhydro bridge. These bridges are responsible for the gelation that is typical to these compounds, by forming a double helix during the process. |FRAME: nu-Carrageenan| is sulfated at position 4 of the beta-1,4 linked D-galactose units and positions 2 and 6 of the alpha-1,3-linked galactose units.

Compound.name: a polyunsaturated fatty acid
Comment: |FRAME: Fatty-Acids "A fatty acid"| is a carboxylic acid with a long unbranched aliphatic tail. Even though fatty acids derived from natural fats and oils, such as CPD-195, are usually at least 8 carbon atoms long, carboxylic acids as short as BUTYRIC_ACID (4 carbon atoms) are considered to be fatty acids. When a fatty acid contains only single bonds, it is referred to as |FRAME: Saturated-Fatty-Acids|. When it contains one or more double bonds, it is referred to as |FRAME: Unsaturated-Fatty-Acids|. |FRAME: Polyunsaturated-fatty-acids "Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs)"| are fatty acids that contain more than one double bond in their backbone. This class includes many important compounds, such as essential fatty acids and those that give drying oils their characteristic property. About nomenclature : Several nomenclatures are used for unsaturated fatty acids, and are not complementary. Systematic names (or IUPAC names) begin counting the carbon atoms from the carboxylic acid end, and the double bonds are labeled with cis / trans or (preferably) E/Z notation, e.g. (8 E ,10 E ,12 Z )-octadeca-8,10,12-trienoate. However, unsaturated fatty acids are often described using the omega nomenclature, which begins counting the carbon atoms from the terminal methyl carbon (designated as n or ω). In addition, unsaturated fatty acids are often referred to by trivial names, or by the "lipid number" as in 18:3, where 18 is the number of carbons, and 3 is the number of double bonds. This notation is ambiguous, as it does not specify the location of the double bonds.

Compound.name: a glycosaminoglycan
Comment: Glycosaminoglycans (also known as mucopolysaccharides) are important components of connective tissues. They are composed of long unbranched polysaccharides consisting of a repeating disaccharide unit. The repeating units consist of an N -acetyl-hexosamine and a hexose or hexuronic acid, either or both of which are often sulfated. Members of the glycosaminoglycan family vary in the type of hexosamine, hexose or hexuronic acid unit they contain (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-12521|, |FRAME: CPD-12515|, galactose, CPD-12557, |FRAME: CPD-12541|). Glycosaminoglycans are divided into four main classes: |FRAME: Chondroitin-sulfates| and |FRAME: Dermatan-Sulfate|; |FRAME: HEPARIN| and |FRAME: Heparan-Sulfate|; |FRAME: Hyaluronan|; and |FRAME: KERATAN-6-SULFATE "keratan sulfate"|. With the exception of hyaluronan, the polysaccharide chains are linked covalently at the reducing end to a core protein through an O -glycosidic linkage to a serine residue. The modified proteins are known as |FRAME: Proteoglycans proteoglycans|. Most glycosaminoglycans are attached via a specific tetrasaccharide known as the |FRAME: GlcA-Gal-Gal-Xyl-Proteins "glycosaminoglycan-protein linkage region"|.

Compound.name: an a-series ganglioside
Comment: | About the nomenclature of gangliosides Ganglioside naming is somewhat complex. Two ganglioside nomenclature systems are currently in use. The most commonly used is a short-hand nomenclature suggested by Svennerholm, which was initially based on the migration order of |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs "ganglio-series"| gangliosides in chromatography 14066623. The more comprehensive system formulated by IUPAC 9826173 is applied much less frequently. A typical ganglioside name using the old system looks like |FRAME: Ganglioside-GQ1b "ganglioside GQ1b"|. The first letter refers to the glycosphingolipid series. For example, the "G" stands for the |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs "ganglio series"|. The next letter describes the number of sialic acid residues: (A = 0, M =1, D = 2, T = 3, Q = 4, P = 5, H = 6, S = 7). The following number describes the number of the non-sialic residues, and is derived in a rather complex manner. It was initially assumed that the number of such residues does not exceed 5. The number in the name was calculated as (5 - the number of uncharged carbohydrates). In addition, several sub-series of gangliosides have been defined based on the number of sialic acids attached to the galactose residue of the lacosylceramide core. If no sialic residues are present at that position, the compounds belong to the |FRAME: 0-Series-Ganglioside "0-series |. Those with one sialic acid at that position are named the |FRAME: A-Series-Gangliosides a-series |, those with two sialic acids belong to the |FRAME: B-Series-Gangliosides b-series |, and so on. |FRAME: C-Series-Gangliosides "C-series"| or higher gangliosides are rare in adult mammals and birds, but are abundant in fish and amphibians. Confusingly, GM1b and GD1c are both 0-series gangliosides, despite having a b and c in their names. So, for example, the |FRAME: Ganglioside-GQ1b "ganglioside GQ1b"| is named as follows: G = belongs to the ganglio series, Q = 4 sialic acids, 1 = 4 non-sialic residues, and b = belongs to the b-series, meaning two of the sialic acids are attached to the inner galactose.

Compound.name: a mannosylerythritol lipid
Comment: |FRAME: CPD-25639 "Mannosylerythritol lipids"| (MELs) are amphiphilic glycolipids that display high surface activity and act as biodetergents (biosurfactants). The compounds are produced by yeast strains that belong to the |FRAME: TAX-5269| and |FRAME: TAX-63261| genera. They show excellent surface-active properties and versatile biochemical actions. The compounds were first described in 1956 from an |FRAME: TAX-5269| species 13276861. However, the most common MEL producing species are members of the |FRAME: TAX-63261| genus, such as |FRAME: TAX-84753|, |FRAME: TAX-84754|, |FRAME: TAX-84752|, and |FRAME: TAX-203536| 25723622. The lipids are acylated at positions O-2' and O-3' by a range of fatty acyl residues. In |FRAME: TAX-5270| the fatty acid at O-2' ranges from C2 to C6, while that at O-3' ranges from C12 to C16. In addition, MELs differ in their acetylation status. Four general types are produced differing in the acetylation of positions O-4' and O-6'. Mel-D has no acetylation, MEL-B is acetylated only at the O-6' position, MEL-C is acetylated only at the O-4' position, and MEL-A is acetylated at both positions |CITS: [Kitamoto90a][Kitamoto90][10570818][17898510]|. The biological function of MELs is still unknown, but they are of growing biotechnological interest as a sustainable alternative for chemical surfactants |CITS: [18585066][22901730]|.

Compound.name: a plastoquinol
Comment: Plastoquinones are found in the chloroplasts of higher plants, red, brown and green algae, and in cyanobacteria, and are important members of the photosynthetic electron transfer chain, where they carry electrons from |FRAME: CPLX490-3506| to the |FRAME: CPLX-9022|. In fact, it has been shown that in cyanobacteria essentially all electron transport through unbound quinones proceeds via PQ in cyanobacterial thylakoids. Apart from PQ the only quinone found in thylakoids is vitamin K1, which is associated with PS I Vermaas01. Plastoquinones also serve as cofactors involved in the desaturation of phytoene in the synthesis of carotenoids (see |FRAME: PWY-6475|). They are analogs of |FRAME: Ubiquinones "ubiquinones"| (Coenzyme Q), with two methyl groups substituting the methoxy groups found in Q. Plastoquinone can function as acceptor/donor for one or two electrons. The fully reduced form is called |FRAME: Plastoquinols|. Plastoquinone was isolated originally in 1946 from alfalfa, but was not identified at the time. It was rediscovered in 1959 and its structure was described in the same year (see 7022156). Please note that the structure shown here is that of |FRAME: CPD-12829| and is not accurate for this generic class of compounds, which contains plastoquinols with different side-chain lengths.

Compound.name: an E vitamin

Structurally tocotrienols and tocopherols differ only in the degree of unsaturation of their side-chain. The tocotrienol chain comprises three trans -double bonds, whereas the tocopherol chain is fully saturated. In addition, the alpha, beta, gamma, and delta species of both compound groups vary in the methylation pattern of the chromanol ring 12897790. Vitamin E compounds are synthesized only by photosynthetic organisms, although they are essential dietary components for animals (including humans), where they act primarily as antioxidants. Their presumed role in plants involve protection of chloroplast lipids and chlorophylls against oxidative damages. The tocotrienols are mostly found in monocots Padley94 and a few dicots 17110122, whereas tocopherols are wider spread in the plant kingdom and dominate in the dicots 8827691.

They are used to treat tuberculosis, leprosy, and mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) infections. Compound.name: a galactomannan
Comment: Mannans are polymers composed of beta(1->4)-linked |FRAME: MANNOSE| residues. Pure mannans are rarely found, and most contain alpha(1,6)-linked galactopyranosyl side chains. The extent of galactosylation varies greatly, and the mannose : galactose ratio is one of the main characteristics of the polymer as it determines their physicochemical properties, such as solubility in water, density, and the viscosity of the solution Ebringerova05. On one hand, slightly galactosylated linear mannans (about 4% galactose), have been isolated from the seed endosperm of vegetable ivory nut (|FRAME: TAX-115507|) and date (|FRAME: TAX-42345|). They are water-insoluble, resemble cellulose in conformation of the individual molecular chains, and occur in cellulose microfibrils of the plant tissues Reid95. On the other hand, heavily galactosylated polymers (up to 96%) are abundant in the cell walls of storage tissues (endosperm, cotyledons, perisperm) of many seeds. Those from the endosperm of some leguminous seeds, such as guar (|FRAME: TAX-3832|), locust bean or carob (|FRAME: TAX-20340|), and tara gum (|FRAME: TAX-191904|), are widely used commercially Reid95. Another important feature is the distribution of the galactopyranose residues along the mannan backbone, which affects the molecular interactions of the chains among themselves (self-association) and with other polysaccharides (cooperative associations) in solution Ebringerova05.

Compound.name: an I antigen
Synonyms: an N -acetyl-beta-D-galactosyl-1,4-[beta-D-galactosyl-1,4- N -acetyl-beta-D-glucosyl-1,6]- N -acetyl-beta-D-glucosaminyl-1,3-beta-D-galactosyl-1,4- N -acetyl-D-glucosaminyl-[glycoprotein] // an N -acetyl-beta-D-galactosyl-(1,4)-[beta-D-galactosyl-(1,4)- N -acetyl-beta-D-glucosyl-(1,6)]- N -acetyl-beta-D-glucosaminyl-(1,3)-beta-D-galactosyl-(1,4)- N -acetyl-beta-D-glucosaminyl-R // an I histo-blood group antigen // a beta-D-Gal-(1->4)-beta-D-GlcNAc-(1->3)-[beta-D-Gal-(11->4)-beta-D-GlcNAc-(1->6)]-beta-D-Gal-(1->4)-beta-D-GlcNAc-R
Comment: The |FRAME: Lower-case-i-Antigens "i antigen"| is found on membrane proteins in red blood cells and many other cell types as well as various body secretions of developing fetuses and newborn infants |CITS: [13767181][4971635]|, while the |FRAME: Upper-case-I-antigens "I antigen"| is found in all adults 13292836. The i antigen undergoes gradual conversion to the I antigen in newborn infants, a process that completes in about 18 months. Both antigens are based entirely on Type 2 (|FRAME: BETA-D-GALACTOSYL-ETCETERA-GLUCOSAMINE " N -acetyllactosamine"|) chains. The basic i structure is an unbranched polylactosamine comprising at least two N - acetyllactosamine units connected by a beta(1->3) linkage |CITS: [823020][22356451]|. The crucial step in the transition from the i antigen to the I antigen is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.150|, also known as the I-branching enzyme, which introduces the branching by adding a GlcNAc residue by a beta(1->6) linkage to the galactose residue to which other residues are already attached by a 1,3 linkage 6490658. Note that the structure shown here is the core structure that defines I antigenicity. Most I antigens are further glycosylated. (Reviewed in Daniels13).

Compound.name: a thiazoline siderophore
Comment: Siderophores are small, high-affinity iron chelating compounds usually produced and secreted by microorganisms. Once outside the cell, siderophores bind |FRAME: FE+3| with high affinity, and the iron-siderophore complexes are imported back into the cell by active-transport mechanisms. Siderophores are very common in pathogenic bacteria, since iron in the host organism is usually tightly bound to proteins, resulting in an extremely low concentration of free iron in the blood. Most siderophores belong to one of three major groups: the |FRAME: Catecholate-siderophores "catechols"|, |FRAME: Hydroxamate-siderophores "hydroxamates"| and |FRAME: Thiazoline-siderophores "thiazolines"|. Some grasses are known to make siderophores as well. These |FRAME: Phytosiderophores "phytosiderophores"| are also known as mugineic acids. Thiazoline siderophores are named based on the presence of a thiazoline (5-membered heterocyclic compound containing both sulfur and nitrogen in the ring) element in their structures.

Compound.name: an N -linked glycoprotein
