In most cases, each of these compounds mutarotates quickly to form a mixture of the two, and thus it is the general rule to use this non-specific form in reactions unless it is specifically known that an enzyme can accept only one of the forms.

Compound.name: a [lipoyl-carrier protein]- N 6 -[( R )-lipoyl]-L-lysine
Synonyms: protein N6-(lipoyl)lysine // lipoyl-domain // a lipoylated protein lipoyl-domain // an [enzyme] N 6 -(lipoyl)lysine // an enzyme N 6 -(lipoyl)lysine
Comment: |FRAME: LIPOIC-ACID "Lipoate"| is an organosulfur compound that is used as an essential cofactor by many enzyme complexes. The functional group of lipoate is a ditholane ring, which is a cyclic disulfide. The enzyme complexes that require lipoate have a dedicated |FRAME: Lipoyl-Protein "lipoyl domain"|, and lipoate is actually produced on this domain. The precursor |FRAME: CPD-195| molecule is first attached to a specific |FRAME: LYS| residue within the lipoyl domain (producing |FRAME: Octanoylated-domains|), and is then converted to lipoate by the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX0-782|, resulting in |FRAME: Lipoyl-Protein-N6-lipoyllysine|. |FRAME: CPLX0-782 "Lipoate synthase"| not only catalyzes the reaction, but is also the source of the two sulfur atoms.

Compound.name: cellulose
Comment: Cellulose is the most common organic compound on Earth. It is a polysaccharide consisting of a linear chain of several hundred to over ten thousand beta(1->4) linked D-glucose units, and is the structural component of the primary cell wall of green plants, many forms of algae and the oomycetes. Cellulose is a straight chain polymer. Unlike |FRAME: Starch starch| or |FRAME: Glycogens glycogen|, there is no coiling or branching, and the molecule adopts an extended and stiff rod-like conformation. The multiple hydroxyl groups on the glucose moieties from one chain form hydrogen bonds with oxygen atoms on neighbor chains, holding the chains firmly together side-by-side and forming microfibrils with high tensile strength. Several different crystalline structures of cellulose are known, corresponding to the location of hydrogen bonds between and within strands. Known crystalline forms are named cellulose I, cellulose II, cellulose III and cellulose IV. Cellulose I is further divided into Ialpha and Ibeta, with the former formed by bacteria and algae and the latter by higher plants. Crystalline cellulose is not soluble. It is converted to a soluble, amorphus structure only at a temperature of 320 °C. Molecules with very small chain length, known as |FRAME: Cellodextrins cellodextrins|, are typically soluble in water and organic solvents.

Compound.name: naringenin
Comment: |FRAME: NARINGENIN-CMPD| is a flavanone that is abundant in citrus fruit, where it mainly occurs as glycosides such as |FRAME: NARINGENIN-7-O-BETA-D-GLUCOSIDE| (naringenin-7-glucoside), |FRAME: NARINGIN| (the predominant flavanone in grapefruit), or |FRAME: CPD-7059|. It is also present in tomato. The naringenin and its glycosides content undergoes significant changes upon phytopathogen attack, and thus it appears that these compounds participate in the defense mechanism of TAX-2706 species and may act as fungicides 15053528. |FRAME: NARINGIN Naringin| has been investigated with respect to its ability to scavenge oxygen free radicals involved in the oxidation of hemoglobin 12967034, lowering the plasma total cholesterol level 14738906 and blocking the cytotoxity and apoptosis of |FRAME: CPD-15099| (Ara-C), a chemotherapeutical drug used for acute leukemia 15135655. The bitterness of certain citrus species such as grapefruit (TAX-37656), bitter orange (TAX-43166) and pummelo (TAX-37334) is caused by flavanone neohesperidosides such as naringin, in which a rhamnose is attached via the C-2 hydroxyl group of glucose. Flavanone rutinosides such as |FRAME: CPD-7059|, in which the L-rhamnose attached to the C-6 hydroxyl group of the glucose moiety, are tasteless and occur predominantly in sweet citrus fruits such as orange (TAX-2711) and mandarin ( Citrus reticulata ) 15361143. |FRAME: CPD-14042| is not found in nature, and is only formed by chemical synthesis.

Compound.name: a maltodextrin
Comment: Maltodextrins are linear polymers of glucose molecules joined by an O -glycosidic (alpha-1->4) bond. The term is usally used to describe a mixture of chains that vary from 3-17 glucose units long. Maltodextrin is commonly used as a food additive, and is commercially produced from corn and wheat |FRAME: Starch| by partial hydrolysis.

Compound.name: an O -linked mannose glycan
Comment: O-Linked mannose glycans are initiated by covalent linkage of mannose to the hydroxyl oxygen of a serine or threonine amino acid residue. O-Mannose may then be extended by the addition of other monosaccharides and functional groups to form a variety of glycan structures.

Compound.name: a Lewis b epitope
Synonyms: an Le b antigen // a Lewis b antigen // a histo-blood group Lewis b antigen

Compound.name: a glucosylceramide
Synonyms: a glucocerebroside // a D-glucosylceramide // a glucosyl cerebroside // a GlcCer // a glucosyl ceramide
Comment: Cerebrosides consist of |FRAME: Ceramides| with a single sugar residue at the 1-hydroxyl moiety. The sugar residue can be either glucose or galactose, and the two major types are thus named |FRAME: Glucosyl-ceramides glucocerebrosides| and |FRAME: D-galactosylceramide galactocerebrosides|. Galactocerebrosides are typically found in neural tissue, while glucocerebrosides are found in other tissues. Based on the notation GlcCer(m:n)-p used to name subclasses of glucosylceramides, the total number of carbons present in the sphingoid base and the fatty amide is "m" while the total number of double bonds is "n." The total number of hydroxyl groups (not including the hydroxyl group used as the site of the head group attachment) is "p." The length, hydroxylation position, double bond position, and double bond orientation of the groups attached at R1 and R2 will differ between individual members of this group of compounds.

Compound.name: a 1,2-diacyl-3-(6-sulfo-alpha-D-quinovosyl)- sn -glycerol
Comment: |FRAME: SULFOQUINOVOSYLDIACYLGLYCEROL "Sulfoquinovosyl diacylglycerol"| (SQDG) is an abundant class of sulfolipids composed of a glycoside of |FRAME: CPD-10247| and |FRAME: 1-2-Diglycerides diacylglycerol|, which are found in many photosynthetic organisms, including all photosynthetic plants, algae, cyanobacteria, and purple sulfur and non-sulfur bacteria. SQDG is synthesized from |FRAME: UDP-SULFOQUINOVOSE| by the action of |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.M2|. The synthesis of SQDG is not crucial under normal growth conditions. It only becomes important when phosphate is limited 9465123. Under such conditions, the increase of SQDG levels compensates for the decrease in phospholipids and ensures a constant proportion of anionic lipids in photosynthetic membranes 14675442. SQDG is localized in photosynthetic membranes (in plants in the thylakoid membranes), where it is closely associated with certain membrane proteins.

Compound.name: a 5,10-methenyltetrahydrofolate
Comment: |FRAME: THF-GLU-N Tetrahydrofolate| (vitamin B9) and its derivatives, commonly termed folates, are required in a variety of reactions in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, where they act as carriers of one-carbon units in various oxidation states. These one-carbon units are utilized in the biosynthesis of several cellular components, including glycine, methionine, formylmethionine, thymidylate, pantothenate and purine nucleotides. During folate biosynthesis (as described in FOLSYN-PWY) the enzyme |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.12|, adds a glutamate residue to |FRAME: 7-8-DIHYDROPTEROATE|, resulting in |FRAME: DIHYDROFOLATE|, also known as H 2 PteGlu 1 . This molecule in turn is reduced by EC-1.5.1.3 (FolA) to |FRAME: THF| (H 4 PteGlu 1 , or tetrahydrofolate), which can be converted to several other folate molecules 11501996. Most folate molecules are modified in cells by successive additions of glutamate residues, forming folate polyglutamates (or folylpoly-gamma-glutamates). The glutamate residues are added by an amide linkage to the gamma-carboxylate group of the folate or folate derivative. Since these isopeptide bonds are not the normal amide bonds they are not hydrolyzed by peptidases or proteases, which are specific for alpha-carboxyl-linked peptide bonds. The addition of glutamyl residues probably occurs after the reduction of newly synthesized dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate and its conversion to other tetrahydrofolate derivatives. The glutamylation of folate residues serves several goals: it prevents the efflux of folates out of the cell, it increases the binding of folate cofactors to the enzymes of folate interconversion and biosynthesis, and in mammals, it allows the accumulation of folates in the mitochondria, which is required for glycine synthesis 10598551. This class stands for 5,10-methenyltetrahydrofolates with an unspecified number of glutamate residues.

Compound.name: a plant arabinogalactan
Comment: Arabinogalactans are biopolymers consisting of arabinose and galactose residues. Two main classes of arabinogalactans are found in nature: |FRAME: Plant-Arabinogalactans "plant arabinogalactan"| and |FRAME: Mycobacterial-Arabinogalactans "microbial arabinogalactan"|. |FRAME: Plant-Arabinogalactans "Plant arabinogalactans"| (AGs) are widely spread throughout the plant kingdom. Many edible and inedible plants are rich sources of these polysaccharides. AGs are associated with the pectin cell-wall component by physical bonds, and some of them are covalently linked to the complex pectin molecule as neutral side chains Ebringerova05. AGs occur in two structurally different forms described as |FRAME: Plant-Arabinogalactans-I "type I"| and |FRAME: Plant-Arabinogalactans-II "type II"|. AG of type I has a linear (1->4)-beta-D-Galp backbone, bearing 20-40% of alpha-L-Araf residues (1->5)-linked in short chains, in general at position 3. It is commonly found in pectins from citrus, apple and potato. Type I AG has been isolated from the skin of Opuntia ficus indica pear fruits 15063212. AG of type II, known as arabino-3,6-galactan, has a (1->3)-beta-D-Galp backbone heavily substituted at position 6 by mono- and oligosaccharide side chains composed of arabinosyl and galactosyl units. It is more widespread than the AG type I and occurs in cell walls of dicots and cereals often linked to proteins (known as arabinogalactan proteins). AG type II, along with galactomannans and cellulose, comprises the predominating polysaccharides of green arabica coffee beans11217967. In some case type II AGt contains a small amount of beta-glucuronate. AG type II occurs as minor, water-soluble components in softwoods. It is very abundant in the wood of larch trees (members of the genus |FRAME: TAX-3325|) - certain parts of the western larch (|FRAME: TAX-3327|) contain up to 35% AG Whistler93. However, larch AG type II is located in the lumen of the tracheids and ray cells, and is thus not a cell-wall component and by definition, not part of the |FRAME: Hemicelluloses| of these trees.

Compound.name: a phenolphthiodiolenone A
Comment: |FRAME: Phenolphthiodiolenone Phenolphthiodiolenones| are intermediates in |FRAME: Phenolphthiocerols phenolphthiocerol| biosynthesis. Phenolphthiocerol glycolipids have been found in many Mycobacterium species, including |FRAME: TAX-1769|, |FRAME: TAX-1768|, |FRAME: TAX-1765|, |FRAME: TAX-1781|, and |FRAME: TAX-78331| 3113946. Two types of phenolphthiodiolenone exist. In |FRAME: Phenolphthiodiolenone-A "phenolphthiodiolenone A"| the oxo and the methyl groups are attached at positions 3 and 4, respectively, and the hydroxyl groups are at positions 9 and 11. In |FRAME: Phenolphthiodiolenone-B "phenolphthiodiolenone B"| a methyl group is missing from the beginning of the molecule, and thus the oxo and methyl groups are attached at positions 2 and 3, respectively, and the hydroxyl groups are at positions 8 and 10.

Compound.name: a 3-oxoacyl-CoA
Synonyms: a beta-ketoacyl-CoA // 3-oxoacyl-CoA // a 3-oxo-acyl-CoA // RCOCH2CO-CoA // a 3-ketoacyl-CoA // beta-ketoacyl-CoA
Comment: ACYL-COA are oxoacids that have been activated by |FRAME: CO-A|. They are often classified by the length of their acyl moiety. |FRAME: Medium-Chain-Acyl-CoAs "Medium-chain acyl-CoAs"| are derived from fatty acids with aliphatic tails of 6-12 carbons. |FRAME: Long-Chain-Acyl-CoAs "Long-chain acyl-CoAs"| are derived from fatty acids with aliphatic tails of 13-21 carbons. |FRAME: VERY-LONG-CHAIN-FATTY-ACYL-COA "Very long-chain fatty acyl-CoAs"| are derived from fatty acids with aliphatic tails of 22 carbons or longer.

Compound.name: a very long-chain alkane
Comment: Alkanes are saturated acyclic hydrocarbons. They consist only of hydrogen and saturated carbon atoms and are bonded exclusively by single bonds. They could be either branched or unbranched. Linear alkanes are often classified by the length of their acyl moiety. |FRAME: Short-Chain-Alkanes "Short-chain alkanes"| contain less than 6- carbons. |FRAME: Medium-Chain-Alkanes "Medium-chain alkanes"| contain 6-12 carbons. |FRAME: Long-Chain-Alkanes "Long-chain alkanes"| contain 13-22 carbons. |FRAME: Very-Long-Chain-Alkanes "Very-long-chain alkanes"| contain 23 carbons or longer.

Compound.name: Man 7 (GlcNAc) 2 -[protein] (isomer 7A 1,2,3 B 3 )
Comment: This is one of four isomers of Man 7 GlcNAc 2 chains that are found in N glycans. The nomenclature used to identify high mannose glycans has not been standardized. Several earlier systems were insufficient to describe all possible isomers |CITS: [7954510][17719235][17685584]|. The nomenclature used here is that proposed by Prien et al 19181540, which can represent all processing isomers. According to this nomenclature, the other three Man 7 GlcNAc 2 isomers are named |FRAME: Man7GlcNAc2-protein-A123B2 "isomer 7A 1,2,3 B 2 "|, |FRAME: Man7GlcNAc2-protein-A123B1 "isomer 7A 1,2,3 B 1 "| and |FRAME: Man7GlcNAc2-protein-A12B12 "isomer 7A 1,2 B 1,2 "|.

Compound.name: an (8E)-4-hydroxysphing-8-enine ceramide
Comment: The predominant long-chain base in animal ceramides is sphingosine, which is only present in trace amount in plant ceramides. In contrast, sphinganine, 4-hydroxysphinganine, and 4-hydroxy-8-sphingenine are the prevalent long-chain bases in plants. The acyl chain of plant ceramides contains alpha-hydroxylated very long chain fatty acids. The plant ceramide (IV) in MetaCyc represents plant ceramides with 4-hydroxy-8-sphingenine as the long-chain base.

Compound.name: a [glycerolipid]-(9Z,12E)-octadecadienoate
Synonyms: a [glycerolipid]- trans -Δ12 linoleic acid // a [glycerolipid]-18:2Δ9 cis ,12 trans // a [glycerolipid]-(9Z,12E)-octadeca-9,12-dienoate // a [glycerolipid]- trans -Δ12 linoleate
Comment: |FRAME: CPD-8203 "(9Z,12E)-Octadecadienoate"| is an unusual unsaturated fatty acid that contains a trans double bond. It is usuall found |FRAME: CPD-17285 "attached to a lipid"|.

Compound.name: a pyrimidine
Comment: |FRAME: PYRIMIDINE-RING Pyrimidine| is a heterocyclic aromatic compound similar to benzene, containing two nitrogen atoms at positions 1 and 3 of the ring. The name pyrimidines is also used for compounds derived from the basic pyrimidine compound, including |FRAME: Pyrimidine-Bases "three of the bases"| found in nucleic acids, namely |FRAME: CYTOSINE|, THYMINE, and |FRAME: URACIL|. This class stands for all compounds that have a pyrimidine as part of their structure.

Compound.name: a lactone
Comment: A |FRAME: Lactones "lactone"| is a cyclic ester, the product of condensation of an alcohol group and a carboxylate group within the same molecule. It is characterized by a closed ring consisting of two or more carbon atoms and a single oxygen atom, with a ketone group in one of the carbons adjacent to the ring oxygen. There are several types of lactones - |FRAME: Beta-lactones| contain 3 carbons in the ring, Gamma-lactones contains 4, Delta-lactones contains 5, and Epsilon-lactones contains 6 carbons. The most stable structure for lactones are gamma-lactones and delta-lactones, because of the minimal angle strain in their structure. In fact, gamma-lactones are so stable that, in the presence of dilute acids at room temperature, 4-hydroxy acids esterify and cyclize spontaneously to form lactones. beta-lactones, on the other hand, are not very stable. The name lactone is derived from the lactone of |FRAME: L-LACTATE|, which is called |FRAME: CPD-9549|, although it is really a di-lactone.

Compound.name: a brevianamide
Comment: The brevianamides are a class of indole alkaloids originally isolated from |FRAME: TAX-5074|. They are derived from |FRAME: PRO|, |FRAME: TRP|, and one or two isoprene units |CITS: [5419195][4751807][1186436][16345847]|. The two main producers of |FRAME: CPD-15274| are |FRAME: TAX-5074| and |FRAME: TAX-60134|. The brevianamides belong to a diverse family of biologically active prenylated indole alkaloids isolated mainly from various |FRAME: TAX-5073| and |FRAME: TAX-5052| species of fungi that contains a unique bicyclo[2.2.2]diazaoctane core ring system, and are derived from |FRAME: TRP|, a cyclic amino acid (|FRAME: PRO|, |FRAME: L-PIPECOLATE| or a derivative of one of those compounds), and one or two isoprene units. In addition to their structural diversity, members of this family have been attributed a variety of bioactivities, including (but not limited to) insecticidal, cytotoxic, anthelmintic, and antibacterial properties. The bicyclo[2.2.2]diazaoctane-containing compounds can be divided into two sub-categories: the diketopiperazines (DKPs) and the monoketopiperazines (MKPs). DKPs include the |FRAME: Stephacidins stephacidins|, |FRAME: Brevianamides brevianamides|, and |FRAME: Notoamides notoamides|, while MKPs include the |FRAME: Paraherquamides paraherquamides|, |FRAME: Asperparalines asperparalines|, |FRAME: Marcfortines marcfortines|, |FRAME: Chrysogenamides chrysogenamides|,and |FRAME: Malbrancheamides malbrancheamides|. Two distinct stereochemical configurations have been noted with respect to the relative configuration of the bridging amide of the bicyclo[2.2.2]diazaoctane core. Most compounds have a syn -configuration (in which the the C-19 position (brevianamide numbering) and the bridging amide point at the same direction), but a few (such as |FRAME: CPD-25433| and |FRAME: CPD-25434|) have an anti configuration. The brevianamides display the anti configuration, as well as a spiro-indoxyl moiety and an unsubstituted indole ring 22502590. |FRAME: CPD-15274 "Brevianamide A"| possesses antifeedant and insecticidal effects Paterson87. |FRAME: CPD-15265 "Brevianamide F"| (cyclo-L-Trp-L-Pro) serves as the precursor for several secondary metabolites that lack the bridging bicycle, such as the |FRAME: CPD-15266 fumitremorgins| and spirotryprostatins in |FRAME: TAX-746128| 18763205.

Compound.name: a (1,4)-beta-D-mannan
Comment: beta-1,4-Mannans are major constitutents of hemicelluloses in plant tissue and are polymers composed of beta(1->4)-linked mannose residues. Some contain galactopyranosyl side chains (see |FRAME: Galactomannans|). Slightly galactosylated mannans (4% galactose), considered as linear beta(1->4)-D-mannans, have been isolated from the seed endosperm of vegetable ivory nut (|FRAME: TAX-115507|) and date (|FRAME: TAX-42345|) Reid95. Note that there are several types of mannans. The proteins in yeast cell walls contain particularly complex N -glycans referred to as alpha-mannans in which the core N -glycan is extended by ~200 alpha-1,6-mannose units that are also decorated with alpha-linked mannose side chains 4882958. In some yeasts, such as the human pathogen |FRAME: TAX-5476|, beta-1,2-mannose residues cap the alpha-mannans side chains, and extended beta-1,2-mannan chains are attached to the alpha-mannan via phosphate bridges 26286752. beta-1,2-Mannans also fulfill an important storage role in |FRAME: TAX-5658 Leishmania| parasites 12902334.

Compound.name: a phthiodiolone A
Comment: |FRAME: Phthiodiolones Phthiodiolones| are intermediates in |FRAME: Phthiocerols phthiocerol| biosynthesis. They contain an oxo group where phthiocerols contain a methoxyl group. Two types of phthiodiolone exist. In |FRAME: Phthiodiolone-A "phthiodiolone A"| the oxo and the methyl groups are attached at positions 3 and 4, respectively, and the hydroxyl groups are at positions 9 and 11. In |FRAME: Phthiodiolone-B "phthiodiolone B"| a methyl group is missing from the beginning of the molecule, and thus the oxo and methyl groups are attached at positions 2 and 3, respectively, and the hydroxyl groups are at positions 8 and 10.

Compound.name: an alkali metal cation
Comment: The alkali metals (along with hydrogen) form Group IA of the periodic table. They are very reactive, electropositive, monovalent metals forming strongly alkaline hydroxides.

Compound.name: a cardiac glycoside
Comment: Cardiac glycosides are plant-made compounds (mostly by members of the |FRAME: TAX-4163| genus, or Foxgloves) that have beneficial effects over patients with cardiac failure. The treatment of congestive heart failure (dropsy), among other ailments like tuberculosis, by the use of Foxglove is mentioned in writings as early as 1250 A. D., when the Welsh Physicians of Myddva collected foxglove as one of their many herbs and included it in their remedies. 28561136. The cardiac glycosides are composed of two structural features: a sugar moiety that may contain one or more saccharides, and a steroid aglycone. Cardiac glycosides having a terminal glucose are called primary glycosides whereas those lacking such a sugar are termed secondary glycosides. There are two classes of cardiac glycosides differing by the group attached at the 17-position of the aglycone: the |FRAME: Cardenolide-Glycosides "cardenolides"|, which have a five-membered unsaturated lactone ring (but-2-en-4-olide ring) and the |FRAME: Bufadienolide-Glycosides bufadienolides|, which have a six membered doubly unsaturated lactone ring (penta-2,4-dien-5-olide ring). The steroid nucleus of the cardiac glycosides have a unique configuration: rings A/B and C/D are cis - fused while rings B/C are trans - fused. The nucleus has beta configured hydroxyls at the positions C-3 and C-14, and many compounds have additional hydroxyl groups at positions 12 and 16. The sugars found in the glycoside moiety range from common hexoses and pentoses (such as |FRAME: D-Glucose|, |FRAME: L-rhamnose|, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE|, and |FRAME: D-Xylose|) to very uncommon sugars, some of which have only been found in cardiac glycosides (e.g. |FRAME: D-quinovopyranose|, |FRAME: CPD-22597|, |FRAME: D-Digitoxose|, |FRAME: CPD-22572|, |FRAME: D-Olivose|, and |FRAME: D-Fucoses|). While the mechanism whereby cardiac glycosides cause a positive inotropic effect and electrophysiologic changes of the hurt is still not completely clear, the most widely accepted mechanism involves the ability of cardiac glycosides to inhibit the membrane bound Na+/K+-ATPase pump responsible for Na+/K+ exchange KAUTE08.

Compound.name: an alpha-limit dextrin
Synonyms: a glycogen phosphorylase-limit dextrin // a glycogen phosphorylase-limited dextrin
Comment: |FRAME: CPD0-971 "A limit dextrin"| is the name given to the highly-branched core of the polysaccharide fragments remaining at the end (limit) of exhaustive hydrolysis of |FRAME: CPD-7043 amylopectin| or |FRAME: Glycogens glycogen| by alpha-1,4-glucan hydrolase enzymes such as |FRAME: GLYCOPHOSPHORYL-CPLX| and |FRAME: MALDEXPHOSPHORYL-CPLX|. These enzymes shorten the chains, but are not able to hydrolyze the alpha-1,6 bonds at branch points. Since the branching residues block the enzymes from getting close, the enzymes leave a tail of 4 alpha-1,4-linked residues next to the branch points.

Compound.name: a penem
Comment: This compound class stands for |FRAME: Lactams lactams| in which the amide bond is contained within a four-membered ring, which includes the amide nitrogen and the carbonyl carbon. beta-Lactam compounds imitate the naturally occurring |FRAME: D-ALA-D-ALA| substrate for the group of enzymes known as penicillin binding proteins (PBPs), which cross-link the peptidoglycan in bacterial cell wall, and thus act as powerful antibiotics 6109324. Naturally occurring |FRAME: Beta-Lactams "beta-lactam antibiotics"| are classified into several groups according to their chemical structure: In |FRAME: Monolactams monolactams| the beta-lactam ring is not fused to another ring. This class includes compounds such as the |FRAME: Nocardicins nocardicins| 3427723 and the |FRAME: Monobactams monobactams| 3909315. In |FRAME: Penams penams| the beta-lactam ring is fused to a saturated five atom ring (a 4:5 structure). Penams contain a sulfur atom at position 1 of the five atom ring (for example, the |FRAME: PENICILLIN penicillins|) 6335599. Related classes include the |FRAME: Carbapenams carbapenams|, which contain a carbon atom in that position 12890666, and the |FRAME: Clavams oxopenams| (also known as clavams), which contain an oxygen atom at that position (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-9261|) 3304182. |FRAME: Penems Penems| are molecues similar to penams in which the five atom ring is unsaturated at positions 2-3. Similarly, penems contain a sulfur atom at position 1 of the five atom ring, while |FRAME: Carbapenems carbapenems| contains a carbon atom in that position 16413506. In |FRAME: Cephams cephams| and |FRAME: Cephems cephems| the beta-lactam ring is fused to a six-atom ring (a 4:6 strcuture) that contains a sulfur atom at position 1. In cephams the ring is saturated, while cephems have an unsaturated bond at positions 3-4 |CITS: [1164170][12722308]|. 1-Oxocephams/1-oxacephems conain an oxygen atom at position 1 |CITS: [11671696][11078187]|.

Compound.name: a jasmonate
Comment: The |FRAME: Jasmonates jasmonates| are a group of important phytohormones, structurally similar to animal |FRAME: Prostaglandins prostaglandins| and ubiquitous in the plant kingdom. Many forms exist, based on the structure of |FRAME: Jasmonic-Acids "Jasmonate"| (jasmonic acid, JA). The jasmonates act as regulatory molecules in many developmental processes that include fertility, sex determination, root elongation and fruit ripening. They are also potent signals activating plant defences against pathogens, herbivory, wounding and abiotic stress. The jasmonate regulation system includes the COI1 receptor protein and several JAZ ( JA smonate Z IM domain) repressors, which, in the absence of jasmonate, are bound to the MYC2 transcription factors, preventing transcription. In the presence of active jasmonate molecules, COI1 interacts with the JAZ repressors, causing their |FRAME: PWY-7511 ubiquitylation|. The ubiquitylated repressors are targeted for proteasome degradation, releasing the MYC2 transcription factors and activating transcription 19716757. Only two of the four stereoisomers of jasmonate occur naturally: |FRAME: CPD-731| and |FRAME: CPD-734| |CITS: [8074303][19349968]|. These two forms are present in equilibrium within cells and can interconvert spontaneously through epimerization |CITS: [8074303][19349968]|. The exact ratio of these stereoisomers within a cell has not been conclusively determined, and it may vary based on species, cell type, and physiological state. But, in the systems tested so far, |FRAME: CPD-734| is found at higher levels than |FRAME: CPD-731| 19349968. The biological activity of these stereoisomers can be quite different 8074303. In addition, enzymes involved in JA metabolism may have different preferences for the different stereoisomers 17291501.

Compound.name: a K vitamin
Comment: Vitamin K is a name given to a group of derivatives of 2-methyl-1,4-naphthoquinone that are required by mammals for the posttranslational modification of certain proteins, mostly involved in blood coagulation. These compounds, while essential for mammals, are not synthesized by them, and are thus considered vitamins. The natural forms of the vitamin are vitamin K 1 (|FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE|) and vitamin K 2 (|FRAME: Menaquinones|). Since menaquinones produced by different organisms have different tail lenghts, there are many variations of vitamin K 2 , usually specified based on the number of carbons in their tails, such as in Vitamin K 2 (45). Menaquinones are synthesized by gut bacteria, and are absorbed into the blood. Thus, dietary deficiency is extremely rare in healthy individuals. There are also several synthetic forms- vitamin K 3 through K 9 . Vitamin K 3 (|FRAME: CPD-3766|) is the most active of the synthetic forms.

Compound.name: a purine ribonucleoside
Comment: Nucleosides are glycosylamines consisting of |FRAME: Bases| bound to a |FRAME: CPD0-1110 ribose| or |FRAME: 2-DEOXYRIBOSE| sugar via a beta-glycosidic linkage. The nucleosides are called |FRAME: Ribonucleosides ribonucleosides| when the sugar is |FRAME: CPD0-1110 ribose|, and |FRAME: Deoxy-Ribonucleosides deoxyribonucleosides| when it is |FRAME: 2-DEOXYRIBOSE|. Common |FRAME: Ribonucleosides ribonucleosides| include |FRAME: CYTIDINE|, |FRAME: URIDINE|, |FRAME: ADENOSINE|, |FRAME: GUANOSINE| and |FRAME: INOSINE|. Examples of |FRAME: Deoxy-Ribonucleosides deoxyribonucleosides| include |FRAME: THYMIDINE| and |FRAME: DEOXYADENOSINE|. Purines are heterocyclic aromatic compounds that contain a |FRAME: PYRIMIDINE-RING| ring fused to an |FRAME: IMIDAZOLE-RING| ring. Two of the ribonucleosides in nucleic acids, |FRAME: ADENOSINE| and |FRAME: GUANOSINE|, are purines.

The term is also often used to describe the carbohydrate portion of a glycoconjugate, such as a glycoprotein, glycolipid, or a proteoglycan.

Comment: |FRAME: Phthiodiolones Phthiodiolones| are intermediates in |FRAME: Phthiocerols phthiocerol| biosynthesis. They contain an oxo group where phthiocerols contain a methoxyl group. Two types of phthiodiolone exist. In |FRAME: Phthiodiolone-A "phthiodiolone A"| the oxo and the methyl groups are attached at positions 3 and 4, respectively, and the hydroxyl groups are at positions 9 and 11. In |FRAME: Phthiodiolone-B "phthiodiolone B"| a methyl group is missing from the beginning of the molecule, and thus the oxo and methyl groups are attached at positions 2 and 3, respectively, and the hydroxyl groups are at positions 8 and 10.

Compound.name: a [2Fe-2S] iron-sulfur cluster
Synonyms: an iron-sulfur center (ambiguous) // Fe 2 S 2 iron-sulfur cluster // a 2Fe-2S center // a 2Fe-2S cluster // 2Fe-2S // Fe 2 S 2 // an Fe 2 S 2 iron-sulfur center // [2Fe-2S] // [2Fe-2S] cluster // Iron-sulfur (2Fe-2S)
Comment: |FRAME: FeS-Centers "Iron-sulfur clusters"| consist of nonheme iron complexed to sulfur in several ways. They serve as prosthetic groups of many proteins, which function as intracellular electron carriers with a low reduction potential. In addition to their roles in electron transfer reactions, iron-sulfur clusters are also known to participate in the activation of substrates, the stabilization of radicals and structures, the protection of proteins from enzymes and the storage of iron and sulfur. They act as sensors of iron, dioxygen, the superoxide ion, and possibly nitric oxide, and participate in gene expression regulation 16466637. In |FRAME: CPD-6| the irons are coordinated to the sulfurs of 4 cysteine side chains.

Compound.name: a fatty acyl-CoA
Comment: Fatty acyl-CoAs are |FRAME: ACYL-COA "acyl-CoAs"| derived from |FRAME: Fatty-Acids "fatty acids"|. Many enzymes that act on fatty acids, as well as the corresponding |FRAME: Fatty-Acyl-CoAs "fatty acyl-CoAs"|, |FRAME: Fatty-Alcohols alcohols|, and |FRAME: Fatty-Aldehydes aldehydes|, have evolved to recognize substrates with a limited range of chain lengths. To classify these enzymes, it is helpful to divide the substrates into smaller groups based on their chain length. The following subgroups have been defined: |FRAME: Short-Chain-Acyl-CoAs "Short-chain acyl-CoAs"| are derived from |FRAME: Short-chain-fatty-acids "fatty acids that have 3-5 carbons in the longest chain"|. |FRAME: Medium-Chain-Acyl-CoAs "Medium-chain acyl-CoAs"| are derived from |FRAME: Medium-chain-fatty-acids "fatty acids that have 6-12 carbons in the longest chain"|. |FRAME: Long-Chain-Acyl-CoAs "Long-chain acyl-CoAs"| are derived from |FRAME: Long-Chain-Fatty-Acids "fatty acids that have 13-22 carbons in the longest chain"|. |FRAME: VERY-LONG-CHAIN-FATTY-ACYL-COA "Very-long-chain fatty acyl-CoAs"| are derived from |FRAME: Very-long-chain-fatty-acids "fatty acids that have 23-27 carbons in the longest chain"|. |FRAME: Ultra-Long-Chain-Acyl-CoAs "Ultra-long-chain fatty acyl-CoAs"| are derived from |FRAME: Ultra-long-chain-fatty-acids "fatty acids that have more than 27 carbons in the longest chain"|.

Compound.name: a Co alpha-[alpha-(aden-7-yl)]-cobamide
Comment: |FRAME: Cobamides "A cobamide"| is a corrinoid molecule based on the structure of |FRAME: CPD-20843|, a cobalt-corrinoid hexaamide that is formed from |FRAME: COBINAMIDE| by the attachment of an alpha-D-ribofuranose 3-phosphate residue at the 2 position of the aminopropanol chain. Biologically active forms of cobamides contain an upper (beta) and a lower (alpha) axial ligands. The most common upper axial ligand are either a methyl group or a 5'-deoxyadenosyl group, although some other forms exist. More variability is found with the lower axial ligand, where more that 16 different forms have been described. This class includes all cobamides that have an adenine base as their lower axial ligand. Cobamides that have an adenine molecule as the lower ligand are known as pseudocobalamins. They are known to be produced by different bacterial genera |CITS: [10552882][10940017][17888910][24055007][27040778][27737643]|. Many cyanobacterial species produce pseudocobalamin, which is used as a cofactor in their specialized methionine synthase (MetH) |CITS: [20086323][28028206]|.

Compound.name: a protopanaxadiol-type ginsenoside
Comment: |FRAME: Ginsenosides Ginsenosides| or panaxosides are a class of steroid glycosides and triterpene saponins found exclusively in the plant genus |FRAME: TAX-4053| (ginseng). They are the principal components responsible for the pharmaceutical activities of ginseng. Ginsenosides are composed of an aglycone and sugar moieties. Based on the structure of their aglycones, ginsenosides have been categorized into three broad types; |FRAME: Protopanaxadiol-type-ginsenosides "protopanaxadiol-type ginsenosides"| (PPD), which contain hydroxyl groups at positions 3 and 20, |FRAME: Protopanaxatriol-type-ginsenosides "protopanaxatriol-type ginsenosides"| (PPT), which contain hydroxyl groups at positions 3, 6 and 20, and |FRAME: Oleanonic-acid-type-ginsenosides "oleanonic-acid-type saponins"|. Although ginsenosides only have three kinds of aglycones, more than 60 kinds of ginsenosides have been identified by now due to the variability in the type of sugar moieties, their number, and the carbon positions they link to. The biological activity of ginsenoside increases with the decrease of the number of the sugar moieties. All of the ginsenosides found in large quantities in wild ginseng (known as major ginsenosides) are heavily glycosylated, while the more active less-glycosylated ginsenosides are found in much smalller quantities (and are commonly referred to as the minor ginsenosides). Following oral intake of ginseng, the large low-solubility and poor-permeability major ginsenosides cannot be absorbed by the human body directly Su06, and are deglycosylated into smaller forms in the gastrointestinal tract by intestinal bacteria and/or digestive enzymes 8923812. Glycosidase enzymes that can convert the major ginsenosides to minor ginsenosides are not common and are of commercial interest.

Compound.name: a mycofactocin
Comment: |FRAME: Mycofactocins Mycofactocins| (MFT) are a family of related electron acceptors that are used by dehydrogenases that belong to the TIGR03971, TIGR03989, and TIGR04266 families. The identity of the cofactor has not been known until 2019, and enzymes that require it were initially analyzed using artificial electron acceptors. The first clue to mycofactocin's identity came in 2011 when bioinformatic analysis demonstrated the co-occurrence of the genes mftABCDEF in over 600 bacterial species, including pathogens such as |FRAME: TAX-1773|, |FRAME: TAX-1764|, and |FRAME: TAX-1809|, with genes encoding the dehydrogenases of the above mentioned families 21223593. Further studies have shown that mycofactocins originate from a ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptide (MftA). The C terminus of the peptide, consisting of |FRAME: VAL|-|FRAME: TYR|, is oxidatively decarboxylated and cyclized by a radical SAM enzyme and cleaved, followed by oxidative deamination to generate the |FRAME: CPD-22872| aglycone, which contains the redox center of MFT. Mature mycofactocins are glycosylated by sugar chains consisting of up to nine beta-1,4-linked glucose units, and some of them are methylated on the second glucose unit Pena-Ortiz19. See also |FRAME: PWY-8122|.

Compound.name: a peptidoglycan
Comment: The bacterial bag-shaped envelope (sacculus) can resist turgor pressures of 2-5 atmospheres in Gram-negative bacteria, and up to 20 atm in Gram-positive bacteria. This remarkable tensile strength, combined with elasticity, is achieved by the structure of the cell wall's main component, peptidoglycan (also known as "basal structure", "mucopeptide", "glycopeptide", "glycosaminopeptide" and "murein"). Peptidoglycan is best described as a fisherman's net. The net is made of parallel, rather inextensible glycan threads consisting of alternating |FRAME: N-ACETYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSAMINE| (GlcNAc) and |FRAME: CPD-19950| (MurNAc) sugars, which are held together by small elastic peptide crosslinks which are formed between the side-chains of the different strands, allowing the net to expand or shrink 10532377. The structure below shows a region of peptidoglycan consisting of two monomers with pentapeptide side chains. R1 and R2 refer to the parts of the polymer upstream and downstream. Many variations exist in regard to the composition of the side chain.

They are categorized by the number of C5 isoprene units as follows: |FRAME: Hemiterpenes Hemiterpenoids| (one C5 unit), |FRAME: Monoterpenes monoterpenoids| (C10; two C5 units), |FRAME: Sesquiterpenes sesquiterpenoids| (C15; three C5 units), |FRAME: Diterpenes diterpenoids| (C20; four C5 units), |FRAME: Sesterterpenes sesterterpenoids| (C25; five C5 units), |FRAME: Triterpenes triterpenoids| (C30; six C5 units), |FRAME: C35-Terpenes "sesquarterpenoids"| (C35; seven C5 units), and |FRAME: Tetraterpenes tetraterpenoids| (C40; eight C5 units).

Compound.name: an aminated amino group donor
Comment: |FRAME: Amine-Donors "An amino group donor"| is a compound that can donate an amino group to another compound in a reaction catalyzed by enzymes that belong to the |FRAME: EC-2.6.1 transaminase group"| (often called aminotransferases). Prior to donating the amino group the compound is |FRAME: Aminated-Amine-Donors| and after donating it the compound is |FRAME: Deaminated-Amine-Donors|. Since tranmination reactions are reversible, the distinction between an amino group donor and an amino group acceptor is not determined by the actual chemical entity, but by the role it plays in a particular reaction. However, some compounds, such as |FRAME: GLT| and |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE|, are often used as amino group donors by the aminotransferases in reactions that are physiologically unidirectional. This particular entry is used when the identity of the amino group donor (or acceptor) is not known or cannot be defined.

The enzyme complexes that require lipoate have a dedicated |FRAME: Lipoyl-Protein "lipoyl domain"|, and lipoate is actually produced on this domain. The precursor |FRAME: CPD-195| molecule is first attached to a specific |FRAME: LYS| residue within the lipoyl domain (producing |FRAME: Octanoylated-domains|), and is then converted to lipoate by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.8.1.8|, resulting in |FRAME: Lipoyl-Protein-N6-lipoyllysine|. |FRAME: CPLX0-782 "Lipoate synthase"| not only catalyzes the reaction, but is also the source of the two sulfur atoms (see several pathway variants under |FRAME: Lipoate-Biosynthesis|).

Compound.name: an A antigen
Synonyms: an A histo-blood group antigen // a histo-blood group substance A // an N -acetyl-alpha-D-galactosaminyl-(1,3)-[alpha-L-fucosyl-(1,2)]-beta-D-galactosyl-R // a [glycoprotein]- N -acetyl-alpha-D-galactosaminyl-(1,3)-[alpha-L-fucosyl-(1,2)]-D-galactose

The majority of the A, B and H antigens are linked to the ends of long polylactosamine chains attached mainly to band 3 protein (encoded by SLC4A1), the anion exchange protein of the red blood cells. A minor fraction of the antigens is attached to a ceramide moiety, forming neutral glycosphingolipids.

Compound.name: alginate
Comment: |FRAME: ALGINATE Alginate| is a major component of the cell walls of |FRAME: TAX-2870| (brown algae), and can make up to 45% of the total algal material. It is a linear polysaccharide of (1-4)-linked |FRAME: CPD-15205|, with variable amounts of its C-5 epimer |FRAME: CPD-15204| Schmidt26. The |FRAME: CPD-15205| (M) and |FRAME: CPD-15204| (G) residues are arranged in homopolymeric regions of M and G blocks, interspaced with regions of alternating structure (MG blocks). The physicochemical properties of alginate depend on both the overall M to G ratio and the relative proportions of the three block types in the chain. G block-rich alginate forms a high-strength gel in presence of divalent cations such as calcium, and is found in more rigid parts of the alga. Alginates rich in M or MG blocks are more flexible. The composition varies among species, and within an organism according to the nature and the age of the tissues as well as to the season and to the growing area. Depending on its composition, alginate can absorb 200 300 times its own weight in water, forming a viscous gum. Historically, alginate extracted from seaweed has had a wide variety of uses. Its unique physical properties enable it to be used as a stabilizer, viscosifier, and gelling agent in the food and beverage, paper and printing, biomaterials, and pharmaceutical industries |CITS:[9283015][9393029][11018131][12149954][16183570][20581859][25300542]|. Commercial varieties of alginate are extracted from several species, including the giant kelp |FRAME: TAX-35122|, |FRAME: TAX-52969|, and various types of |FRAME: TAX-33637|. The alginates formed by brown algae are non-acetylated. An acetylated form of alginate is produced by bacteria that belong to the |FRAME: TAX-286| and |FRAME: TAX-352| genera. The higher the degree of O-acetylation, the higher the viscosity and pseudoplastic rheology of the alginate Skjak-Braek88. The biological function of alginates differs between the two genera. In |FRAME: TAX-286| alginate is associated with biofilms, promoting bacterial adherence to target cell walls 3155514. Alginate production is a major contributing factor in chronic pulmonary infections by |FRAME: TAX-287|, the causative agent of cystic fibrosis 3155514. Most strains of |FRAME: TAX-287| do not produce alginate, although alginate is always produced in the lung of CF pateints. it is believed that alginate encapsulation protects the infecting bacterial cells from phagocytosis, as well as from antibiotic therapy. In |FRAME: TAX-352| alginate is a structural element in the wall of the cyst, a desiccation-resistant capsule that is formed under adverse environmental conditions 16912921.

Compound.name: a pyrimidine nucleoside
Comment: Nucleosides are glycosylamines consisting of |FRAME: Bases| bound to a |FRAME: CPD0-1110 ribose| or |FRAME: 2-DEOXYRIBOSE| sugar via a beta-glycosidic linkage. The nucleosides are called |FRAME: Ribonucleosides ribonucleosides| when the sugar is |FRAME: CPD0-1110 ribose|, and |FRAME: Deoxy-Ribonucleosides deoxyribonucleosides| when it is |FRAME: 2-DEOXYRIBOSE|. Common |FRAME: Ribonucleosides ribonucleosides| include |FRAME: CYTIDINE|, |FRAME: URIDINE|, |FRAME: ADENOSINE|, |FRAME: GUANOSINE| and |FRAME: INOSINE|. Examples of |FRAME: Deoxy-Ribonucleosides deoxyribonucleosides| include |FRAME: THYMIDINE| and |FRAME: DEOXYADENOSINE|. When nucleosides are phosphorylated on the sugar's primary alcohol group, the resulting phosphonucleosides are called |FRAME: Nucleotides nucleotides|. Pyrimidine is a heterocyclic aromatic compound similar to benzene, containing two nitrogen atoms at positions 1 and 3 of the ring. The name pyrimidines is also used for compounds derived from the basic pyrimidine compound, including three of the nucleosides found in nucleic acids, namely |FRAME: CYTIDINE|, THYMIDINE, and |FRAME: URIDINE|.

Compound.name: a [glycerolipid]-linoleate
Synonyms: a [glycerolipid]-cis,cis-9,12-octadecadienoate // a [glycerolipid]-(9Z,12Z)-octadeca-9,12-dienoate // a [glycerolipid]-9,12-linoleic acid // a [glycerolipid]-9-cis,12-cis-octadecadienoate // a linoleoyl-[glycerolipid]

Linoleate is produced by many organisms, including bacteria, plants, fungi and some insects. It is abundant in many vegetable oils, especially safflower and sunflower oils. While mammals require linoleate, which is found in their membranes and is used as the precursor for production of |FRAME: CPD-8117|, |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID|, |FRAME: Prostaglandins prostaglandins|, |FRAME: Leukotrienes leukotrienes|, and |FRAME: Thromboxanes thromboxanes|, they are not able to produce it since they lack |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.6|. Thus linoleate is an essential fatty acid, and must be obtained through the diet. Like other fatty acids, |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID| is rarely found in its free form. It is usually found either as |FRAME: CPD-18| or |FRAME: Linoleoyl-groups "incorporated into a lipid"|.

Compound.name: a levan
Comment: Levan is a non-structural polysaccharide present in several microorganisms and a few plant species. It consists almost solely of fructosyl residues linked via beta-2,6 linkages, and is packed into nano-sized spherical forms, giving it a very low intrinsic viscosity. Levan is a main ingredient in natto, a traditional Japanese food. Plants synthesize levan in the vacuole by the concerted action of various fructosyltransferases such as |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.10|. When acting alone, this enzyme synthesizes linear levan chains from sucrose via the trisaccharide intermediate |FRAME: 6-KESTOSE| (it can also use |FRAME: 1-KESTOTRIOSE| and |FRAME: NEOKESTOSE| as the initial fructose acceptors). Plant fructans generally have a low degree of polymerization (DP <10 to 100). The occurrence of levansucrase is widespread in Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. Bacterial levans reach much higher molecular masses and contain up to 10,000 fructosyl units. Species that belong to the |FRAME: TAX-1301|, |FRAME: TAX-1243|, and |FRAME: TAX-1578| genera also contain |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.9|, which forms beta-(2,1) fructosyl-fructose linkages. When expressed together with levansucrase, that enzyme creates branching points that connect multiple beta-(2,6) linked levan chains, forming a branched polymer known as |FRAME: Graminans graminan| 27178733.

Mucin-type O -glycosylation, consisting of glycans attached via O-linked |FRAME: CPD-3604|, is one of the most abundant forms of protein glycosylation in animals. Eight core-type structures of mucin-type O -glycans have been proposed, including |FRAME: Core1 "core 1"|, |FRAME: Core2 "core 2"|, |FRAME: GLUCOSAMINYL-13-N-ETCETERA-GALACTOSAMINY "core 3"|, |FRAME: GLUCOSAMINYL-16-ETCETERA-GALACTOSAMINYL- "core 4"|, |FRAME: Core5 "core 5"|, |FRAME: Core6 "core 6"|, |FRAME: Core7 "core 7"| and |FRAME: Core8 "core 8"| 16413314. Compound.name: a chitodextrin
Synonyms: a chtin fragment // a chitin oligosaccharide
Comment: |FRAME: CHITIN Chitin| is a polymer of repeating units of beta-(1,4)-linked |FRAME: N-ACETYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSAMINE| (beta-GlcNAc n ). It may be the second most abundant biopolymer in the world, after cellulose. It is the main component of the cell walls of fungi, the exoskeletons of arthropods such as crustaceans and the insects, the radula of mollusks, and the beaks of cephalopods. In nature, chitin polymers are likely to have a high degree of polymerization and are insoluble in water 20559485. |FRAME: Chitodextrins Chitodextrins| are polymers that are still purely composed of beta-(1,4)-linked |FRAME: N-ACETYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSAMINE| residues, but have smaller degrees of polymerization than native |FRAME: CHITIN chitin|. Though the specific upper limit for defining a chitodextrin is hard to define, a class of related compounds referred to as chitooligosaccharides, composed of both |FRAME: N-ACETYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSAMINE| and |FRAME: GLUCOSAMINE| typically have a degree of polymerization of 20 or fewer residues 20559485. In the structure shown for this compound, R1 will be a hydrogen if the |FRAME: N-ACETYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSAMINE GlcNAc| residue that it is attached to is the terminal residue on the non-reducing end of the compound. R2 will be a hydrogen if the |FRAME: N-ACETYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSAMINE GlcNAc| residue that it is attached to is the terminal residue on the reducing end of the compound. However, R1 and/or R2 may also be a single |FRAME: N-ACETYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSAMINE GlcNAc| residue or a chain of n |FRAME: N-ACETYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSAMINE GlcNAc| residues.

Compound.name: an XLXG xylogulcan

Comment: |FRAME: Xyloglucan Xyloglucan| is the major hemicellulose in dicotyledon type I cell walls. The cross-linking between xyloglucan chains is a major factor in the stability of the three-dimensional matrix between adjacent cellulose microfibrils Whitney95. Xyloglucan has a backbone of beta-1,4-linked cellotetraose units, which are substituted in C-6 by alpha-D-xylosyl residues at two or three of the first three glucosyl residues, but not in the position closest to the reducing end 8252539. Some of the xylosyl residues are subsequently further substituted by (1,2)-beta-D-galactosyl residues at the second and/or third xylose residue and by (1,2)-alpha-L-fucose at the galactosyl unit of the third xylose residue |CITS:[12837954] [17011813]|. A common terminology uses G for basic non-substituted glucosyl units within a xylosylglycan, X for glucose residues substituted by alpha-D-xylose, L for glucose residues substituted by alpha-D-xylose and beta-D-galactose, and F for glucose residues substituted by alpha-D-xylose, beta-D-galactose and alpha-L-fucose Fry93. Most xylosylglucans consist of repeating heptasaccharide |FRAME: Xyloglucans-Xylose XXXG| units.

Synonyms: an L-1-phosphatidyl- sn -glycerol // a 1,2-diacyl- sn -glycero-3-phospho-(1'- sn -glycerol) // a 1-phosphatidylglycerol
Comment: The structure of |FRAME: L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-GLYCEROL phosphatidylglycerol| (PG) was determined in 1958 from lipid isolates of single-cell green algae from the |FRAME: TAX-3087| genus 13510267. Its structure is analogous to phosphatidylinositol (PI), but with a glyceryl moiety replacing the inosityl moiety of PI. Within a decade it has been found in higher plants Benson61, Gram-negative bacteria |CITS: [4868364][4295332]| and mammals 5660098. It was later discovered in the archaeon |FRAME: TAX-2246|, indicating that it is produced by all three domains of life. The biosynthetic pathway was elucidated in the early 60s 14033231, and a laboratory synthesis was completed a few years later 5916374. The abundance of PG is relatively low compared with phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) in prokaryotes or with either PE or phosphatidylcholine (PC) in eukaryotes |CITS: [18216768][20671299][21172818]|. It is typically more concentrated in plant systems than in animals, forming 1.5-4·5% of the lipid fraction |CITS: [23532185][3592680]| Since its discovery, biochemical research into PG has been dominated by its roles in the surfactant of lung tissue (PG is the second largest lipid constituent of lung surfactant in almost all mammals), chloroplast membranes (PG is the only phospholipid found in chloroplast thylakoids) and in both bacterial and mammalian systems.

Compound.name: a steroidal estrogen

Compound.name: an iron-sulfur cluster
Synonyms: an FeS center // an FeS cluster // an [FeS] iron-sulfur center // an [FeS] iron-sulfur cluster // an iron-sulfur center
Comment: Iron-sulfur clusters are cofators of |FRAME: FeS-Proteins "iron-sulfur proteins"| and consist of a cluster of two to four iron atoms linked to sulfides, some of which are cysteine residues of the protein. Several cluster types have been described, including |FRAME: CPD-6|, |FRAME: CPD-23|, |FRAME: 3FE-4S| and |FRAME: CPD-7|. The [3Fe-4S] cluster is relatively rare, and 3Fe/4Fe interconversion may occur with minimal protein reorganization. In another type of Fe-S cluster, known as |FRAME: CPD0-1098|, two of the 4 cysteine residues that are coordinated with the iron atoms in regular |FRAME: CPD-6| are substituted by histidine residues. Although the clusters contain several iron atoms, each one usually transfers only one electron, so, for example, a protein with two [4Fe-4S] clusters will usually transfer two electrons. Small electron transfer proteins that contain only [2Fe-2S] or [4Fe-4S] clusters are called |FRAME: Ferredoxins ferredoxins|. When Fe-S clusters occur in larger (and sometimes membrane-bound) proteins together with other prosthetic groups and/or metal cofactors, the proteins are designated as complex Fe-S proteins. In addition to their roles in electron t ransfer reactions, iron-sulfur clusters are also known to participate in the activation of substrates, the stabilization of radicals and structures, the protection of proteins from enzymes and the storage of iron and sulfur. They can also act as sensors of iron, dioxygen, the superoxide ion, and possibly nitric oxide, and participate in gene expression 16466637. In some cases iron-sulfur clusters serve as sources of sulfur in enzymatic reactions. In such cases the cluster needs to be reassembled before the enzyme can catalyze the next round 29051382.

Comment: Strigolactones are plant hormones that stimulate the branching and growth of symbiotic arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, but inhibit plant shoot branching. They promote the probability of establishment of a symbiotic association between the plant and the fungi. The first strigolactone (|FRAME: CPD-14655|) was described from |FRAME: TAX-3635| (cotton) infected by the root parasitic weeds |FRAME: TAX-4169| (witchweed) (hence the name). It has been shown that the seeds of the parasites germinated only if they were exposed to stimulant molecules present in the root exudate of the host. Although the nature of strigol was not understood at the time, it was observed that it was active at hormonal levels 17780042. Discovery of additional strigolactones from other plants followed, such as |FRAME: CPD-14659| from |FRAME: TAX-4558| Hauck92, |FRAME: CPD-14660| from |FRAME: TAX-3917| Mueler92 and |FRAME: CPD-14657| from |FRAME: TAX-57577| (red clover) Yokota98. The real purpose of strigolactones, which was understood 40 years after the discovery of strigol, is to promote the formation of symbiotic associations known as arbuscular mycorrhiza, which consist of close interaction between the plants roots and |FRAME: TAX-214504| fungi |CITS: [15944706][16574693]|. Arbuscular mycorrhiza, which are found in more than 80% of higher plant species, are one of the most ancient symbioses of land plants. The fungi acquire and deliver nutrients to the plants, which in return provides the fungi with carbohydrates produced by photosynthesis 15944687. The lactones induce extensive hyphal branching in germinating spores of the fungi, which increases the chance of contact with the root and subsequently infecting it. The branching phenomenon has been known for more than 30 years before the identity of the chemical signal that promotes it has been traced to strigolactone Mosse73. Since strigolactones are very labile and active at concentrations as low as picomolar, they are active only in close proximity to potential host roots, ensuring successful interactionbetween the fungi the roots. Study of mutants lacking strigolactones suggest that the hormones are also involved in the regulation of shoot branching, acting as branch-inhibiting hormones |CITS: [15268852][15342640]|.

Comment: This compound class stands for generic and unspecified bacterial endotoxins. These are components from the outer membrane and cell wall of bacteria, which are toxic to humans and can cause sepsis. The Gram negative bacteria produce lipopolysaccharides, whereas the Gram positive bacteria produce the less active lipoteichoic acids and muramyl peptides.

Compound.name: acetan
Comment: |FRAME: Acetan Acetan| is an acidic heteropolysaccharide produced by the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-28448| (previously known as Acetobacter xylinum ) that consists of a cellulose backbone with side-chains attached to alternate glucose units. The polymer is composed of repeating units of a heptasaccharide with the following structure: alpha-L-rhamnose-(1->6)-beta-D-glucose-(1->6)-alpha-D-glucose-(1->4)-beta-D-glucuronate-(1->2)-alpha-D-mannose-(1->3)-beta-D-glucose-(1->4)-beta-D-glucose. These repeating units are attached to each other via beta(1->4) links between the terminal two glucose units, forming a cellulose backbone with alternating pentasaccharide branches |CITS: [8370027][7780996]|. Acetan is structurally related to |FRAME: Xanthan|.

Compound.name: a [lipoyl-carrier protein]-L-lysine
Comment: |FRAME: LIPOIC-ACID "Lipoate"| is an organosulfur compound that is used as an essential cofactor by many enzyme complexes. The functional group of lipoate is a ditholane ring, which is a cyclic disulfide. The enzyme complexes that require lipoate have a dedicated |FRAME: Lipoyl-Protein "lipoyl domain"|, and lipoate is actually produced on this domain. The precursor |FRAME: CPD-195| molecule is first attached to a specific |FRAME: LYS| residue within the lipoyl domain (producing |FRAME: Octanoylated-domains|), and is then converted to lipoate by the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX0-782|, resulting in |FRAME: Lipoyl-Protein-N6-lipoyllysine|. |FRAME: CPLX0-782 "Lipoate synthase"| not only catalyzes the reaction, but is also the source of the two sulfur atoms.

Compound.name: a medium-chain fatty alcohol
Comment: Fatty alcohols are aliphatic |FRAME: Alcohols alcohols| consisting of a chain of 3 or more carbon atoms. They may be saturated or unsaturated and may be branched or unbranched. Many enzymes that act on |FRAME: Fatty-Acids "fatty acids"|, as well as the corresponding |FRAME: Fatty-Acyl-CoAs "fatty acyl-CoAs"|, |FRAME: Fatty-Alcohols alcohols|, and |FRAME: Fatty-Aldehydes aldehydes|, have evolved to recognize substrates with a limited range of chain lengths. To classify these enzymes, it is helpful to divide the substrates into smaller groups based on their chain length. The following subgroups have been defined: |FRAME: Short-Chain-Alcohols "Short-chain alcohols"| have 3-5 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Medium-Chain-Alcohols "Medium-chain alcohols"| have 6-12 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Long-chain-alcohols "Long-chain alcohols"| have 13-22 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Very-Long-Chain-Alcohols "Very-long-chain alcohols"| have 23-27 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Ultra-Long-Chain-Alcohols "Ultra-long-chain alcohols"| have more than 27 carbons in the longest chain.

Compound.name: a pyrone
Comment: Pyrones (also called pyranones) are a class of heterocyclic chemical compounds. They contain a six-membered heterocyclic, non-aromatic ring consisting of five carbon atoms and one oxygen atom and containing two double bonds and a ketone functional group. Most pyones belong to either of two isomers based on the |FRAME: CPD-11706| (2-pyrone) or |FRAME: CPD-26550| (4-pyrone) structure. The 2-pyrone structure common in nature as part of the |FRAME: Coumarins "coumarin"| ring system, while the 4-pyrone structure is found in some natural chemical compounds such as |FRAME: CPD-26551|, |FRAME: CPD-15508| and |FRAME: KOJIC-ACID|. 3-Pyrone structures exist, but are far less common.

Compound.name: a [protein]-(L-serine/L-threonine/L-tyrosine)
Comment: This generic class describes either an |FRAME: SER|, an |FRAME: THR|, or an |FRAME: TYR| within a protein.

Compound.name: a monobactam
Comment: A class of beta-lactam antibiotics that lack the double ring construction of the traditional beta-lactam antibiotics. Monolactams are not sensitive to metallo-beta-lactamases 3909315. |FRAME: CPD-9235 Aztreonam| is a U.S. Food and Drug Administration-approved monobactam in clinical use, and has proved efficacious in the clinical treatment of many multidrug-resistant infections, eradicating those caused by bacteria resistant to the most broadly active antibiotics, including meropenem, vancomycin, and imipenem 22274165.

Compound.name: a 1,2-diacyl-3-O-[beta-D-galactosyl-(1->6)-beta-D-galactosyl]- sn -glycerol
Synonyms: a (beta-D-galactosyl-(1->6)-beta-D-galactosyl)-1,2-diacyl- sn -glycerol // an beta-D-galactosyl-beta-D-galactosyldiacylglycerol // DGDG // a beta,beta digalactosyldiacylglycerol

Compound.name: a 1,6-beta-D-glucan
Comment: This compound class stands for 1,6-beta-D-glucosyl polymers.

Compound.name: a sterol
Comment: Sterols are steroids carrying a hydroxyl group at C-3 and most of the skeleton of cholestane. Additional carbon atoms may be present in the side chain.

Compound.name: a soyasaponin
Comment: Saponins are a class of secondary metabolites that have been grouped together phenomenologically by the foaming they produce when shaken in aqueous solutions, and structurally by their composition of one or more hydrophilic glycoside moieties combined with a lipophilic triterpene derivative. They are particularly abundant in various plant species, but are also found in marine organisms. Soyasaponins are saponins found in soy beans. The aglycones of these compounds are |FRAME: Soyasapogenols soyasapogenols|. Triterpene saponins have diverse biological actions including antiinflammatory, antifungal, antimicrobial, antiparasitic, and antitumor activities.

Compound.name: an icosanoid
Comment: Icosanoids (often spelled eicosanoids) are signaling molecules generated by oxidation of 20-carbon fatty acids. Icosanoids participate in many cellular processes including promoting or inhibiting inflammation; responding to allergy, fever and other immune system challenges; regulating normal childbirth; contributing to the perception of pain; regulating cell growth; controlling blood pressure; and modulating the regional flow of blood to tissues. There are multiple subfamilies of icosanoids, the main of which are the |FRAME: Prostaglandins prostaglandins|, |FRAME: Thromboxanes thromboxanes|, |FRAME: Leukotrienes leukotrienes|, |FRAME: Lipoxins lipoxins|, |FRAME: Resolvins resolvins|, and |FRAME: Eoxins eoxins|. Each family can have up to 4 series of compounds, which are derived from the ω-3 fatty acid |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE|), the ω-6 fatty acids |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| [(5Z,8Z,11Z,14Z)-icosatetraenoate] and |FRAME: CPD-8120| [(8Z,11Z,14Z)-icosatrienoate], and the ω-9 fatty acid |FRAME: CPD-24529|, respectively.

Compound.name: a 3-(3-hydroxyalkanoyloxy)alkanoate
Comment: This class contains molecules that are composed of two 3-hydroxy fatty acid chains of varying length (represented here in part by R1 and R2) linked to each other through an ester bond between the beta-hydroxyl group of one chain and the carboxyl group of another chain. They have been found to be constituents of rhamnolipids (see |FRAME: Mono-Rhamnolipids| and a |FRAME: Di-Rhamnolipids|) |CITS: [11813309] [16160828] [20336292]|.

Compound.name: an alkane
Comment: Alkanes are saturated acyclic hydrocarbons. They consist only of hydrogen and saturated carbon atoms and are bonded exclusively by single bonds. They could be either branched or unbranched. Alkanes are often classified by the length of their acyl moiety. |FRAME: Short-Chain-Alkanes "Short-chain alkanes"| contain less than 6- carbons. |FRAME: Medium-Chain-Alkanes "Medium-chain alkanes"| contain 6-12 carbons. |FRAME: Long-Chain-Alkanes "Long-chain alkanes"| contain 13-22 carbons. |FRAME: Very-Long-Chain-Alkanes "Very-long-chain alkanes"| contain 23 carbons or longer.

Compound.name: an [HPr protein]- N π -phospho-L-histidine
Comment: HPr (histidine protein) is one of two sugar-non-specific protein constituents of the phosphoenolpyruvate:sugar phosphotransferase system (PTS). It accepts a phosphoryl group from phosphorylated Enzyme I (PtsI) and then transfers it to the EIIA domain of any one of the many sugar-specific enzymes (collectively known as Enzymes II) of the PTS.

Compound.name: an oligosaccharide
Comment: An oligosaccharide is a saccharide polymer containing a small number (typically three to six) of component monosaccharides (also known as simple sugars). Oligosaccharides are often found either O - or N -linked to compatible amino acid side chains in proteins or to lipid moieties.

Compound.name: a dimycocerosyl phthiocerol
Comment: |FRAME: CPD-18580 Phthiocerol| glycolipids have been found in many species of |FRAME: TAX-1762|. The two secondary alcohol functions are often esterified by |FRAME: Mycocerosic-Acids "mycocerosic acids"| 3113946. |FRAME: CPD-18612 "Dimycocerosyl phthiocerol"| (DIM) and |FRAME: CPD-18579| (PGL) are important virulence factors 24028583.

Compound.name: a xyloglucan
Comment: |FRAME: Xyloglucan Xyloglucan| is the major component of the |FRAME: Hemicelluloses| in cell walls of dicotyledon type I and non-graminaceous monocotyledon plants. It also exists in some seeds of trees growing in the tropical zone. Xyloglucan interacts with cellulose microfibrils via hydrogen bonds to form a structural network that is assumed to play a key role in cell wall integrity. Cross-linking between the xyloglucan chains is a major factor in the stability of the resulting three-dimensional matrix Whitney95. Xyloglucan has a backbone of beta-1,4-linked glucose residues, most of which are substituted in C-6 by alpha-D-xylosyl residues 8252539. In most plants some of the xylosyl residues are further substituted by (1,2)-beta-D-galactosyl residues, and some of the galactosyl residues are capped by (1,2)-alpha-L-fucose |CITS:[12837954] [17011813]|. Other types of xyloglucans, for example those found in the Poaeceae and Solanaceae, feature xylose units that bear alpha-L-arabinosyl instead of beta-D-galactosyl residues. A common terminology uses G for basic non-substituted glucosyl units within a xylosylglycan, X for glucose residues substituted by alpha-D-xylose, L for glucose residues substituted by alpha-D-xylose and beta-D-galactose, and F for glucose residues substituted by alpha-D-xylose, beta-D-galactose and alpha-L-fucose Fry93. Fucosyl residues are typically absent from seed xyloglucans but present on the xyloglucans in the vegatative portions of the same plant Mishra09. Most xylosylglucans consist of repeating heptasaccharide |FRAME: Xyloglucans-Xylose XXXG| units. The average molecular weight of xyloglucan is more than 50,000 Mishra09. A common form of xyloglucan that is often used in enzyme assays is produced from tamarind (|FRAME: TAX-58860|) seeds.

Compound.name: a D- erythro sphinganine
Comment: |FRAME: DIHYDRO-SPHINGOSINE Sphinganines| can have C14, C16, C18 or C20 skeletons. They also exist as different stereoisomers. The |FRAME: D-erythro-Shinganines "D- erythro isomers"| are the biologically relevant forms 21421810.

Compound.name: a uronate
Comment: Uronic acids are carbohydrate acids formally derived by oxidation of the terminal hydroxyl group of any |FRAME: Aldoses aldose| or |FRAME: Ketoses ketose| to a carboxy group.

Compound.name: a glycoconjugate
Comment: Glycoconjugate is the general term used for carbohydrates that are covalently linked with other chemical species such as proteins, peptides, lipids and saccharides. Examples for glycoconjugates include |FRAME: Glycoconjugates glycoproteins|, glycopeptides, |FRAME: Peptidoglycans peptidoglycans|, |FRAME: Glycolipids glycolipids|, |FRAME: Glycosides glycosides| and |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharides|. Glycoconjugates are often involved in cell-cell interactions, cell-cell recognition, cell-matrix interactions, and detoxification processes.

Compound.name: a [glycerolipid]-crepenynate
Comment: |FRAME: CREPENYNATE Crepenynate| (crepenynic acid) is a fatty acid with an 18-carbon chain containing a cis double bond at position 9 and a triple bond at position 12. Like other fatty acids, |FRAME: CREPENYNATE| is rarely found in its free form. It is usually found |FRAME: Glycerolipid-crepenynate "incorporated into a lipid"|. |FRAME: CREPENYNATE Crepenynate| makes up to 70% of the fatty acids in triacylglycerol from the seed oil of the plant |FRAME: TAX-72610| Banas97.

Compound.name: a [glycerolipid]-(8Z,11Z,14Z,17Z)-icosatetraenoate
Comment: |FRAME: CPD-8121 Icosatetraenoate| (also spelled eicosatetraenoate, or ETA) is a polyunsaturated fatty acid that contains four cis double bonds at positions 8, 11, 14 and 17. The last double bond is located at the third carbon from the end of the molecule, making it an ω-3 fatty acid. |FRAME: CPD-8121 Icosatetraenoate| is an intermediate between |FRAME: CPD-12653| and |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE|. It appears to act as as a dual inhibitor of |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| oxygenation by both the cyclooxygenase (COX) and lipoxygenase pathways, and may be responsible for the anti-inflammatory effect of |FRAME: TAX-38949| (green-lipped mussels), in which it is found in high concentrations 12042477. Like other fatty acids, |FRAME: CPD-8121| is rarely found in its free form. It is usually found as either |FRAME: CPD-14394| or |FRAME: CPD-17281 "incorporated into a lipid"|.

Compound.name: a pyrrolidine

Compound.name: core 6
Synonyms: N -acetyl-beta-D-glucosaminyl-1,6- N -acetyl-D-galactosaminyl-R // N -acetyl-beta-D-glucosaminyl-1,6- N -acetyl-D-galactosaminyl-[glycoprotein] // an N -acetyl-beta-D-glucosaminyl-(1->6)- N -acetyl-alpha-D-galactosaminyl-[protein] // N -acetyl-beta-D-glucosaminyl-(1->6)- N -acetyl-alpha-D-galactosaminyl-[glycoprotein]
Comment: O -Linked glycans are polysaccharide or oligosaccharide that are linked to a protein via the oxygen atom in the side chain of a |FRAME: SER| or |FRAME: THR| residue. Most commonly O -glycosylation begins with the attachment of |FRAME: CPD-3604| to the free hydroxyl group of the amino acid, although O-linkages to fucose, glucose, mannose, xylose and other sugars are known. In eukaryotes, O -linked glycans are assembled in the Golgi apparatus one sugar at a time, while attached to the core protein. Mucin-type O -glycosylation, consisting of glycans attached via O-linked |FRAME: CPD-3604|, is one of the most abundant forms of protein glycosylation in animals. Eight core-type structures of mucin-type O -glycans have been proposed, including |FRAME: Core1 "core 1"|, |FRAME: Core2 "core 2"|, |FRAME: GLUCOSAMINYL-13-N-ETCETERA-GALACTOSAMINY "core 3"|, |FRAME: GLUCOSAMINYL-16-ETCETERA-GALACTOSAMINYL- "core 4"|, |FRAME: Core5 "core 5"|, |FRAME: Core6 "core 6"|, |FRAME: Core7 "core 7"| and |FRAME: Core8 "core 8"| 16413314. Compound.name: an alkaloid
Comment: Alkaloids are naturally occurring heterocyclic compounds that contain nitrogen and an alkaline pH (hence the name). Alkaloids are secondary metabolites, and have a marked physiological action on animal physiology. They are produced by a large variety of organisms, including bacteria, fungi, plants, and animals.

The peptides listed under this class could be generated by hydrolysis of larger polypeptides, or could be synthesized by other means, such as |FRAME: Non-ribosomal-peptide-synthetases "non-ribosomal peptide synthases"| (NRPSs) or by chemical synthesis. The majority of the aminoglycosides consist of a unique aminocyclitol |FRAME: CPD-10151| core, which is decorated with various aminosugars, leading to diverse structural molecules,including |FRAME: Kanamycins kanamycin|, |FRAME: CPD-14154 tobramycin|, |FRAME: Gentamycins gentamycin|, |FRAME: CPD-14143 ribostamycin|, |FRAME: CPD-14140 butirosin|, |FRAME: Neomycins neomycin|, |FRAME: CPD-14177|, |FRAME: Lividomycins lividomycin|, |FRAME: CPD-14157 apramycin|, and |FRAME: HYGROMYCIN-B|.

Compound.name: a menaquinone
Comment: Menaquinones and demethylmenaquinones are isoprenoid quinones of the naphthalene series, and are constituents of bacterial plasma membranes, where they play important roles in electron transfer and oxidative phosphorylation. Menaquinones are the most widespread respiratory quinones in biological systems Fujimoto12. Menaquinones and demethylmenaquinones are named MK- n or DMK- n , respectively, where the n refers to the number of prenyl units present in the side chain. The most common length of the side chain in bacteria is 8, although minor amounts of MK-1 through MK-14 have been found 7022156. Many bacteria and archaea have |FRAME: Dihydromenaquinones "dehydrogenated menaquinones"|, which are named MK- n (H 2 ). The degree and location of dehydrogenation depends on the species. Some organisms have menaquinones with modifications of the head group, for example |FRAME: TAX-2302| possess both |FRAME: CPD-15875 thermoplasmaquinones| (TPQ), which contains an extra methyl group, and |FRAME: CPD-15876 methionaquinones| (MTK), which contains a methylthio group 11157962. Menaquinones are also known as vitamin K 2 . Vitamin K is a name given to a group of derivatives of 2-methyl-1,4-naphthoquinone that are required by mammals for the posttranslational modification of certain proteins, mostly involved in blood coagulation. These compounds, while essential for mammals, are not synthesized by them, and are thus considered vitamins. The natural forms of the vitamin are vitamin K 1 (|FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE|) and vitamin K 2 (|FRAME: Menaquinones "menaquinone"|). Since menaquinones produced by different organisms have different tail lengths there are many variations of vitamin K 2 , usually specified based on the number of carbons in their tails, such as in Vitamin K 2 (45). The reduced form of menaquinone is called |FRAME: Menaquinols|.

Compound.name: a beta-lactone
Comment: A |FRAME: Lactones "lactone"| is a cyclic ester, the product of condensation of an alcohol group and a carboxylate group within the same molecule. It is characterized by a closed ring consisting of two or more carbon atoms and a single oxygen atom, with a ketone group in one of the carbons adjacent to the ring oxygen. There are several types of lactones - |FRAME: Beta-lactones| contain 3 carbons in the ring, Gamma-lactones contains 4, Delta-lactones contains 5, and Epsilon-lactones contains 6 carbons.

Compound.name: compound 0
Comment: |FRAME: Compound-0 "Compound 0"|, |FRAME: Compound-I|, and |FRAME: Compound-II| are the names given to intermediate states of the heme-iron center that is formed at the active sites of cytochrome P-450 enzymes and peroxidases during catalysis. I. Cytochrome P-450 In cytochrome P-450 the proximal coordinatioin position of the heme iron, which is bound to the 4 nitrogen atoms of the tetrapyrrole ring, is tethered to the protein via a cysteine thiolate ligand. At its rest state, the iron is found at a low-spin ferric state (III valency). At this state the iron also binds a water molecule as a sixth ligand at the distal axial coordination position. Binding of a substrate to the low-spin ferric enzyme leads to displacement of the water as the sixth ligand and a high spin shift. The substrate-bound complex has a greater reduction potential and more easily accepts a single electron from the redox partner, which can be either |FRAME: EC-1.6.2.4 "a cytochrome P450 reductase"|, |FRAME: Ferredoxins|, or |FRAME: Cytochromes-b5|). After the first reduction, the heme iron binds oxygen, forming an oxy-heme complex. The oxygen is bound at the distal axial coordination position, from which the water molecule has been displaced. Following the transfer of the second electron from the redox partner and two subsequent protonations, a peroxo adduct is formed, known as |FRAME: Compound-0|. Next, the O-O bond is cleaved heterolytically, releasing a water molecule and leaving behind an oxygen atom with only six valence electrons. This highly active oxene oxygen removes one electron from the iron and one from the porphyrin, oxidizing the iron to the unusual valency of IV (ferryl iron) and generating an additional oxidizing equivalent that is delocalized over the porphyrin and thiolate ligands. This ferryl/porphyrin radical cation complex is known as |FRAME: Compound-I| 21071661. When the substrate nears the active site, |FRAME: Compound-I| abstracts an electron from it, converting the substrate into a radical and becoming a protonated non-radical ferryl compound known as |FRAME: Compound-II|. At this point the substrate radical reacts with the oxygen of |FRAME: Compound-II|, forming a new carbon oxygen bond. The product is released, and the iron returns to a valency of III (compound III) OrtizdeMontellano15. II. preoxidases In peroxidases the proximal coordinatioin position of the heme iron, which is bound to the 4 nitrogen atoms of the tetrapyrrole ring, is tethered to the protein via a histidine residue. |FRAME: Compound-I "Compound I"| is produced when the heme iron is oxidized by |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE|. A single one-electron reduction step of |FRAME: Compound-I| from an electron donor substrate yields |FRAME: Compound-II|, followed by a second one-electron transfer that returns the enzyme to the ferric oxidation state, thus completing the catalytic cycle. Each electron transfer event converts a substrate molecule to a radical cation, forming two such radicals during a catalytic cycle. In the presence of high concentrations of |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE| and the absence of a reducing substrate, |FRAME: Compound-II| can be oxidized to |FRAME: Compound-III|, a catalytically inactive form of the enzyme. |FRAME: Compound-III "Compound III"| is converted back to the resting state by spontaneous autoxidation or by oxidation with two molecules of the substrate radical cation 18581264.

Compound.name: arabinose
Comment: |FRAME: Arabinoses Arabinose| is an aldopentose - a monosaccharide containing five carbon atoms. Unlike many other aldoses, which are more abundant in nature as the "D"-form, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE| is far more common in nature than |FRAME: D-ARABINOSE|. Free |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE| rarely exists in the nature (though it has been found in the core of coniferous trees Pingman57). However, it is widely distributed as a component of complex nonstarch polysaccharides in plant cell walls, including many plants common in the human diet such as maize, wheat, rye, rice, sugar beets, and plant gums, and in bacterial polysaccharides. L-arabinose has many biomedical and health effects, especially intestinal sucrase inhibition effect 8931641. In recent years it has been used as a low-caloric sweetener, with approximately 50% of the sweetness of sucrose Hu18.
