Comment: |FRAME: Ginsenosides Ginsenosides| or panaxosides are a class of steroid glycosides and triterpene saponins found exclusively in the plant genus |FRAME: TAX-4053| (ginseng). They are the principal components responsible for the pharmaceutical activities of ginseng. Ginsenosides are composed of an aglycone and sugar moieties. Based on the structure of their aglycones, ginsenosides have been categorized into three broad types; |FRAME: Protopanaxadiol-type-ginsenosides "protopanaxadiol-type ginsenosides"| (PPD), which contain hydroxyl groups at positions 3 and 20, |FRAME: Protopanaxatriol-type-ginsenosides "protopanaxatriol-type ginsenosides"| (PPT), which contain hydroxyl groups at positions 3, 6 and 20, and |FRAME: Oleanonic-acid-type-ginsenosides "oleanonic-acid-type saponins"|. Although ginsenosides only have three kinds of aglycones, more than 60 kinds of ginsenosides have been identified by now due to the variability in the type of sugar moieties, their number, and the carbon positions they link to. The biological activity of ginsenoside increases with the decrease of the number of the sugar moieties. All of the ginsenosides found in large quantities in wild ginseng (known as major ginsenosides) are heavily glycosylated, while the more active less-glycosylated ginsenosides are found in much smalller quantities (and are commonly referred to as the minor ginsenosides). Following oral intake of ginseng, the large low-solubility and poor-permeability major ginsenosides cannot be absorbed by the human body directly Su06, and are deglycosylated into smaller forms in the gastrointestinal tract by intestinal bacteria and/or digestive enzymes 8923812. Glycosidase enzymes that can convert the major ginsenosides to minor ginsenosides are not common and are of commercial interest.

Compound.name: a colanic acid
Comment: |FRAME: CPD0-1099 "Colanic acid"| is an exopolysaccharide secreted by |FRAME: TAX-562| and a number of other |FRAME: TAX-543| that encapsulates the organism, resulting in a mucoid appearance 13963285. Colanic acid is thought to promote biofilm formation and to protect the organism when exposed to harsh environments such as acidic conditions |CITS: [11371548][16706906]|. Even though it wasn't identified as such, colanic acid was first described in 1927 by Dorothea Smith, who isolated a polysaccharide from a mucoid strain of |FRAME: TAX-562| 19869322. Fourteen years later, in a study on the antigens of the Enterobacteriaceae , it was noticed that one antigen was common to several mucoid strains of |FRAME: TAX-57045| Kauffmann41. It was soon reported that the same antigen, which was named "M" antigen, is produced by mucoid Escherichia coli strains 15406247. In 1954 Kauffmann reported that the antigen was common to all mucoid Salmonella species Kauffmann54. Similar exopolysaccharides were reported from a number of mucoid strains and species |CITS: [13475241][13641209][13963285][14073028][5324934]|. In the early 60s it was reported that a large number of Salmonella and Escherichia strains that are not normally mucoid can be induced to form slime exopolysaccharides when grown at 15 to 20°C in high phosphate concentration |CITS: [Anderson61][Anderson63]|, and the exopolysaccharide was named "colanic acid" after |FRAME: TAX-562| from which it was isolated 13963285. In a paper describing the discovery of the same polysaccharide in |FRAME: TAX-83333| it was suggested that colanic acid and the "M antigen" reported in the earlier studies are identical 14206589. A confirmation was obtained in 1969 when it was shown that colanic acid of identical composition is produced by strains from the genera Salmonella , Escherichia , and Aerobacter . At that time the exact structure was not known, though it was known that the polysaccharide contains glucose, galactose, fucose, and glucuronate, as well as some O -acetyl groups 4902806. Additional structural studies have shown that colanic acid from different organisms is very similar, with the polysaccharide composed of a hexasaccharide repeating unit consisting of glucose, two fucoses, two galactoses, and glucuronate. In addition, one fucose and one galactose may be acetylated to varying degrees, and the terminal galactose residue is modified. The repeat units are connected by a linkage between the first and third residues, with the remaining three residues forming a side chain |CITS: [4311825][4902692]|. Differences are found in the modifications of the terminal galactose residue, which was found to contain a 4,6-pyruvoyl group, a 3,4-pyruvoyl group, a 3,4-ethylidene group, or a 4,6-methylene group in different strains 4941627. The structure shown here was published in 2007, correcting several errors in earlier reports 17227761. While colanic acid was considered exclusively an exopolysaccharide that is only loosely associated with the cell surface, the 2007 study also found that colanic acid can be attached to the lipid A core of lipopolysaccharide instead of the O antigen, forming a novel type of lipopolysaccharide which was named |FRAME: CPD0-1101 M LPS | 17227761.

Compound.name: an excited coelenteramide monoanion
Comment: |FRAME: OPLOPHORUS-LUCIFERIN Coelenterazine| and its analogues are the luciferase substrate (=luciferin) in the light-emitting process of bioluminescent coelenterates as well as various, distantly related, types of organisms such as squids, shrimps, fishes, and some chaetognaths |CITS: [Shimomura80][Campbell90][20972255]|. It is also found in many nonluminous organisms 9336010. In bioluminescent systems, |FRAME: OPLOPHORUS-LUCIFERIN coelenterazine| is bound by either |FRAME: Coelenterazine-binding-proteins| or by an aequorin protein, depending on the species. In the first system, upon binding of Ca 2+ ions the coelenterazine-binding protein releases coelenterazine, which is then oxidized and decarboxylated by the luciferase enzyme, resulting in |FRAME: CPD-20235|. In the second system, aequorin binds and oxidizes coelenterazine, retainning it in the form of bound |FRAME: CPD-20222|. Upon binding of Ca 2+ ions, the enzyme catalyzes the decarboxylation and formation of |FRAME: CPD-20235|. In vitro the excited coelenteramide relaxes to the ground state by emission of blue light. However, in vivo the excitation energy is transferred to |FRAME: GFP| by Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) |CITS: [4151620][33175]|. Coelenterazine is a derivative of imidazopyrazinone. Its biosynthetic origin is not known. However, it has been shown that the hydromedusa |FRAME: TAX-6100| is not able to synthesize it, and is dependent on a dietary supply of this luciferin for bioluminescence 11572972. The only report of de novo biosynthesis of coelenterazine is from the bioluminescent shrimp |FRAME: TAX-576189| Thomson95. Studies of the excited state of coelenteramide have shown that emission occurs exclusively from the electronic singlet excited state of the monoanion form |CITS: [Hori73][12797][36127]|.

Compound.name: a phenylpropanoid

The pathway that starts from |FRAME: PHE| forms |FRAME: COUMARATE| as a main intermediate. The name "phenylpropanoid" is derived from this compound, which consists of an aromatic phenyl group and a propene tail. Further processing results in the biosynthesis of many types of compounds, including |FRAME: Lignols monolignols| (precursors to |FRAME: Lignins lignin| and lignocellulose), |FRAME: Flavonoids flavonoids|, |FRAME: Coumarins coumarins|, |FRAME: Stilbenoids stilbenoids|, and phenolic acids. Phenylpropanoids are found throughout the plant kingdom, where they serve as essential components of a number of structural polymers, provide protection from ultraviolet light, defend against herbivores and pathogens, and also mediate plant-pollinator interactions as floral pigments and scent compounds.

Compound.name: a gentamicin
Comment: Gentamicins are a family of |FRAME: Aminoglycoside-Antibiotics "aminoglycoside antibiotics"| produced by Gram-positive bacteria of the |FRAME: TAX-1873| genus. They were discovered in 1963 by a group of scientists at the Schering Corporation 14274893. Gentamicins are particularly active against Gram-negative bacteria, and are bactericidal. They act by binding the 30S subunit of the bacterial ribosome, interrupting protein synthesis. Despite their high antibacterial activity, intravenous use is limited by their ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity. However, they are used commonly as a topical treatment to skin infections. The most common form of gentamycin is the |FRAME: GENTAMICIN-C "C complex"|, which consists of a mixture of |FRAME: CPD-14213|, |FRAME: CPD-14216|, |FRAME: CPD-14211|, |FRAME: CPD-14212| and |FRAME: CPD-15231|. While the name can be written as both gentamicin and gentamycin, the former is more common, to emphasize the biological origin of the antibiotics.

Compound.name: a kanamycin
Comment: |FRAME: Kanamycins Kanamycins| are a group of |FRAME: Aminoglycoside-Antibiotics "aminoglycoside antibiotics"| produced by the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1967|. The compounds were discovered in 1957 by researchers in the National Institute of Health of Tokyo, Japan |CITS: [13513509][13595489]|. Due to their wide range of activity, especially against severe staphylococcal and mycobacterial infections, these antibiotics gained almost immediate acceptance, and the most common form, |FRAME: CPD-4821|, was produced commercially within a year of its discovery 13566481. Kanamycins interact with the 30S subunit of the prokaryotic ribosome, inducing substantial amounts of mistranslation and indirectly inhibiting translocation during protein synthesis, resulting in death |CITS: [391568][9662506]|. Kanamycins are currently used to treat a wide variety of infections. Kanamycins share several biosynthetic intermediates with other aminoglycosides, including the core moiety |FRAME: CPD-10151| and the pseudodisaccharides |FRAME: CPD-14126|, |FRAME: CPD-14125| and |FRAME: CPD-14137|. While the main product produced by |FRAME: TAX-1967| is |FRAME: CPD-4821| (R1 = NH2; R2 = OH), additional products are also produced, including |FRAME: CPD-4822| (R1 = R2 = NH 2 ), |FRAME: CPD-4823| (R1 = OH; R2 = NH 2 ) |CITS: [13563334][13587408]|, |FRAME: CPD-14138| (similar to |FRAME: CPD-4821|, but contains a glucose moiety instead of the kinosamine moiety) Adams96 and |FRAME: CPD-4824| (R1 = R2 = OH) Chang80.

Compound.name: a gaburedin
Comment: The |FRAME: Gaburedins gaburedins| are a family of gamma-aminobutanoate (GABA)-derived ureas whose biosynthesis is encoded by a silent gene cluster in the |FRAME: TAX-54571| genome. The cluster, which consists of the three genes |FRAME: G-124751|, |FRAME: G-124752|, and gbnC , is located adjacent to a putative regulatory system homologous to the the mmfR - mmfLHP - mmyR cluster of |FRAME: TAX-100226|. The products of the mmfLHP genes are the |FRAME: MMFs "methylenomycin furans"|, which act as inducers of |FRAME: CPD-27200 methylenomycin| production in |FRAME: TAX-100226|, while MmfR and MmyR are ArpA-like transcriptional repressors, which repress |FRAME: CPD-27200 methylenomycin| production 18988741. Based on the sequence homology, it was hypothesized that the gbnABC genes encode a natural product(s), whose production is controlled by a regulatory system encoded by the mmfR - mmfLHP - mmyR genes homologs. The gbn cluster contains highly conserved DNA sequence, which were predicted to be binding motifs for the transcriptional repressor GbnR, the mmyR homolog. To test this hypothesis, the gbnR gene was knocked out. Indeed, the mutant produced six new metabolites, the products of the gbnABC genes, which were named gaburedin A-F. The compounds structures were shown to be gamma-aminobutanoate (GABA)-derived ureas, containing an amino acid linked by a ureido bridge Sidda14.

Based on the phenotype of a ΔpruA mutation it has been suggested that the enzyme catalyzes the reduction of |FRAME: CPD-11770| to |FRAME: CPD0-2101|, and that |FRAME: CPD0-2101| is part of a signaling cascade to control biofilm formation in |FRAME: TAX-358| |CITS: [26126849][32482721]|.

The hydroxyl groups of the carbohydrate core are partially or totally esterified with phenolic groups such as |FRAME: CPD-183| in |FRAME: Gallotanins gallotannins| or |FRAME: CPD-17769| in |FRAME: Ellagitannins ellagitannins|.

Compound.name: a VB type gamma-butyrolactone
Comment: The Gram-positive, soil-inhabiting, filamentous bacteria of the genus |FRAME: TAX-1883| use a number of chemical compounds including |FRAME: Gamma-Butyrolactones "gamma-butyrolactones"|, |FRAME: MMFs "methylenomycin furans"|, |FRAME: CPD-19905|, and |FRAME: Butenolides "gamma-butenolides"|, as chemical signalling molecules or microbial hormones, which, together with their specific receptors, regulate morphological and/or physiological differentiation 2268871. At least 60% of Streptomyces species appear to produce gamma-butyrolactones, although (as of 2011), only a small number of which have been identified 21090718. Based on their structures, these gamma-butyrolactones have been classified into three types: the |FRAME: A-factor-type-lactones "A-factor type"|, |FRAME: Virginiae-butanolides "virginiae butanolide (VB) type"|, and |FRAME: IM-2-type-lactones "IM-2 type"|, all of which share the cyclic butanolide skeleton |CITS: [14523609][19778723]|. The VB-type compounds were originally isolated from |FRAME: TAX-1961|, where they control |FRAME: CPD-19910 virginiamycin| production. Compound.name: a very-long-chain fatty alcohol

The following subgroups have been defined: |FRAME: Short-Chain-Alcohols "Short-chain alcohols"| have 3-5 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Medium-Chain-Alcohols "Medium-chain alcohols"| have 6-12 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Long-chain-alcohols "Long-chain alcohols"| have 13-22 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Very-Long-Chain-Alcohols "Very-long-chain alcohols"| have 23-27 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Ultra-Long-Chain-Alcohols "Ultra-long-chain alcohols"| have more than 27 carbons in the longest chain.

Compound.name: starch
Comment: Starch is a glucose-based polysaccharide produced by plants, green algae, and cyanobacteria. Starch combines two polymeric carbohydrates (polysaccharides) called |FRAME: Alpha-Amyloses "alpha-amylose"| and |FRAME: CPD-7043|. |FRAME: Alpha-Amyloses "alpha-Amylose"| contains up to several thousand alpha-glucosyl units linked almost exclusively in linear alpha(1->4) linkages, with very few branches of alpha(1->6) linkages. In |FRAME: CPD-7043|, on the other hand, branching is common, and occurs approximately every 24-30 glucose monomer units. Amylopectin is one of (if not the) largest biological polymer known and contains from 10 5 –10 6 glucose residues 9730163. Unlike |FRAME: Glycogens glycogen| molecules, which is limited to ~55,000 glucose units, the starch branched structure leads to clusters of chains that allow for indefinite growth of the polysaccharide. |FRAME: Alpha-Amyloses "alpha-Amylose"| accounts for 30% of starch, while |FRAME: CPD-7043| accounts for the other 70%. The dense packing of branches at the root of the clusters generates tightly packed glucan chains that are close enough to align and form parallel double helical structures. The helices within a single cluster and neighbouring clusters align and form sections of crystalline structures separated by sections of amorphous material (containing the branches) thereby generating the semi-crystalline nature of amylopectin and of the ensuing starch granule. The crystallized chains become insoluble and typically collapse into a macrogranular solid that is osmotically inert 9730163. The enzymes of starch synthesis and mobilization are unable to interact directly with the solid structure, with the exception of |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.242 "granule-bound starch synthase"| 14502990. The solid semi-crystalline starch and hydrosoluble |FRAME: Glycogens glycogen| define two distinct physical states of the same type of storage polysaccharide. Glycogen is by far the most widespread form of storage, as it is found in Archaea, Bacteria, and Eukaryotes. The appearance of semi-crystalline storage polysaccharides appears linked to the requirement of unicellular diazotrophic cyanobacteria to fuel nitrogenase and protect it from oxygen through respiration of large amounts of stored carbon 21220783.

SOXYDENIT-MONOMER combines with SOXZDENIT-MONOMER, a sulfur compound chelating protein, to form the CPLX-881 complex. A thiosulfate ion can be transferred the free thiol group of a conserved cysteine residue (Cys138) of SOXYDENIT-MONOMER to form |FRAME: SoxY-Thiocysteine-Sulfate|, the first covalently bound sulfur adduct in the sulfur oxidation pathway of |FRAME: TAX-82367|. The reaction is catalyzed by the |FRAME: CPLX-7149| complex 14651972. The attachment of sulfite to the same cysteine residue, which produces |FRAME: SoxY-Systeine-Sulfinate|, is not dependent on |FRAME: CPLX-7149| 24030319. The residues of SOXYDENIT-MONOMER, SOXZDENIT-MONOMER, and SOXBDENIT-MONOMER involved in the interactions among them have been identified 16084835. In native gradient polyacrylamide gels CPLX-881 sometimes appears as a 50-kDa alpha 2 beta 2 heterotetramer 10940005 . Neither SoxY nor SoxZ contains a cofactor or metal.

Comment: |FRAME: THF-GLU-N Tetrahydrofolate| (vitamin B9) and its derivatives, commonly termed folates, are required in a variety of reactions in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, where they act as carriers of one-carbon units in various oxidation states. These one-carbon units are utilized in the biosynthesis of various cellular components, including glycine, methionine, formylmethionine, thymidylate, pantothenate and purine nucleotides. During folate biosynthesis (as described in FOLSYN-PWY) the enzyme |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.12|, adds a glutamate residue to |FRAME: 7-8-DIHYDROPTEROATE|, resulting in |FRAME: DIHYDROFOLATE|, also known as H 2 PteGlu 1 . This molecule in turn is reduced by EC-1.5.1.3 (FolA) to |FRAME: THF| (H 4 PteGlu 1 , or tetrahydrofolate), which can be converted to several other folate molecules 11501996. Most folate molecules are modified in cells by successive additions of glutamate residues, forming folate polyglutamates (or folylpoly-gamma-glutamates). The glutamate residues are added by an amide linkage to the gamma-carboxylate group of the folate or folate derivative. Since these isopeptide bonds are not the normal amide bonds they are not hydrolyzed by peptidases or proteases, which are specific for alpha-carboxyl-linked peptide bonds. The addition of glutamyl residues probably occurs after the reduction of newly synthesized dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate and its conversion to other tetrahydrofolate derivatives. The glutamylation of folate residues serves several goals: it prevents the efflux of folates out of the cell, it increases the binding of folate cofactors to the enzymes of folate interconversion and biosynthesis, and in mammals, it allows the accumulation of folates in the mitochondria, which is required for glycine synthesis 10598551. This class stands for tetrahydrofolates with an unspecified number of glutamate residues.

Comment: |FRAME: Sphingomyelins Sphingomyelins| are a type of |FRAME: SPHINGOLIPIDS sphingolipids| found in animal cell membranes, especially in the membranous myelin sheath that surrounds some nerve cell axons. It usually consists of |FRAME: PHOSPHORYL-CHOLINE| and |FRAME: Ceramides|, but |FRAME: PHOSPHORYL-ETHANOLAMINE| can replace |FRAME: PHOSPHORYL-CHOLINE|. Sphingomyelins are found in all tissues and lipoproteins; for example, they account for ~5% of the lipid phosphate in liver and 25% in pancreas 2187537. Sphingomyelins have a function in signal transduction 8086039. Sphingomyelins are highly enriched in the plasma membrane of cells, and were considered to be found largely in the exoplasmic leaflet of the cell membrane. Moreover, neutral sphingomyelinase-2, an enzyme that breaks down sphingomyelins into ceramides, has been found to localize exclusively to the inner leaflet, further suggesting that there may be sphingomyelin present there. Sphingomyelin can accumulate in a rare hereditary disease called Niemann-Pick Disease . The disease is caused by a deficiency in the enzyme sphingomyelinase, rsulting in accumulation of sphingomyelin in the spleen, liver, lungs, bone marrow, and the brain, causing irreversible neurological damage.

It is involved in crosslinking cellulose and hemicellulose fibers, which provides rigidity to the cell wall. The characteristic structure of pectin is a linear chain of alpha-(1-4)-linked |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| that forms the pectin-backbone, |FRAME: 1-4-alpha-D-galacturonosyl|. Diferent components of pectin have different substitutions and additions. A common type is |FRAME: Rhamnogalacturonans-I "rhamnogalacturonan I"| (RG-I), which makes up 20-35% of pectin. In RG-I some of the |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| units in the backbone are replaced by (1-2)-linked |FRAME: L-rhamnose|, to which side chains of various neutral sugars branch off, mostly |FRAME: D-Galactose|, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE| and |FRAME: CPD-25028|. Another common type is |FRAME: CPD-14581 "rhamnogalacturonan II"| (RG-II), which makes up about 10% of pectin. RG-II is based on a backbone of 8-9 galacturonate units, which are decorated by four side chains consisting of 12 different types of sugars in more than 20 different linkages. RG-II usually forms dimeric structures via the formation of crosslinks by a 1:2 borate diol ester between apiosyl residues in one of the side chains. Other types of pectin include chains of |FRAME: Apiogalacturonans apiogalacturonan|, |FRAME: 1-4-alpha-D-galacturonosyl homogalacturonan|, and |FRAME: Xylogalacturonan xylogalacturonan|. There is currently no consensus as to how the pectic polysaccharides are linked to each other, or to other polymers, in the wall. However, it is thought that the different peptides are covalently linked to each other via their backbones, forming a large linear structure with many side branches |CITS: [11423143][12162553][Coenen07]|. In nature, around 80% of the carboxyl groups of the galacturonate units are esterified with |FRAME: METOH|. Some plants, including sugar beet, potatoes and pears, contain pectins with acetylated galacturonate in addition to methyl esters. The salt of partially esterified pectins is called a pectinate, and if the degree of esterification is below 5%, |FRAME: PECTATE|. Pectin is used in the animal feed industry and in the food industry as a gelling agent. Phytopathogenic and saprophytic bacteria and fungi can produce variety of extracellular and intracellular enzymes that degrade pectin and its derivatives. Pectinolytic enzymes such as esterases, hydrolases and lyases, are used in the food, fiber and animal feed industries. There is commercial interest in pectinolytic enzymes to convert the pectin-rich by-products from citrus peel and sugar beet processing to higher value material. Compound.name: a fatty acid
Comment: The term "fatty acid" was originally coined to describe aliphatic monocarboxylic acids derived from or contained in esterified form in an animal or vegetable fat, oil or wax. However, over the years the term has been expanded to refer to additional, shorter monocarboxylic acids with an aliphatic tail such as |FRAME: PROPIONATE| and |FRAME: BUTYRIC_ACID| (but not the shorter |FRAME: FORMATE| and |FRAME: ACET|). The length of a fatty acid is determined by the length of the longest carbon chain, including the carbon of the carboxy group. Common natural fatty acids usually have an even number of carbons in the longest chain and can be either saturated or unsaturated. In many organisms they are often modified by branching, hydroxylation, methylation, epoxidation and other types of modifications. Inside living cells fatty acids are rarely found in free form. They are usually bound to coenzyme A or acyl-carrier proteins, or form part of |FRAME: Triacylglycerides triglycerides|, |FRAME: Phospholipids phospholipids|, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharides|, and |FRAME: Cholesterol-esters cholesterol esters|. Many enzymes that act on fatty acids, as well as the corresponding |FRAME: Fatty-Acyl-CoAs "fatty acyl-CoAs"|, |FRAME: Fatty-Alcohols alcohols|, and |FRAME: Fatty-Aldehydes aldehydes|, have evolved to recognize substrates with a limited range of chain lengths. To classify these enzymes, it is helpful to divide the substrates into smaller groups based on their chain length. The following subgroups have been defined: |FRAME: Short-chain-fatty-acids "Short-chain fatty acids"| (SCFA) have 3-5 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Medium-chain-fatty-acids "Medium-chain fatty acids"| (MCFA) have 6-12 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Long-Chain-Fatty-Acids "Long-chain fatty acids"| (LCFA) have 13-22 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Very-long-chain-fatty-acids "Very-long-chain fatty acids"| (VLCFA) have 23-27 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Ultra-long-chain-fatty-acids "Ultra-long-chain fatty acids"| (ULCFA) have more than 27 carbons in the longest chain. Most of the natural fatty acids have an even number of carbon atoms, since their biosynthesis involves the addition of two-carbon-atom units. When a fatty acid contains only single bonds, it is referred to as |FRAME: Saturated-Fatty-Acids|. When it contains one or more double bonds, it is referred to as |FRAME: Unsaturated-Fatty-Acids|. If it contains a double bond in the trans configuration, it is often referred to as a trans fatty acid. Most fatty acids in the trans configuration are not found in nature and are the result of human processing.

Compound.name: an opine
Comment: |FRAME: Opines Opines| are a large family of low molecular weight compounds. The vast majority of opines are secondary amine derivatives resulting from the reduction of the imine formed by condensation of an amino acid with either a keto acid or a sugar. Opines from the |FRAME: CPD-308| family are formed when |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| serves as the keto substrate in the condensation reaction, while those of the |FRAME: CPD-309| family are formed when |FRAME: PYRUVATE| is involved in the condensation reaction. Opines of the |FRAME: CPD-15773| and |FRAME: CPD-26410| families are formed by the condensation of an amino acid with a sugar. A small, separate class of opines is the |FRAME: Agrocinopines agrocinopines|, which are sugar-phosphodiesters (e.g., |FRAME: CPD-15774|, which is a phosphodiester of sucrose and L-arabinose). While opines are found in marine invertebrates, fungi, higher plants and mammals, they are most commonly found in plant crown gall tumors or hairy root tumors, where they are produced by bacteria of the genera |FRAME: TAX-357| and |FRAME: TAX-379|, respectively. However, the first opine to be identified (in 1927), octopine, was isolated from an octopus muscle, hence its name, which was later extended for naming the opine family. Biosynthesis of opines in crown gall tumors is performed by enzymes encoded by genes contained in T-DNA (transfer DNA), which is part of the Ti plasmid (in |FRAME: TAX-357|) or Ri plasmid (in |FRAME: TAX-379|). The plasmids are inserted by the bacteria into the plant genome, where they are integrated and expressed. Those opines are used by the bacteria as energy, carbon and nitrogen sources. Each strain of |FRAME: TAX-357| and |FRAME: TAX-379| induces and catabolizes a specific set of opines, determined by the specific Ti or Ri plasmid they possess, and Ti-plasmids are classified as nopaline-type, octopine-type, agropine-type, vitopine-type, succinamopine-type, and chrysopine-type 31386108. Over 30 different opines have been described.

Compound.name: chitosan

Chitosan is mostly produced commercially by deacetylation of |FRAME: CHITIN| , which is the structural element in the exoskeleton of crustaceans. Linalool is a primary compound in floral scent research. Both enantiomeric forms, |FRAME: CPD-8996| and |FRAME: CPD-8997|, occur in nature. Linalool is involved as an attractant in plant interactions with pollinators, herbivores and parasitoids RAGUSO. It has also been shown to be induced by artificial wounding and by jasmonic acid 17440821. The de novo synthesis of linalool has been demonstrated in floral tissues 17440821, barks and roots RAGUSO. Junipers, dicots and monocots emit linalool along with other monoterpenoids RAGUSO. It accounts for roughly 10-20% of the phospholipid fatty acid content of skeletal muscle cells. In addition to being involved in cellular signaling as a lipid second messenger, arachidonate is also a key inflammatory intermediate and can also act as a vasodilator. Like other fatty acids, |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| is rarely found in its free form. It is usually found either as |FRAME: ARACHIDONYL-COA| or |FRAME: CPD-17284 "incorporated into a lipid"|.

Comment: The nomenclature of isoprenoids and their derivatives is somewhat confusing. Here are some guidelines for understanding these names: Isoprenoids are composed of repeating isoprene units. The units can be attached in either a trans conformation (the two carbons are on opposite sides of the double bond) or a cis conformation (the two carbons are on the same side of the double bond). It is common to use E and Z instead of trans and cis , respectively. The numbering of carbons in the molecule starts from the carbon attached to the hydroxyl or phosphate group. The isoprene unit furthest from the C1 carbon is called the ω unit. Unlike all other isoprene units, the ω unit is not a stereo center since the last carbon is attached to two identical methyl groups. There are two widely used naming systems, and unfortunately they refer to the isoprene units in opposite order. One method describes the molecule starting with the unit with the lowest carbon number (ie the one furthest from the ω unit), naming each of the stereo-active carbons by its number, followed by its stereo designation. For example, CPD-11977 is referred to as 2,6- cis ,10- trans -tetraprenyl diphosphate or (2 Z ,6 Z ,10 E )-tetraprenyl diphosphate. According to the other method, the molecule is described by the stereoconfiguration of the molecule starting with the ω unit. For example CPD-11977 is referred to as ω, E,Z,Z tetraprenyl diphosphate. On top of this, many of the shorter molecules have trivial names that are commonly used. Some of these names are specific for a particular stereoisomer and some are used for all stereoisomer. For example, |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP "geranylgeranyl diphosphate"| is commonly used for the all- trans isomer of the molecule with four isoprene units, while farnesyl diphosphate is used for all four isomers of the molecule with three isoprene units - FARNESYL-PP, CPD-9444, CPD-11293 and CPD-11990.

Compound.name: candicidin
Comment: Candicidin is an aromatic polyene macrolide antibiotic produced by some species of |FRAME: TAX-1883|. It has a complex structure composed of a macrolide ring, the amino sugar |FRAME: CPD-16768|, and an aromatic moiety, |FRAME: CPD-16769|. Lechevalier first described this antibiotic as C135 and it was renamed candicidin due to its strong action against |FRAME: TAX-5475 Candida | species including one of the most common human fungal pathogens |FRAME: TAX-5476| 13159187. The increased susceptibility of immunocompromised patients to fungal attacks has stimulated research efforts to isolate effective antifungal agents (reviewed in |CITS: [19362642][12664141]|). The same compound was isolated independently from |FRAME: TAX-206662|, and named FR-008. Despite initial reports that FR-008 is different from candicidin, it was later shown that the two compounds are in fact identical 18559273. Structural elucidation of candicidin revealed that it consists of three components named |FRAME: CPD-13108|, |FRAME: CPD-17190|, and |FRAME: CPD-17191|. All structural variants have been characterized (18559273 and reviewed in 19362642).

The compounds in this class are often classified by the length of their aliphatic chains. |FRAME: Short-Chain-234-Saturated-Fatty-Acids "Short-chain 2,3,4-saturated fatty acids"| are 2,3,4-saturated fatty acids with aliphatic chains of less than 6 carbons. |FRAME: Medium-Chain-234-Saturated-Fatty-Acids "Medium-chain 2,3,4-saturated fatty acids"| are 2,3,4-saturated fatty acids with aliphatic chain of 6-12 carbons. |FRAME: Long-Chain-234-Saturated-Fatty-Acids "Long-chain 2,3,4-saturated fatty acids"| are 2,3,4-saturated fatty acids with aliphatic chains of 13-22 carbons. |FRAME: Very-Long-Chain-234-Saturated-FAs "Very-long-chain 2,3,4-saturated fatty acids"| are 2,3,4-saturated fatty acids with aliphatic chains of 23 carbons or longer.

Compound.name: a rhodoquinone
Comment: Rhodoquinone (RQ) is a modified ubiquinone, where the methoxyl group in position 3 is replaced by an amino group. The compound was originally isolated from TAX-1085 |CITS:[Glover62][14293762] [14285535]|, where is it used for the reduction of fumarate to succinate under anaerobic conditions. Rhodoquinone is not limited to prokaryotes. It was soon discovered that some eukaryotic parasites such as the nematodes |FRAME: TAX-6253| and |FRAME: TAX-6252| |CITS: [5796154][811785]|, as well as parasitic helminths 4795616 also contain rhodoquinone, which is essential for fumarate reduction under anaerobic conditions 2843227. Later it was shown that rhodoquinone is present in all eukaryotes that reduce fumarate during anoxia, including freshwater snails, mussels, lugworms, and oysters 8537365.

Compound.name: a (6 S )-5-formyltetrahydrofolate
Synonyms: a folinic acid // an (6 S )- N 5 -formyltetrahydrofolate
Comment: |FRAME: THF-GLU-N Tetrahydrofolate| (vitamin B9) and its derivatives, commonly termed folates, are required in a variety of reactions in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, where they act as carriers of one-carbon units in various oxidation states. These one-carbon units are utilized in the biosynthesis of several cellular components, including glycine, methionine, formylmethionine, thymidylate, pantothenate and purine nucleotides. During folate biosynthesis (as described in FOLSYN-PWY) the enzyme |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.12|, adds a glutamate residue to |FRAME: 7-8-DIHYDROPTEROATE|, resulting in |FRAME: DIHYDROFOLATE|, also known as H 2 PteGlu 1 . This molecule in turn is reduced by EC-1.5.1.3 (FolA) to |FRAME: THF| (H 4 PteGlu 1 , or tetrahydrofolate), which can be converted to several other folate molecules 11501996. Most folate molecules are modified in cells by successive additions of glutamate residues, forming folate polyglutamates (or folylpoly-gamma-glutamates). The glutamate residues are added by an amide linkage to the gamma-carboxylate group of the folate or folate derivative. Since these isopeptide bonds are not the normal amide bonds they are not hydrolyzed by peptidases or proteases, which are specific for alpha-carboxyl-linked peptide bonds. The addition of glutamyl residues probably occurs after the reduction of newly synthesized dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate and its conversion to other tetrahydrofolate derivatives. The glutamylation of folate residues serves several goals: it prevents the efflux of folates out of the cell, it increases the binding of folate cofactors to the enzymes of folate interconversion and biosynthesis, and in mammals, it allows the accumulation of folates in the mitochondria, which is required for glycine synthesis 10598551. Among the many folates 5-FORMYL-THF is the most enigmatic compound involved in the folate biosynthesis. 5-FORMYL-THF is the only folate derivative that does not serve as a cofactor in C1-metabolism, but it is the most frequent and stable form of folates found in plants 8480361. Moreover, 5-FORMYL-THF is known to inhibit most of the folate dependent enzymes at physiological concentrations. The biological role of this compound is still poorly understood but it has been discussed as factor involved in the regulation of essential biosynthetic steps such as the formation of serine during photorespiration |CITS: [15888445][12207015]|. This class stands for (6 S )-5-formyltetrahydrofolates with an unspecified number of glutamate residues.

Compound.name: an N -acylethanolamine

These compounds exert a variety of biological actions through their interactions with various receptors. One of the N -acylethanolamines, |FRAME: CPD-7598|, has received much attention because it is an endocanabinoid (an endogenous ligand of the cannabinoid receptors CB1 and CB2). The other N -acylethanolamines do not bind to cannabinoid receptors.

Compound.name: a lankacidin-group antibiotic
Comment: The |FRAME: Lankacidins "lankacidins"| are a class of unique 17-membered carbocyclic polyketide natural products isolated from Streptomyces spp. that show promising antimicrobial activity. |FRAME: CPD-27267 "Lankacidin C"| was originally isolated in 1960 from |FRAME: TAX-68280| under the name lankacidin Gaumann60. It was subsequently isolated from multiple other species such as |FRAME: TAX-146922| Sakamoto62 and Streptomyces sp. 6642-GC 5796585, sometimes under the name bundlin A. In 1971 a group of related antibiotics, which included lankacidin C, was isolated from |FRAME: TAX-885435| (previously named strain T-2636). These compounds, which were referred to as "T-2636 antibiotics", have been studied extensively. The antibiotics were found to be active against a number of organisms, particularly Gram-positive bacteria, including many strains that are resistant to macrolide antibiotics |CITS: [5541329][5541328][5541330][4833376][1212749][4792112][4792113][1126865][240790]|. X-ray crystallographic analysis revealed that lankacidin C and |FRAME: CPD-27278| (a 14-membered macrolide antibiotic also produced by |FRAME: TAX-885435|) inhibit peptide formation synergistically by binding to neighboring sites in the large bacterial ribosomal subunit |CITS: [20080686][21282615]|. In addition, the lankacidins were shown to have considerable antitumor activity against certain cell line models |CITS: [4801122][1148][27718573]|. |FRAME: CPD-27267 "Lankacidin C"| is currently used in veterinary medicine. In 1994 it was found that the genes encoding the biosynthesis of the lankacidin-group antibiotics reside on the linear plasmid pSLA2-L 7844039. Sequencing of the region suggested that lankacidin biosynthesis is mediated by one PKS/NRPS hybrid (LkcA) and three PKSs (LkcC, LkcF, and LkcG) 10767533. A starter glycine molecule is extended by eight malonyl-[acp] molecules. The methyl groups at C-2, C-4, C-10, and C-16 are added by C-methylation from |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| Uramoto78. The formation of the delta-lactone ring is catalyzed by the thioesterase domain of LkcG. Once removed from the PKS machinary, the molecule is cyclyzed by an |FRAME: MONOMER-124699 "amine oxidase"| (LkcE) |CITS: [15734652][18057700][21953738]|.

Compound.name: a fatty alcohol
Comment: Fatty alcohols are aliphatic |FRAME: Alcohols alcohols| consisting of a chain of 3 or more carbon atoms. They may be saturated or unsaturated and may be branched or unbranched. The following subgroups have been defined: |FRAME: Short-Chain-Alcohols "Short-chain alcohols"| have 3-5 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Medium-Chain-Alcohols "Medium-chain alcohols"| have 6-12 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Long-chain-alcohols "Long-chain alcohols"| have 13-22 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Very-Long-Chain-Alcohols "Very-long-chain alcohols"| have 23-27 carbons in the longest chain. |FRAME: Ultra-Long-Chain-Alcohols "Ultra-long-chain alcohols"| have more than 27 carbons in the longest chain.

Compound.name: rubber
Comment: Natural rubber is an important raw material in an enormous number of products. The backbone of natural rubber comprises a ( cis )-1,4-polyisoprene with two or three trans -isoprene units at the ω-terminus, formed by the sequential condensation of |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (IPP) units in cis configuration onto a short all-trans prenyl diphosphate. It is very similar in structure to |FRAME: DOLICHOL dolichols|, but the chain length is much longer (C>1500). Natural rubber is produced from latex - a material that makes up the cytoplasmic content of the latecifers or latex vessels of |FRAME: TAX-3981| (the Brazilian rubber tree) 17545224. Although over 2000 plant species capable of producing rubber have been identified, only a few synthesize the high molecular weight rubber that is required for the production of high quality rubber products, and natural rubber is currently produced commercially only from |FRAME: TAX-3981|. A potential alternative source is the Russian rubber-producing dandelion (|FRAME: TAX-333970|), which was cultivated in the former Soviet Union during World War II to satisfy the demand for natural rubber 22504822. Rubber biosynthesis is carried out by |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.20|. The enzyme is localized at the surface of cytosolic vesicles known as rubber particles, and biosynthesis is initiated through the binding of an allylic pyrophosphate primer, such as |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| |CITS: [Tanaka01][14622254][18799172]|. The R in the structure stands for an unspecified number of ( cis )-connected isoprene units.

Compound.name: a vaccenate

Another isomer, |FRAME: CPD-9247|, is produced from |FRAME: CPD-9245| by bacteria and plants. It is one of only two unsaturated fatty acids in |FRAME: TAX-562| 6988423 (see |FRAME: PWY-5973|). Compound.name: a glycosphingolipid
Comment: |FRAME: Glycosphingolipids Glycosphingolipids| are a family of complex lipids composed of |FRAME: Ceramides| and mono- or oligosaccharide moieties that play an important role in various cellular functions including recognition, cell adhesion, proliferation and differentiation 8490246. The lipid portion is embedded in the outer plasma membrane leaflet and the sugar chains extended to the outer environment, acting as an antigen. Together with |FRAME: Glycoproteins glycoproteins| and |FRAME: Glycosaminoglycans glycosaminoglycans|, the glycosphingolipids contribute to the glycocalyx that covers eukaryotic cell surfaces. Glycosphingolipids are synthesized by the sequential addition of sugar residues to ceramide by glycosyltransferases that are specific to each glycosidic linkage. |FRAME: Lactosyl-Ceramides Lactosylceramide|, a product of the second glycosylation step in the biosynthesis of many glycosphingolipids, is an important branching point, being a common precursor for the synthesis of the four major classes of glycosphingolipids: the |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs "ganglio series"|, the |FRAME: Globo-Series-GSLs "globo series"|, the |FRAME: Lacto-Series-GSLs "lacto series"|, and the |FRAME: Neolacto-Series-GSLs "neolacto series"| 10320813. One of these fucosyltransferases, encoded by the |FRAME: HS10249| gene, is bifunctional and can fucosylate both the 3 and 4 positions of the penultimate sugar in the precursor disaccharide. The alpha(1,4)-fucosyltransferase activity is only relevant when the substrates are derived from the |FRAME: beta-Gal-13-beta-GlcNac-R "type 1 precursor disaccharide"|, as that position is already occupied in the |FRAME: B-Gal-14-NacGlc-R "type 2 disaccharide"|. However, the alpha(1,3) fucosylation of the N -acetylglucosaminyl residue of |FRAME: B-Gal-14-NacGlc-R| leads to formation of several related antigens known as the |FRAME: CPD-8594 "Lewis x epitope"| (also known as SSEA-1, for stage-specific embryonic antigen 1), |FRAME: Antigen-Ley "Lewis y epitope"|, and the |FRAME: sLea-Antigen "sialyl-Lewis x epitope"| (see |FRAME: PWY-7831|).

Compound.name: a short-chain 3-hydroxy fatty acyl-CoA
Comment: Fatty acyl-CoAs are |FRAME: ACYL-COA "acyl-CoAs"| derived from |FRAME: Fatty-Acids "fatty acids"|. To classify these enzymes, it is helpful to divide the substrates into smaller groups based on their chain length. The following subgroups have been defined: |FRAME: Short-Chain-Acyl-CoAs "Short-chain acyl-CoAs"| are derived from |FRAME: Short-chain-fatty-acids "fatty acids that have 3-5 carbons in the longest chain"|. |FRAME: Medium-Chain-Acyl-CoAs "Medium-chain acyl-CoAs"| are derived from |FRAME: Medium-chain-fatty-acids "fatty acids that have 6-12 carbons in the longest chain"|. |FRAME: Long-Chain-Acyl-CoAs "Long-chain acyl-CoAs"| are derived from |FRAME: Long-Chain-Fatty-Acids "fatty acids that have 13-22 carbons in the longest chain"|. |FRAME: VERY-LONG-CHAIN-FATTY-ACYL-COA "Very-long-chain fatty acyl-CoAs"| are derived from |FRAME: Very-long-chain-fatty-acids "fatty acids that have 23-27 carbons in the longest chain"|. |FRAME: Ultra-Long-Chain-Acyl-CoAs "Ultra-long-chain fatty acyl-CoAs"| are derived from |FRAME: Ultra-long-chain-fatty-acids "fatty acids that have more than 27 carbons in the longest chain"|.

Compound.name: a sialyl-Lewis a epitope
Synonyms: an sLe a antigen // alphaNeuNAc-(2->3)-betaGal-(1->3)-[alphaFuc-(1->4]-betaGlcNAc-[protein] // a histo-blood group sialyl Lewis a epitope
Comment: The |FRAME: sLea-Antigen "sialyl-Lewis a epitope"| (SLe a ) was discovered in 1979 with the use of a monoclonal antibody 94699. While the antigen is believed to play an important role during embryogenesis 6381330, in adults only low amounts of the antigen are present on normal epithelial cells |CITS: [6751528][6381289]|. When the selectin family of adhesion molecules was described, it was found that SLe a , along with the |FRAME: sLex-Antigen "sialyl-Lewis x antigen"|, is a ligand for E-selectin. Higher expression of the SLe a antigen in adults is strongly associated with cancer. It was found in high amounts on the surface of human pancreatic, colon and gastric cancer cell lines |CITS: [7142214][6188455]| and in human adenocarcinomas of the colon, stomach, pancreas and gall-bladder |CITS: [94699][6751528][2910493]|. The expression of the antigen has been linked to tumor progression. A gradual increase in SLe a was found in colon and rectum during neoplastic transformation and progression 2863413, and its presence was restricted to tumorigenic and invasive human urothelial cell lines 8900435. The antigen is responsible for adhesion of colon, pancreas, urinary bladder and gastric cancer cells to endothelium via its interaction with selectin E |CITS: [1716885][7687590][7678075][8900435][9578490]|. The expression level of the SLe a antigen is used as a prognostic factor for colorectal carcinoma, and is associated with high incidence of recurrence and the length of survival time |CITS: [8273774][7697593][9303355]|.

Compound.name: ι-carrageenose
Comment: |FRAME: Carrageenans Carrageenans| and |FRAME: Carrageenoses carrageenoses| are sulfated polysaccharides that are extracted from sea weeds belonging to the |FRAME: TAX-2763| (red algae), mainly from |FRAME: TAX-2769|, and species from the |FRAME: TAX-31444| and |FRAME: TAX-33664| genera. They are laid out in the cell wall at a high density and can constitute up to 50% of the algae dry mass. The basic units of |FRAME: Carrageenans carrageenans| are repeats of alternating alpha-1,3-linked D-galactose and beta-1,4-linked D-galactose units, which are often substituted by sulfate. Carrageenans are classified according to the number and the position of sulfated ester 1367970. In |FRAME: Carrageenoses carrageenoses| the alpha-1,3-linked galactose units are modified by having a 3,6-anhydro bridge. These bridges, which form a double helix during aggregation, are responsible for the gelation that is typical to these compounds. Despite this distinction, carrageenoses are often referred to as carrageenans. The three most industrially exploited carrageenans, namely, |FRAME: kappa-Carrageenan|, |FRAME: iota-Carrageenan| and |FRAME: Lambda-Carrageenan|, are distinguished by the presence of one, two or three ester-sulfate groups per repeating disaccharide unit respectively. |FRAME: iota-Carrageenan| is sulfated at position 4 of the beta-1,4-linked D-galactose units and position 2 of the alpha-1,3-linked 3,6-anhydrogalactose units.

Compound.name: a beta-lactam
Comment: This compound class stands for |FRAME: Lactams lactams| in which the amide bond is contained within a four-membered ring, which includes the amide nitrogen and the carbonyl carbon. beta-Lactam compounds imitate the naturally occurring |FRAME: D-ALA-D-ALA| substrate for the group of enzymes known as penicillin binding proteins (PBPs), which cross-link the peptidoglycan in bacterial cell wall, and thus act as powerful antibiotics 6109324. Naturally occurring |FRAME: Beta-Lactams "beta-lactam antibiotics"| are classified into several groups according to their chemical structure: In |FRAME: Monolactams monolactams| the beta-lactam ring is not fused to another ring. This class includes compounds such as the |FRAME: Nocardicins nocardicins| 3427723 and the |FRAME: Monobactams monobactams| 3909315. In |FRAME: Penams penams| the beta-lactam ring is fused to a saturated five atom ring (a 4:5 structure). Penams contain a sulfur atom at position 1 of the five atom ring (for example, the |FRAME: PENICILLIN penicillins|) 6335599. Related classes include the |FRAME: Carbapenams carbapenams|, which contain a carbon atom in that position 12890666, and the |FRAME: Clavams oxopenams| (also known as clavams), which contain an oxygen atom at that position (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-9261|) 3304182. |FRAME: Penems Penems| are molecues similar to penams in which the five atom ring is unsaturated at positions 2-3. Similarly, penems contain a sulfur atom at position 1 of the five atom ring, while |FRAME: Carbapenems carbapenems| contains a carbon atom in that position 16413506. In |FRAME: Cephams cephams| and |FRAME: Cephems cephems| the beta-lactam ring is fused to a six-atom ring (a 4:6 strcuture) that contains a sulfur atom at position 1. In cephams the ring is saturated, while cephems have an unsaturated bond at positions 3-4 |CITS: [1164170][12722308]|. 1-Oxocephams/1-oxacephems conain an oxygen atom at position 1 |CITS: [11671696][11078187]|.

Compound.name: scyllo -inositol
Comment: |FRAME: Inositols Inositol| is the generic name for 1,2,3,4,5,6-cyclohexanehexol. Epimerization of the six hydroxyl groups results in nine stereoisomers. Among the isomers, |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| is the most abundant in nature and it is an essential compound in eukaryotic cell membranes as a phosphatidylinositol moiety, which plays an important role in signal transduction. Some other forms, such as |FRAME: CPD-8050|, are also found in nature, although they are less abundant. Nomenclature of cyclitols can be quite confusing. Two alternative naming schemes are possible for inositol compounds since carbon-1 could be assigned to either of two enantiotopic carbons. The two methods result in 1D-stereochemistry and 1L-stereochemistry based names. If carbon-1 is placed at the top of the molecule, L-numbering proceeds clockwise, while D-numbering proceeds counter-clockwise. Both the 1D or 1L designations can be employed currently. However, the symbol Ins implies myo-inositol with D- numbering. Additional information on the nomenclature of myo -inositol compounds can be found in the 1973 document Nomenclature of cyclitols by the Nomenclature Committee of the International Union of Biochemistry (NC-IUB), and the 1988 publication Numbering of atoms in myo -inositol , published by the same body, whose aim was to relax some of the rules specified in the 1973 publication. To aid in following the transformations in inositol compounds in pathways, the structures of inositol stereoisomers in MetaCyc have been formatted to show carbon 1 at the top of the ring, with numbering proceeding clockwise. An exception is the structure of |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL|, which is presented with carbon 3 at the top and counter-clockwise numbering. The reason is that carbon 3 of |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| (which is based on L-numbering) matches the carbon-1 of 1D numbering, which is used for the various phosphorylated and otherwise modified forms, and by presenting the molecule in this way, it is much easier to show structural relationships in reactions and pathways (see for example |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL-1-KINASE-RXN "EC 2.7.1.64"|). |FRAME: CPD-8050 " Scyllo -inositol"| is a relatively rare form of |FRAME: Inositols inositol| but is sometimes found in organisms. It has been documented in |FRAME: TAX-13422| buds 10830508 and in |FRAME: TAX-4513 barley| seeds, where it is present in phosphatidylinositol 7755633. The phosphatidylinositol synthase of |FRAME: TAX-5919| can act on |FRAME: CPD-8050| 17403152. In mammals, |FRAME: CPD-8050| has been shown to localize in the kidney and brain 5644141, and an enzyme from bovine brain was found to interconvert |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| and |FRAME: CPD-8050| 1267771.

Compound.name: melatonin
Comment: Melatonin is a natural product found in plants and animals. It is primarily known in animals as a hormone released by the pineal gland in the brain at night. Many of its effects are through activation of the melatonin receptors, while others are due to its role as an antioxidant. In plants, it functions to defend against oxidative stress.

Biotin was first discovered at the turn of the 20th century as a yeast growth factor, and was named bios Wildiers01. 30 years later, the compound was purified from egg yolk by Koegl and Toennis Koegl36. In a completely unrelated research, Gyoergy and his colleagues discovered biotin in liver in 1931, and isolated it in 1941. They named it vitamin H (for the German word for skin: Haut) Vigneaud41. At the same time, another group, which was working on Rhizobia bacteria, also identified it as an essential cofactor, which they named coenzyme R Allison38. Already in 1933, Gyoergy suggested that coenzyme R, bios and vitamin H were all the same molecule. The structure of biotin was solved in 1941 -1942 |CITS: [Vigneaud41B][Melville42]|. In 1949 the first evidence was published demonstrating the biochemical role of biotin in carboxylation reactions, Lardy49, and in 1958 it was suggested that biotin was probably associated with an enzyme 13560478. Shortly after this finding, Lynen et al Lynen61 described biotin's biological function as a cofactor in the biotin-dependent carboxylases. (This historical background is adapted from 12658511).

Gluathione is the major thiol not only in eukaryotic organisms but also in Gram negative bacteria and in the majority of Gram positive bacteria. In cigarette smoke nicotine is carried on particulate matter and is rapidly absorbed in the small airways and alveoli of the lung 11712903. In this neutral pH environment it is un-ionized, soluble, and can be transferred across cell membranes and into the blood, where it moves into the pulmonary venous circulation, to the left ventricle of the heart, and into the systemic arterial circulation |CITS: [8646831][10482401]|. Other forms of nicotine (such as nicotine gum, transdermal patches, inhalers, lozenges, and sublingual tablets) are usually buffered at alkaline pH and quickly traverse cell membranes, but most reach the blood and brain more slowly. Comment: |FRAME: THF-GLU-N Tetrahydrofolate| (vitamin B9) and its derivatives, commonly termed folates, are required in a variety of reactions in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, where they act as carriers of one-carbon units in various oxidation states. These one-carbon units are utilized in the biosynthesis of various cellular components, including glycine, methionine, formylmethionine, thymidylate, pantothenate and purine nucleotides. During folate biosynthesis (as described in FOLSYN-PWY) the enzyme |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.12|, adds a glutamate residue to |FRAME: 7-8-DIHYDROPTEROATE|, resulting in |FRAME: DIHYDROFOLATE|, also known as H 2 PteGlu 1 . This molecule in turn is reduced by EC-1.5.1.3 (FolA) to |FRAME: THF| (H 4 PteGlu 1 , or tetrahydrofolate), which can be converted to several other folate molecules 11501996. Most folate molecules are modified in cells by successive additions of glutamate residues, forming folate polyglutamates (or folylpoly-gamma-glutamates). The glutamate residues are added by an amide linkage to the gamma-carboxylate group of the folate or folate derivative. Since these isopeptide bonds are not the normal amide bonds they are not hydrolyzed by peptidases or proteases, which are specific for alpha-carboxyl-linked peptide bonds. The addition of glutamyl residues probably occurs after the reduction of newly synthesized dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate and its conversion to other tetrahydrofolate derivatives. The glutamylation of folate residues serves several goals: it prevents the efflux of folates out of the cell, it increases the binding of folate cofactors to the enzymes of folate interconversion and biosynthesis, and in mammals, it allows the accumulation of folates in the mitochondria, which is required for glycine synthesis 10598551.

The insulin-mimetic effects of IPGs and their analogues have also been widely documented 10501653. |FRAME: CPD-8052|, as a component of IPGs, is more important than |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL|, since the IPGs functioning as the insulin mediators contain |FRAME: CPD-8052| exclusively 2833261. Kanamycins are currently used to treat a wide variety of infections. Kanamycins share several biosynthetic intermediates with other aminoglycosides, including the core moiety |FRAME: CPD-10151| and the pseudodisaccharides |FRAME: CPD-14126|, |FRAME: CPD-14125| and |FRAME: CPD-14137|. Compound.name: arachidonate
Synonyms: (5Z,8Z,11Z,14Z)-icosatetraenoate // arachidonic acid // all-cis -icosa-5,8,11,14-tetraenoate // (5Z,8Z,11Z,14Z)-icosatetra-5,8,11,14-enoate // C20:4 fatty acid
Comment: |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID "Arachidonate"| (arachidonic acid) is a polyunsaturated ω-6 fatty acid with a 20-carbon chain and four cis -double bonds. It is produced de novo at high levels by mosses (see |FRAME: PWY-5353|), some plants, and by some marine bacteria (see |FRAME: PWY-7583|). Mammals cannot synthesize |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| de novo , but most mammals are able to synthesize it from simpler unsaturated fatty acids (see |FRAME: PWY-7592|). In mammals |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| is present in membrane phospholipids (especially phosphatidylethanolamine, phosphatidylcholine, and phosphatidylinositides) and is abundant in the brain, muscles, and liver. It accounts for roughly 10-20% of the phospholipid fatty acid content of skeletal muscle cells. In addition to being involved in cellular signaling as a lipid second messenger, arachidonate is also a key inflammatory intermediate and can also act as a vasodilator. Arachidonate is also a precursor of different classes of icosanoid effectors involved in the regulation of many important functions in mammals 15292371. Many of the compounds derived from arachidonate are listed |FRAME: Arachidonate-Derived-Metabolites here|. Like other fatty acids, |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| is rarely found in its free form. It is usually found either as |FRAME: ARACHIDONYL-COA| or |FRAME: CPD-17284 "incorporated into a lipid"|.

Compound.name: steviol
Comment: Stevia leaf extract is a non-nutritive sweetener derived from the plant |FRAME: TAX-55670|, which contains multiple sweet-tasting compounds called steviol glycosides. The Stevia leaf extract is increasingly used worldwide as natural, low-calorie sweetener that substitutes for sucrose to counteract growing incidence of obesity and diabetes. The two main steviol glycosides are CPD-14504 and CPD-14506. The former is about 300 times sweeter than sucrose |CITS:[18556105][Lemus-Mondaca12]|. Unlike alternative sweeteners such as |FRAME: CPD-5581|, CPD-14504 and CPD-14506 are thermostable, making them suitable for use in cooked foods Lemus-Mondaca12. Stevia leaves were used by indigenous people in South America as both a food sweetener and medicine. Stevia became more popular following its introduction in Japan in the 1970s. It was initially banned from use as a sweetener in many countries including the United States, Europe, Australia, Canada, and other countries, due to gaps in required safety information. In 1995 tt was permitted for use in the US only as a dietary supplement. Following the establishment of safety, metabolism, and clinical data |CITS:[18556105][19427890]|, purified steviol glycosides were approved for the use as sweetener by the FDA and many other national food safety authorities starting in 2008. Approval in the European Union and Canada followed in 2011 and 2012, respectively. Stevia leaf extract compounds are specifically approved for diabetes patients |CITS:[22492420][18555575][14561506]|. Steviol glucosides have also been reported to be effective in various in vitro anticancer tests acting as chemopreventive agents for chemical carcinogenesis 19131254 and offer therapeutic benefits through anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory actions 19000919. The steviol glucosides have been found to be efficient scavengers of reactive oxygen species (ROS) indicating their involvement in the antioxidant defense strategy of plants to thwart oxidative stress 21043580. All of the sweet compounds in the Stevia leaf extract are derivatives of |FRAME: CPD-14501| and are degraded by gut bacteria back into steviol following ingestion. Steviol itself is completely resistant to bacterial degradation 14558786.

It is a cyclic compound made of three units of 2,3-dihydroxybenzoylserine joined in a cyclic structure by lactone linkages (only the delta-cis isomer of the ferric chelate is biologically active). |FRAME: ENTEROBACTIN Enterobactin| binds Fe 3+ with a estimated Kd of 10 -49 M (10 -35 M at physiological pH) 16076215. |FRAME: ENTEROBACTIN Enterobactin| not only is used by the organisms that produce it but also serves as an exosiderophore for many bacteria that are unable to synthesize it, such as |FRAME: TAX-287|, in a strategy of siderophore piracy |CITS: [26431675][30086222]|.

Compound.name: serotonin

In the CNS, serotonin is causally involved in the regulation of mood, sleep, appetite, memory and learning 16615082. Modulation of serotonin at synapses is the modus operandi of several classes of antidepressants. Serotonin in the periphery is expressed in the enterochromaffin cells of the gastrointestinal tract and regulates gut motility. Released from the enterochromaffin cells, it is taken up by platelets and plays a role in primary homeostasis and cell mediated immune responses 19630576. Circulating |FRAME: SEROTONIN| derived from peripheral tissues is primarily metabolized in the liver to |FRAME: 5-HYDROXYINDOLE_ACETATE|, which is excreted in the urine, see |FRAME: PWY-6313|.

Compound.name: strychnine
Comment: The genus |FRAME: TAX-26496| is the most important genus of the |FRAME: TAX-26468| family, which comprises approximately 190 species of trees and lianas. |FRAME: CPD-21554 Strychnine| is a terpene indole alkaloid belonging to the Strychnos family of Corynanthe alkaloids and was the first alkaloid to be identified in plants of the |FRAME: TAX-26496| genus. It is found in the seeds and bark of many plants in this genus. |FRAME: TAX-28545| is a tree native to the tropical forests on the Malabar Coast in Southern India, Sri Lanka and Indonesia. It has an orange-colored fruit that contains five seeds. The toxic effects of these seeds have been well known from the times of ancient India, although the chemical compound itself was not identified. In 1819, Pelletier and Caventou reported the isolation of strychnine, in pure form, as the principal toxin from |FRAME: TAX-28545| and |FRAME: TAX-1037790| Pelletier19. The correct structure was reported in 1946 |CITS: [Briggs46][Holmes46]|. The absolute stereochemistry of strychnine was established by Peerdeman in 1956 with X-ray crystallographic analysis Peerdeman56. Strychnine is one of the most complex natural products of its size, with twenty-four skeletal atoms arranged in seven rings, resulting in six contiguous stereogenic centers. Strychnine is a powerful toxin (a lethal dose of strychnine for an adult human is in the range of 30-100 mg). It is an antagonist of glycine and acetylcholine receptors and affects primarily the motor nerve fibers in the spinal cord which control muscle contraction. It binds noncovalently to the same receptor as glycine, preventing the inhibitory effects of glycine on the postsynaptic neuron and resulting in activation of the motor neurons. This activation causes spastic muscle contractions and eventually death by asphyxiation.

It is synthesized from |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID| by Δ 6 desaturase enzymes. Unlike its precursor, GLA is not an essential fatty acid for animals, since almost all animals possess a Δ 6 desaturase enzyme. GLA is of major importance in animal cells, being the precursor for the synthesis of several Δ 6 -desaturated fatty acids, such as |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| and |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-7592|). Δ 6 -desaturated fatty acids have roles in the maintenance of membrane structure and function, in the regulation of cholesterol synthesis and transport, in the prevention of water loss from the skin, and as precursors of eicosanoids, including prostaglandins and leucotrienes 1334266. Like other fatty acids, |FRAME: CPD-8117| is rarely found in its free form. It is usually found either as |FRAME: GAMMA-LINOLENOYL-COA| or |FRAME: Gamma-linolenoyl-groups "incorporated into a lipid"|.

Compound.name: 17beta-estradiol
Comment: 17beta-estradiol is a sex hormon that belongs to the |FRAME: Estrogens estrogen| group. It is similar to |FRAME: ESTRONE| and |FRAME: ESTRIOL|, which differ in the number of hydroxyl groups (one for |FRAME: ESTRONE|, two for |FRAME: CPD-352| and three for |FRAME: ESTRIOL|), but is about 10 times as potent as estrone and about 80 times as potent as estriol in its estrogenic effect. |FRAME: CPD-352| is the predominant estrogen in non-pregenant women during their reproductive years in terms of serum levels. |FRAME: ESTRONE Estrone| is the predominant circulating estrogen in women during menopause and |FRAME: ESTRIOL| is the predominant circulating estrogen during pregnancy. 17beta-estradiol is also present in males at roughly the same concentration as in postmenopausal women. It is produced as an active metabolic product of testosterone. In premenapausal women 17beta-estradiol is produced by the granulosa cells of the ovaries by the aromatization of |FRAME: ANDROST4ENE| (via |FRAME: ESTRONE|). The same occurs in men in the testes. The reduced form can be oxidized to a |FRAME: FADH "semireduced form"| (semiquinone, FADH) by donating one electron and one proton. The semiquinone is then oxidized back to the fully oxidized form by losing a second electron and proton. Even though FAD has an aromatic ring system, FADH2 does not, making it significantly higher in energy. Many proteins contain a flavin moiety, either in the form of FAD or |FRAME: FMN|. They have also been found in some marine invertebrates such as sponges, tunicates, bryozoans and mollusks, where they may be synthesized by symbiotic bacteria 17119643. For a list of strains shown to produce indolocarbazole compounds see 17119643. In 1986 it was shown to be nanomolar inhibitor of protein kinases 3457562. During the 1990s protein kinases became the second most important drug target after G-protein-coupled receptors, and |FRAME: STAUROSPORINE| became the focus of much research. |FRAME: CPD-11911| (UCN-01) showed antitumor activity in mouse tumor models and entered clinical studies 1893379. The pharmacological actions of THC result from its binding to the cannabinoid receptors CB1, located mainly in the central nervous system, and CB2, mainly present in cells of the immune system. The natural agonists of these reaceptors are the endocannabinoids |FRAME: CPD-7598|, |FRAME: CPD-12600|, |FRAME: CPD-22217| (noladin ether), |FRAME: CPD-22218|, and |FRAME: CPD-22219|.

Comment: Scopolamine is a natural tropane alkaloid produced by some plants from the |FRAME: TAX-4070| (nightshade) family, and particularly members of the |FRAME: TAX-4078|, |FRAME: TAX-4074|, |FRAME: TAX-301914|, |FRAME: TAX-24609|, |FRAME: TAX-24647|, and |FRAME: TAX-195735| genera. Scopolamine is a nonspecific muscarinic antagonist for the M1, M2, M3, and M4 muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, and has a number of uses in medicine, the most well known of which is as an antidote for motion sickness. However, it is also used for a variety of other indications, including the treatment of postoperative nausea and vomiting, gastrointestinal spasms, renal or biliary spasms, irritable bowel syndrome, and eye inflammation (among others). Scopolamine is one of the earlier alkaloids isolated from plant sources, and has been in use since antiquity, and perhaps prehistoric times. It is being used in its purified forms since its isolation in 1881 Ladenburg81. Historically, the various plants that produce scopolamine have been used psychoactively for spiritual and magical purposes. However, it is physically dangerous and officially classified as a deliriant drug. It has been used occassionally as a truth serum, and is still being used by criminals to sedate victims (particularly in Columbia).

Isoprene is used to produce a diverse range of industrial products including a wide variety of specialty elastomers used in surgical gloves, motor mounts and fittings, rubber bands, golf balls, and shoes. This molecule in turn is reduced by EC-1.5.1.3 (FolA) to |FRAME: THF| (H 4 PteGlu 1 , or tetrahydrofolate), which can be converted to several other folate molecules 11501996. Most folate molecules are modified in cells by successive additions of glutamate residues, forming folate polyglutamates (or folylpoly-gamma-glutamates). The glutamate residues are added by an amide linkage to the gamma-carboxylate group of the folate or folate derivative. Since these isopeptide bonds are not the normal amide bonds they are not hydrolyzed by peptidases or proteases, which are specific for alpha-carboxyl-linked peptide bonds. The addition of glutamyl residues probably occurs after the reduction of newly synthesized dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate and its conversion to other tetrahydrofolate derivatives. The glutamylation of folate residues serves several goals: it prevents the efflux of folates out of the cell, it increases the binding of folate cofactors to the enzymes of folate interconversion and biosynthesis, and in mammals, it allows the accumulation of folates in the mitochondria, which is required for glycine synthesis 10598551.

In addition, sucrose is produced by many nonphotosynthetic aerobic methanotrophic and methanol-utilizing bacteria |CITS: [1055047][12656177][14529181][23808151][23865613]|. In photosynthetic organisms, the product of photosynthetic carbon fixation (|FRAME: GAP|) is transported from the chloroplast into the cytoplasm, where it is transformed to hexose phosphate by enzymes of the |FRAME: GLUCONEO-PWY gluconeogenesis| pathway. In plants, these hexose phosphates are used to synthesize sucrose, the form in which most fixed organic carbon is translocated from photosynthetic tissue to non-photosynthetic organs. Sucrose also provides substrates for plant storage glycosides such as |FRAME: Starch starch| and |FRAME: Fructans fructans|. Storage glycosides, including sucrose, are mobilized and utilized during seed germination and plant growth. In marine and freshwater cyanobacteria sucrose fulfils a different role. It is often synthesized in response to salt or temperature stress and seems to maintain the osmotic balance and to stabilize protein and membrane structure and function |CITS: [Reed86][7854254]|. Methanotrophic and methanol-utilizing bacteria also synthesize sucrose as a secondary osmotic compound, along with the major compatible solute |FRAME: ECTOINE| 25577257.

Comment: The nucleotides |FRAME: GUANOSINE-5DP-3DP| (guanosine 3'-diphosphate 5'-diphosphate) and |FRAME: GDP-TP| (guanosine 3'-diphosphate 5'-triphosphate), referred to collectively as (p)ppGpp, have been shown to regulate gene expression during the stringent response in some bacteria. The stringent response is a global regulatory system that operates under conditions of nutrient or energy starvation or other environmental stress. Due to its role as an effector molecule in the stringent response in bacteria, (p)ppGpp has been described as a bacterial alarmone. It can contribute to the regulation of various cellular processes that are affected by nutritional stress such as growth, cell division, motility, adaptation and virulence. Its effect on the pathogenicity of some bacteria has led to the development of ppGpp analogs as possible antibacterial compounds 18776539 and new in vitro synthesis 18789883 and detection 18166051 methods for ppGpp. Different bacteria have different ways of synthesizing and responding to (p)ppGpp, many of which are still being discovered. Compound.name: dopamine
Comment: Dopamine is an amine compound synthesized in plants and most animals. In the brain, dopamine functions as a neurotransmitter - a chemical released by neurons (nerve cells) to send signals to other nerve cells. Outside the central nervous system, dopamine functions primarily as a local paracrine messenger. In blood vessels, it inhibits norepinephrine release and acts as a vasodilator (at normal concentrations); in the kidneys, it increases sodium excretion and urine output; in the pancreas, it reduces insulin production; in the digestive system, it reduces gastrointestinal motility and protects intestinal mucosa; and in the immune system, it reduces the activity of lymphocytes. With the exception of the blood vessels, dopamine in each of these peripheral systems is synthesized locally and exerts its effects near the cells that release it. Many plants synthesize dopamine, with the highest concentrations observed in bananas. The functions of plant catecholamines have not been clearly established, but there is evidence that they play a role in the response to stressors such as bacterial infection, act as growth-promoting factors in some situations, and modify the way that sugars are metabolized. Dopamine has been detected in some types of bacteria, and homologs of all the enzymes used by animals to synthesize dopamine have been detected in some bacteria.

Now, however, it is known that abscission is usually regulated by ethylene, and abscisic acid is involved in the process only in a small number of plants. In most plants the accumulation of ABA appears to be a signal for other processes. In seeds, ABA plays a dual role in embryo growth during developmen. In early embryogenesis ABA prevents seed abortion and promotes embryo growth |CITS: [12417697][14716564]|. In contrast, during late embryogenesis, when the hormone level increases, ABA blocks the embryo growth by counteracting the action of gibberellin to promote germination |CITS: [10759503][11124119]|. In other tissues ABA-mediated signalling plays an important part in plant responses to environmental stress and plant pathogens, such as development of desiccation tolerance |CITS:[10611388][11842158][11779861][12221975]|, suppression of vivipary |CITS: [10753527][11124119][15363412]|, and water stress-induced closure of stomata |CITS: [11559734][12834401]|. In plants, abscisic acid is synthesized from C40 carotenoids. The C15 backbone of ABA is formed after the oxidative cleavage of |FRAME: CPD1F-135|, and the final molecule is formed by two additional reactions, a dehydrogenase and an oxidoreductase, as described in this pathway |CITS: [12692318][15862093]|. Comment: This is a naturally occurring form of |FRAME: Jasmonic-Acids "jasmonic acid"| |CITS:[8074303][19349968]| in plants. Many forms exist, based on the structure of |FRAME: Jasmonic-Acids "Jasmonate"| (jasmonic acid, JA). The jasmonates act as regulatory molecules in many developmental processes that include fertility, sex determination, root elongation and fruit ripening. They are also potent signals activating plant defences against pathogens, herbivory, wounding and abiotic stress. The jasmonate regulation system includes the COI1 receptor protein and several JAZ ( JA smonate Z IM domain) repressors, which, in the absence of jasmonate, are bound to the MYC2 transcription factors, preventing transcription. In the presence of active jasmonate molecules, COI1 interacts with the JAZ repressors, causing their |FRAME: PWY-7511 ubiquitylation|. The ubiquitylated repressors are targeted for proteasome degradation, releasing the MYC2 transcription factors and activating transcription 19716757. Only two of the four stereoisomers of jasmonate occur naturally: |FRAME: CPD-731| and |FRAME: CPD-734| |CITS: [8074303][19349968]|. These two forms are present in equilibrium within cells and can interconvert spontaneously through epimerization |CITS: [8074303][19349968]|. The exact ratio of these stereoisomers within a cell has not been conclusively determined, and it may vary based on species, cell type, and physiological state. But, in the systems tested so far, |FRAME: CPD-734| is found at higher levels than |FRAME: CPD-731| 19349968. The biological activity of these stereoisomers can be quite different 8074303. Comment: |FRAME: Inositols Inositol| is the generic name for 1,2,3,4,5,6-cyclohexanehexol. Epimerization of the six hydroxyl groups results in nine stereoisomers. Among the isomers, |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| is the most abundant in nature and it is an essential compound in eukaryotic cell membranes as a phosphatidylinositol moiety, which plays an important role in signal transduction. Some other forms, such as |FRAME: CPD-8050|, are also found in nature, although they are less abundant. Nomenclature of cyclitols can be quite confusing. Two alternative naming schemes are possible for inositol compounds since carbon-1 could be assigned to either of two enantiotopic carbons. The two methods result in 1D-stereochemistry and 1L-stereochemistry based names. If carbon-1 is placed at the top of the molecule, L-numbering proceeds clockwise, while D-numbering proceeds counter-clockwise. Both the 1D or 1L designations can be employed currently. However, the symbol Ins implies myo-inositol with D- numbering. Additional information on the nomenclature of myo -inositol compounds can be found in the 1973 document Nomenclature of cyclitols by the Nomenclature Committee of the International Union of Biochemistry (NC-IUB), and the 1988 publication Numbering of atoms in myo -inositol , published by the same body, whose aim was to relax some of the rules specified in the 1973 publication. To aid in following the transformations in inositol compounds in pathways, the structures of inositol stereoisomers in MetaCyc have been formatted to show carbon 1 at the top of the ring, with numbering proceeding clockwise. An exception is the structure of |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL|, which is presented with carbon 3 at the top and counter-clockwise numbering. The reason is that carbon 3 of |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| (which is based on L-numbering) matches the carbon-1 of 1D numbering, which is used for the various phosphorylated and otherwise modified forms, and by presenting the molecule in this way, it is much easier to show structural relationships in reactions and pathways (see for example |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL-1-KINASE-RXN "EC 2.7.1.64"|).
